location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic in Kandy, Sri Lanka, is one of the most important Buddhist sites in the world. While several locations claim to house relics of the Buddha, this specific temple is widely recognized for enshrining his left upper canine tooth. The teachings of the Buddha were transmitted by word of mouth passing his canine tooth. The relic holds immense spiritual and political significance; historically, it was believed that whoever possessed the tooth had the right to govern the country. The temple attracts thousands of pilgrims and tourists daily. Its importance to Buddhists is often likened to that of Mecca or the Vatican. During major festivals like the Esala Perahera, when the relic's casket is brought out in a grand procession, the streets become densely packed with devotees and impassable for blocks.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple is considered sacred by Buddhists for hosting the sacred tooth relic of Lord Buddha. It is believed that the tooth of Lord Buddha was taken out from the burning funeral pyre of Lord Buddha by a monk. It is believed that the sacred tooth of Lord Buddha was  taken to Sri Lanka by the members of the royalty of Kalinga kingdom. The temple is very well maintained, clean and serene. The Kandy drums are a joy to listen to. Like other monuments in Sri Lanka, there are no directions/sign boards indicating the entrance / exit routes. The timings of the darshan are not displayed either at the temple premises or on the tickets. For unknown reasons, the doors of the sanctum sanctorum was closed @19.50 Hrs. even though my  guide/driver indicated that the puja is finished only @20.00 Hrs. The shoe stand just before the entrance ticket counter is crowded and too small for the number of foreigners visiting the temple. The crowd management security staff of the temple could be more polite and smiling. Perhaps, a  month long sensitizing training on hospitality management could change the rather hostile attitude of the temple staff. For some strange reasons only Sri Lankan currency / cash was acceptable at the ticket counter and it took a full 15 minutes to get the tickets issued. Too many visitors, too few cash counters. The price of the entrance ticket was reasonable. The crowd management of the temple needs fine tuning. Recommended.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Visiting the Temple of the Tooth (Sri Dalada Maligawa) was one of the most spiritual and meaningful moments of my time in Sri Lanka. The temple is located in the heart of Kandy and holds a sacred relic — a tooth of Lord Buddha — making it one of the most important Buddhist temples in the world. When I arrived, the temple was already full of people offering flowers, lighting lamps, and silently praying. Despite the crowd, there was a strong sense of calm and peace inside. The architecture is beautiful, with intricate carvings, golden interiors, and a quiet reverence that surrounds you. After the visit, I had the incredible opportunity to get close to a temple elephant — and even touched it! It was such a gentle, beautiful creature and truly added something special to the experience. If you’re in Kandy, this is a must-visit location, whether you’re spiritual or simply curious about local culture and tradition. Go early in the morning if possible, and take your time to really feel the atmosphere.

According to this, the tooth has the ability to act as a rainmaker, similar to the Bodhi tree during Buddha's enlightenment. This belief turned the religious relic into an instrument of political power. It passed through the hands of many Indian kings. The respective protector of the tooth was respected because he had religious support and his country could never be ravaged by drought. In Sri Lanka, the tooth was kept in the respective capital of the country. It was a kind of legitimation for the Sinhalese throne. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: On the lake, in the center of Kandy is the Sri Dalada Maligawa (Temple of the Tooth) built by King Sri Rajasinghe in 1807 and still the heart of the Sinhalese Buddhist religion. It actually has more ancient origins (late 1600s early 1700s) and was always thought to guard the sacred tooth of the Buddha, one of his canine teeth, which remained after cremation and was brought to safety here from India. Since ancient times, the sacred tooth has been paraded through the streets of Kandy on the back of an elephant during the Esala Perahera a huge festival that attracts pilgrims from all over. Attending the Esala Perahera, which lasts 10 days between late July and August on dates that vary depending on the full moon, can be a unique experience. The temple itself does not possess the same attractions as other temples in Sri Lanka or other Buddhist countries but the devotion of pilgrims is tangible. The sanctuary is two-story and the interior has parts in exotic woods, lacquer and ivory. The tooth is upstairs. You must wear clothes that cover your legs and shoulders and remove your shoes.

review_text: Kandy, the enchanting hill capital of Sri Lanka, is renowned for its historical significance and natural splendour. This UNESCO World Heritage City, located 116 kilometres from Colombo, is celebrated for its lush landscapes and rich cultural heritage. At the heart of Kandy lies the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic (Dalada Maligawa), a sacred site revered by Buddhists around the globe. This temple, renowned for its beautiful Sinhalese architecture, houses the relic of Buddha’s tooth and continues to host ancient ceremonies with traditional drum performances daily. Kandy's cultural vibrancy is showcased in the Kandy Esala Perahera, an iconic annual festival held in July or August. This 10-day pageant is one of Sri Lanka’s grandest events, featuring a dazzling procession with over 100 richly adorned elephants, thousands of traditional dancers, drummers, and torch bearers. Originating from the 4th century, the Esala Perahera not only honors the sacred tooth relic but also brings together the community to celebrate Kandyan traditions and arts. The procession’s vibrant colors and rhythmic beats make it one of the most captivating cultural experiences in the world.

This time we were lucky enough to see the “Dathu Karaduwa” since the door of the sacred chamber opened during evening pooja. That said, had to wait a long time until the door is opened. It is always packed with worshippers as well as tourists, so was quite uncomfortable with the heat, people, school kids, etc. It could have great if school trips get more organized inside since small kids were everywhere, talking, screaming, and moving in between tourists & others. To me their teachers were totally out of touch and couldn’t control the kids. They were running around looking for them and the kids were going around the room.

We were there around 09:30 on a festival day and it was open. The temple is very beautiful with lots to see but is incredibly busy during the festival. Tickets cost 2000LKR per person so no need to pay for an expensive tour, you can just turn up and buy a ticket. You need to remove your shoes and leave them in a hut, this costs 100LKR each. There is also a museum in the grounds, same ticket for admission, this is definitely worth a visit. It provides the history of Buddhism and has information and relics from all the countries that practice Buddhism. It was fascinating.

You can walk by there. The building built around the temple is not worth it. The ceremony that starts at 09:30 at the entrance of the ancient temple is also not really special. To the accompaniment of drums and whistles, a number of monks walk into the temple and close the door so that you do not see what they are doing. All this takes 40 minutes. All in all disappointing. You don't have to come to Kandy for this.

A guide rushed me to the sanctum because the rite lasts only 15 minutes during which the Sacred Relic is brought out for the worship. I circumambulated with other devotees and got a chance to bow my head to the Tooth Relic. My guide informed me that I was lucky to have caught the morning ceremony. Ceremonials are carried out twice a day at the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic. If you come outside of these two times, you will be unable to see the Relic.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I am writing to express our deep concern and distress over an incident that occurred around 2pm, 27th of May 2024, which we believe contradicts the inclusive principles that Sri Dalada Maligawa, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, has long stood for. On the mentioned date, my wife was denied entry into the temple by the security personnel at the entry security scanning gate to Sri Dalada Maligawa. The reason provided was her attire – specifically, wearing of a “Hijab” (not Burkha as mentioned in website) which is similar to the head coverings of the Christian Nuns. This action was not only humiliating but also seemed to be in direct opposition to the Buddhist ideology of respect for all religions, which the temple is known to uphold. The exclusion based on religious attire is a matter of serious concern, as it directly impacts the fundamental rights of individuals to practice their religion and the values of respect and tolerance. It is imperative that the temple authorities address this issue promptly to ensure that the sacred space remains accessible and welcoming to all devotees, irrespective of their religious expressions. I’ve already requested in writing to the temple authorities to investigate this matter and take appropriate measures to prevent such incidents in the future maintaining respect the diverse backgrounds of visitors and to uphold the temple's commitment to religious harmony. Also, if “Hijab” which is similar to covering head like Nuns prohibited to entry then should mention clearly in websites publicly. So, it will save our time & effort to travel all the way there.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Sri Dalada Maligawa is our favorite place to visit in Kandy. It is a very important place for Sri Lankan Buddhists. Sri Dalada Maligawa, also known as the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, is a Buddhist temple in Kandy, Sri Lanka. It is considered the most sacred place of Buddhist worship in Sri Lanka and perhaps the world, housing the relic of the tooth of the Buddha. The temple is located in the Royal Palace Complex of the former Kingdom of Kandy. The relic has played an important role in Sri Lankan politics since ancient times, as it is believed that whoever holds the relic holds the governance of the country. The relic was historically held by Sinhalese kings. The temple of the tooth is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. A must-see if you are a tourist, this place is revered by Sri Lankan pilgrims.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth Relic offered a stunning view of the Kandy Royal Palace complex. Be prepared to leave your shoes with caretakers who might expect a tip upon retrieval. There's a security check before entering the temple grounds. While the daily rituals create a vibrant atmosphere, they can be quite loud. The tooth relic itself is enshrined upstairs in a multi-layered chamber, supposedly opened by authorized personnel. Overall, it was a memorable experience!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This was something to experience!  It seemed a usual day but the experience was quite something.  Given we were to view a Sacred relic, the crowds were scary.  We pushed into a line which had no regard for vulnerable people e.g. young, elderly.  Once you engaged, you were pushed up stairs  / and into queues to see a gold box quite a distance away.  Quite scary to be in the melee as you get to understand the power of a crowd.  I felt that if I'd tripped I'd be just trodden over.  Same for young children.  Weird, given we are revering a patron of peace.   But worth it if you've got the stomach for it.  Our children certainly learned about the power of crowds.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: As well as viewing the Lake, this was one of the first things we did in the Kandy area. We made sure we were dressed appropriately (shoulders and knees covered). We bought flowers from the flower sellers outside the gates, and at the ticket office we met a guide, and this worked out perfectly for our family (2 adults 2 kids). We quickly gave in our shoes (for a token) and went to the foreign tourist entrance. Our guide walked us through the different parts of the temple, pointed out specific features, the lanterns, the carved wood panels, where to put our flowers and how to present them, the story of the tooth coming to Sri Lanka. We particularly enjoyed the many Buddha statues, and the royal elephant enclosure (with Raja a former royal/processional elephant). You must walk barefoot so it’s a bit hot at times on the walkways. We covered a lot in quite a short time with our guide, learned a lot and enjoyed this beautiful temple visit. It’s also beautiful from the outside with the carved walls, and golden roof. You can see the queen’s bathing hall across the road too. Highly recommend for an easy site to visit in the centre of Kandy and close restaurants, shops and lakefront.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This World Heritage Site is for sure one of the most popular places to see when travelling to Kandy. Be prepared that it's quote crowded and warm, especially inside due to all the visitors. You won't be able to see the actual tooth of Buddha, which is kept in ornamental boxes inside boxes. I found it rather interesting to learn more about people's customs and traditions and enjoyed the beautiful grounds surrounding the temples. People bring offerings like lotus flowers, which vendors will try to sell you. Also, be aware of the "guides" at the entrance trying to chat you up - you are not obliged to hire them and if you do, then better negotiate about the price right from the beginning. Men and Women must be dreased respectfully and wear at least half arm shirts and trousers/skirts covering the knee otherwise you will have to wear a shawl and/or sarong-wrap from the temple. Plan about 30-45 minutes for the visit. You may bring an umbrella and a water bottle in your bag against the very intensive sun, but hats or caps are also not allowed. I always bring a pair of light socks with since you have to remove your shoes when inside the temple.

review_text: This is the heart of all Buddhist Sri Lankan's. Countless times have visited here. Located on a beautiful place in kandy city next to Nuwara Wewa (in ancient time called 'The Milk ocean' which was a big paddy field). The most luckiest thing is any body can worship the sacred tooth of lord Buddha which is saved in a Golden casket. No matter your religion or nationality you are welcome there.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, Sri Lanka, is a mesmerizing UNESCO World Heritage site that holds great cultural and religious significance. It houses the sacred relic of the tooth of the Buddha, making it a focal point for Buddhist pilgrims and visitors alike. The architecture is stunning, reflecting traditional Sri Lankan craftsmanship and intricate design. However, due to its popularity, it can get quite crowded, especially during religious festivals. Overall, it's a must-visit for anyone interested in history, culture, and spirituality.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I had been here almost a decade ago but didn't remember much of our visit. We gathered in a group at just after 1000 on a Sunday morning. Inside the temple, there was much drumming.  Some of the rooms were reasonably crowded, though this apparently was only mild compared to how many visit on some other days. As usual one had to remove shoes before entering.  There was one area dripping with water so I couldn't take a short cut to reach it, but apart from that most surfaces were level including where there were flagstones. The large expanse of lawn outside the temple (though still within its grounds) could do with far more trees to soften and provide shade. It was easy to retrieve shoes.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: When you hear the word “Buddha,” in the imagination of the ignorant, a statue of a man sitting in the “lotus” position immediately appears with a body proportional like a Nyagrodha tree, with membranes between the fingers, with an ushnisha on the top of the head, a smile with forty teeth, etc. In reality, this same Buddha is not just an idol sculpted from one material or another. Siddhartha Gautama Shakyamuni (aka Gautama Buddha) is a key figure in Buddhism: he is a spiritual teacher and the founder of Buddhism, one of the three world religions. Alas, as with all such personalities, there is little reliable information about the biography of the Buddha: a number of Buddhist sutras (texts) in Pali and several Sanskrit scriptures: “Buddacharita”, “Lalitavistara” and others. What is interesting is that when Buddha, at the age of 80, made the “Great Transition into the Absolute Peace of Nirvana,” his body was cremated in accordance with the rite for the Universal Ruler. But then all sorts of Epic Fails begin on the topic of “dividing the relics of the deceased.” If you believe the legends, the remains of the Buddha were divided into eight parts and lie at the base of specially erected stupas-suburgans - these are Buddhist architectural and sculptural religious structures of a hemispherical shape. So, when the relics of Buddha were being divided, someone cunning managed to steal the left fang of the deceased, which was taken to Ceylon. They say that Princess Hemamala and Prince Dantha from the city of Kalinga in India were involved in this action, and this happened during the reign of King Kirti Sri Meghavarna (sometime around 301-328 AD). In Ceylon, the TOOTH was declared a shrine and from that moment the history of the future Temple of the Sacred Relic of the Tooth Relic of Gautama Buddha, the Temple of the Tooth Relic, Sri Dalada Maligawa began!!! All these are names of the same religious building. And not just another Buddhist stupa, but one of the main and most revered shrines of the island!!! In Christianity, this question (I’m talking about sacred relics) is somehow more solid, or something: the Shroud of Turin, the Crown of Thorns, the Spear of Longinus, the Title INRI, the Holy Grail, nails (with which the body of Jesus was nailed to the Cross), and finally the pincers with which they took out those very nails... And then a TOOTH... A whole temple was built over it!!! The same existing Sri Dalada Maligawa in the city of Kandy, the capital of the Central Province of Sri Lanka. Like any shrine, from ancient times this TOOTH was attributed with a certain magical power - whoever owned the fang of the Buddha also had all the power. It is clear that under this “sauce” the Buddha tooth became the property of the ruling Sri Lankan royal dynasty. The fate of the TOOTH was turbulent: it was always kept in the temple at the royal residence, and since the capital “moved” several times (Anuradapura, Pollonnaruwa, Dambadeniya, Yapahuwa, Kurunegala, Kotte Gampola), the TOOTH “traveled” after it. Until he arrived in Kandy at the end of the 16th century. The first “Dalada Madura” (or “Dalada Mandira”, depending on how you write) to store the holy relic (I’m talking about the ZUB, of course) was built during the reign of King Vimaladharmasuriya I in 1592-1604. Alas, during the colonization of the island by the Portuguese, the temple was destroyed. The second sacral was erected on the same site during the reign of King Rajasinghe II from 1635 to 1687. Apparently, Temple of the Tooth was fatally unlucky - and this iconic building was burned, though now by the Dutch. In 1687, King Vimaladharmasuriya II built another Dalada Madura, and it had three floors!!! However, over time, the building fell into disrepair and was destroyed. And finally, his son, King Sri Vera Parakrama Narendrasinghe, who reigned from 1707 to 1739, built the current Dalada Maligawa, which, with minor architectural “adjustments” by subsequent rulers, has survived to this day. The architecture of the sacral is executed in a unique Kandyan style in combination with details and elements of the style of “Dalada Madura” - the forerunner sanctuaries, which previously housed the relic of the Sacred Tooth Relic of Buddha. The location chosen for the temple was simply magical: next to the ancient Royal Palace (the latter is located north of the temple) and a forest reserve called Udavatha Kelaya (to the east). The aura of this magnificent place is brightened by the famous Kandy Lake - the so-called Sea of Milk (also known as Bogambara and Kiri Mukhuda). I was probably lucky - there were practically no people (maybe it was just not the season), I refused the services of a guide - everything that interested me, I read on the internet the day before. I can’t say that I was deeply impressed by what I saw, but I recommend a visit to Sri Dalada Maligawa, if only because it is one of the most famous religious sites on the island.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This place is supposed to have a tooth of Buddha but is not visible to anyone except the monks. One can visit the top floor and move around the temple. This is a live temple and rituals and procedures with prayers are being observed at this place.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We went there as was told it was a "must see".  We took some nice photos as the sun set over the lake. The temple was absolutely mobbed, we were beng shoved and bashed and along with the extremely loud noisy music - mostly drumming we made a quick exit. Not for us but to be fair didn't take time to read up on what we were looking at. Thre was an upper floor but again folk were pushing and shoving to get up the stairs so we gave it a miss.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Foreign visitors are charged 2,000 LKR to enter the Complex where several attractions can be visited. The main attraction here is the Tooth Relic of Buddha. Visitors are required to take off their shoes and dress moderately, no legs exposed. Shoes can be left behind at a counter where one is given a storage number. There lots of steps to take in some areas. The place where the tooth relic is kept has people praying around it. During my visit, there was a ceremony scheduled at 9:45 am to show the relic. Other attractions at the Complex: several museums, cemetery, Elephant Show, etc. Highly recommended is the Buddhist Museum that shows the spread of Buddhism in Asia. Note that taking pictures is not allowed inside the museums.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A fascinating experience but, as everyone mentions, beware of the crowds. There is a lot to see and a guide would probably be helpful. At the end, there is a slow line where you get a closer look at the reliquary containing the tooth and a quicker option where the view is from further away. I think the clause view is really not that b my e essay and line moves very slowly.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I honesty don't know how best to review this location, architecturally it is magnificent, so much detail and for that alone worth a visit. We went at dusk to enter the Temple but not being very religious it felt a little intrusive at what is an important ceremony. I would recommend using a guide to explain a lot of the meanings otherwise you are herded from pillar to post without fully understanding the area's significance. Something not to miss, but ensure you allow proper reverence to the location & beliefs of many people who visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A must visit site in Kandy but be prepared for the crowds. We visited here on the first day of March so many people were coming to prepare for the month ahead. There were lots of queues to enter the shrines or temples because of this combined with the heat, there was a lot of pushing Between crowds. Thankfully our guide, who was a certified, Sri lanka tour guide, managed to get us some priority in a few of the rooms which are not open all the time and close at short notice. Don’t forget, you must have your knees and shoulders covered. If you are visiting and shoes will need to be removed and left at the designated areas outside of the temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is a must-visit attraction in Kandy, but be prepared for very large crowds, especially during the tooth display. Despite the crowds, the temple's impressive architecture and cultural significance make it worth a visit. While the actual tooth is not visible, the ornate casket that houses it is a sight (or glimpse while others push you) to behold. It is a religious place, so wear modestly. No saram (sarong/pareo) rental here, but you can buy from a nearby street vendor (3000lkr negotiable)

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Initially not included in the program, we arrived in Kandy earlier than expected and therefore decided to visit the temple after hearing a lot about this famous tooth in the cultural triangle (Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa). We were delighted with our visit! The temple is magnificent, the fervor is incredible, don't hesitate to buy an offering for Buddha. Buddhists are very welcoming. Seen some comments, yes sometimes we are packed like sardines especially during the ceremony, but you have to be captivated by the atmosphere, it's an incredible moment of human sharing! If you can, go there on a full moon evening, the party is magnificent. Leave the shoes on the right of the temple, paying to collect them but that seems normal to me... however be careful, we took our time when the temple closed to enjoy the garden, we arrived at the lockers just as the guard closed the door, we came close to leaving barefoot...! (at closing you have a little margin, but probably no more than 30min).

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is an interesting temple to visit, but it is more about the history of the tooth relic rather than the temple itself that is not particularly stunning. Our guide provided a good commentary and probably best to have a guide rather than just wandering aimlessly. It is not somewhere we would bother returning to.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I was there without a guide, which I would not recommend. The building is not that interesting without getting to know some of the history, traditions and rituals from the place, so from me I was an average experience. Don’t recommend.

review_text: A serious place of worship. Advised against a guide as they are reported not to be trusted re pricing. State one cost at the beginning but then raise it by the end for frivolous reasons. Approached by many touts but they accepted a form no thank you. Quite expensive entrance fee but is an extraordinary place and a must do in Kandy. Confusing how to enter once tickets purchased and footwear  in the stored location. Peaceful and enchanting walk around. Shame the in house performances are not advertised more openly as we were there mid/ late afternoon and were not able to wait another hour + for this.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth is a captivating blend of art, history, and spirituality. Stepping into its hallowed halls, one is immediately struck by the intricate architecture and rich cultural heritage. I had the pleasure of attending a puja ceremony, where the air was filled with dramatic music and the atmosphere was charged with devotion. Despite the crowd, the experience was deeply moving and immersive. The ticket price of 2000 was a small investment for the spiritual journey and architectural marvel that awaited within. I highly recommend this sacred site to everyone seeking a profound connection to Sri Lanka's cultural and religious heritage.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Definitely worth going for the ceremony…we went during the 9:30–11 one. Great temple throughout, and you don’t need to hang around the central vestibule for more than ten min or  so to get the gist of the ceremony. But be mindful that this is a holy place and the ceremony is a sacred experience for many people… tourists clogging up the aisles upstairs to get selfies while actual worshippers are patiently waiting in the impossible heat with handfuls of flowers to offer was a genuine disappointment.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Fascinating place and culturally significant but very, very busy at the time of the actual tooth ceremony (around 6pm on), so be aware of this. (To may Buddhists this is a "once in a lifetime" visit, and it was an issue to me, how busy the pace was, and some European/American tourists simply wanted a better/closer photo - even at the cost of pushing other people out of the way. The use of a zoom lens is fine. I understand that Sri Lanka needs all the tourist income it can, but there has to be a balance, and they haven't achieved that at the moment)

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Very interesting place and culturally significant but it was also very busy at the time we arrived around 6pm as there is a ceremony at 7pm, so be aware of this. We didn’t end up going anywhere near the tooth and just walked the grounds and went into the other exhibitions because it was so busy and we were waiting in a line for approximately 30 mins and there was no movement.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It is always awkward to intrude on someone else's religious shrine - but our guide made the trip consistently interesting and the people did not mind us.  Not that they would notice.  The shrine is extraordinarily busy - thousands of people walking around and watching the various elements of the 'showing' of the tooth's resting-place.  Other rooms contained gifts of Buddha statues from other countries, thousands of volumes of Buddhist history, and a small museum featuring other gifts from over the centuries.  The overall effect is dizzying, but it is a cultural experience that seems welcoming and is not to be missed.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The tooth temple has its share of stories and we were told it was the wisdom tooth of Buddha that was placed inside and hordes of people come to pray there and in a large hall above . The temple itself had closed doors that day (it was srilanka national day when we visited ) which was disappointing but we did the other rituals of lighting the lamps and incense sticks . The garden was very well maintained. And the guide was very witty !

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Tooth Relic Temple shows how peacefully religions and different faiths can co-exist. One should go and visit the temple and have at utmost respect kindly do not take photos. The arches, the woodwork,  the flowers, the fragrances, the drums and everything is a sensory treat. We asked for Dinesh tour guide who is an authorised guide with an ID for it. He charged reasonably around 3000 LKR for the tour and he helped us with the do's and don'ts. Sorry, I did not take any pictures of the temple as it is very tricky and can cause fines. 077-7710044 is his number.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Its so calm and beautiful there. You have to pay for an entry ticket and remove your shoes at the counter itself. Inside the temple, you can sit, meditate and pray. Also, there is another area with the history of the tooth temple, which is very informative. Got the chance to meet the monk who stays there.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I would highly recommend visiting this important religious site if in Kandy, and I would definitely suggest hiring one of the local site guides to take you around - we nearly didn't and the amount of information we would've missed out on would've been tragic (we had a lovely guide by the name of Dinesh). We toured the temple during the day and then returned at 18:30 for the ceremony and the opportunity to view the gold casket in which Lord Buddhas' tooth is housed (our tour guide explained tickets were valid for the day) and it was so special to have been able to witness this. Remember: shoulders and knees to be covered for both men & women! When we returned in the evening they were not happy with the length of my husband's shorts which were sitting on his knees, but luckily we had thrown a sarong in our bag in the event of this happening.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This sacred site, nestled within the heart of the Kandy city, is a testament to the rich history and religious significance of Sri Lanka. Upon entering the temple complex, the first thing that captures your attention is the magnificent architecture that seamlessly blends different traditional styles. The intricate carvings, vibrant paintings, and the imposing structure create an aura of grandeur, setting the stage for the profound experience that awaits inside. Main highlight of the temple is the sacred tooth relic of Lord Buddha enshrined within. The atmosphere inside the chamber is filled with a sense of reverence and devotion, as pilgrims and visitors alike gather to catch a glimpse of this revered relic. The temple complex also houses various other shrines, each adorned with unique religious artifacts and symbolic representations. Great surroundings with the picturesque Kandy Lake and the lush greenery. You will find knowledgeable guides there to provide insights into the temple's history and significance.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Also known as Sri Dalada Maligawa, the Tooth Relic Temple is an impressive place. It was given recognized as a UNESCO world heritage site in 1988. It is the main attraction in Kandy and definitely worth visiting. It’s located in the Royal Palace complex, with its white buildings and walls. It was bombed in 1989 & 1998 but is now fully restored. Don’t forget to take appropriate clothing to cover your knees and shoulders. I would definitely recommend getting one of the many guides to take you around as it is a huge place and can be quite confusing and also the information from the guides make it a much better experience. As it is one of the most important places of worship for Buddhists it is very busy. If visiting its best to check the opening times of the tooth relic room, the doors are closed at other times. There are plenty of impressive sights to see on the visit including the elephant memorial (Tusker Raja), a full sized taxidermy elephant of the most famous elephant that carried the tooth casket during the festival of the tooth in Kandy each year.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We were unlucky to get here on a full moon. Then it is a holiday for the Buddhists and the temple was packed with people. Absolutely hysterical. My tip is to choose another day. Incidentally, I think the temple is very interesting. For an additional cost, you can choose to stand in a long line and get a quick look at the casket where the Buddha's tooth is said to be kept. Entry 2000 LKR per person plus fee to hand in your shoes for storage. You should also buy with you some flowers that are offered on altars inside the temple. Long skirt or trousers and no bare shoulders. Take off your cap. You are allowed to take pictures but no silly poses.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, Sri Lanka, holds immense cultural and religious significance as it enshrines a tooth believed to be that of Buddha. With opening hours from 5:30 am to 8:30 pm, visitors can immerse themselves in the temple's rich history and witness daily rituals, including puja ceremonies. Prayer time is 5.30am 6.30am 10.30am 6.30pm. Admission tickets, priced at approximately 2000 LKR, provide access to this UNESCO World Heritage Site. To respect local customs, it's advisable to dress modestly, ensuring shoulders and knees are covered. Before entering the temple, visitors are required to remove their shoes, a customary practice symbolizing reverence. The Temple of the Tooth offers a profound spiritual experience amid its historical splendor. A highly recommended destination for those visiting Kandy, the Temple of the Tooth offers a profound and culturally enriching experience, deeply rooted in reverence and historical significance.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited it at 6pm, when the faithful are called to prayer to the rhythm of the drums. I must say that I didn't enjoy the visit very much, the crowd was huge, we couldn't see much. Even the external parts were barely visible at dusk: perhaps we were also tired and felt the weight of the whole day.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I guess you need to be a Buddhist to get deep and meaningful value from the visit. I won’t comment on religion beyond this. But it clear means a lot to our Buddhist friends and it’s good to see that a new roof has been installed to protect this beautiful monument. In terms of an attraction, it’s ok, the flow through is not clear (no guide leaflet provided) necessitating a human guide to fully appreciate the place. Even with our (very good ) guide we still came away a little nonplussed. We visited the elephant memorial (for Raja - the maligawa tusker) and didn’t feel like celebrating the poor creatures long life of service rather its extended ordeal of slavery and suffering for a life lived in chains. Strange how different cultures view these things so differently. On a more practical and safety point - a major roof at the site was undergoing roof repairs which involved removing and dumping hundreds if not thousands of clay tiles. My question to the management- at a site where people are forced to walk barefooted why are you not using bins for this material instead of dumping it across footpaths.?

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: First off the viator pricing advertised on TA is outrageous. Temple entry is 2000LKR for foreigners versus Viator 7700LKR. Yes you can skip queues with TA but not worth that premium as after 10am queues went right down. The temple is truly beautiful inside. Ornate with amazing carvings and paintings. Despite lots of people it was actually quite tranquil inside. Building works at the moment which do impact a little on noise and as of 17th Jan 23 the toilets for foreigners were closed due to building works. You can use the toilets for locals. The museums were interesting. A highlight of the trip and highly recommended.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Kandy, a UNESCO World Heritage site, stands as the last capital of Sri Lanka's ancient kings. Nestled within its verdant hills is the revered Temple of the Tooth, which cradles the Buddha's sacred relic. This relic, symbolizing the living Buddha, has been a spiritual beacon for Buddhists for centuries. Historically, the tooth relic's possession signified governance, with kings seeking its blessings for prosperity and protection. The temple's grandeur reflects diverse architectural influences, from traditional Kandyan designs to intricate Indo-Aryan motifs. Each year, the temple's cultural vibrancy shines during the Esala Perahera, a grand procession drawing thousands with its displays of traditional arts and music. Many Buddhists globally journey to this sanctuary, immersing themselves in Sri Lanka's rich history, art, and traditions. The temple offers glimpses of traditional Kandyan performances, evoking a profound spiritual experience. Its architectural beauty, from the golden roof to delicate carvings, mesmerizes visitors. Beyond its tangible marvels, the Temple of the Tooth epitomizes values of peace, unity, and reverence, standing as a testament to Sri Lanka's historical legacy. To ensure a respectful visit, visitors are advised to observe Puja times at 5.45am 6:30am 10:30am and 6:30pm dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, preferably in white, and remove shoes upon entering."

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Our private driver arranged for an off duty official guide to take us around. We timed it when the tooth room was open in the evening. We also wanted to see the Raja Tusker Museum and would have never found it in the dark without him. Being a religion place you cannot wear shoes and knees and shoulders have to be covered.

review_text: I can confirm a lot of the other reviews. It is very full especially on poya (full moon days). BUT please consider this is a sacred religious place for the locals and as tourists we are lucky to be allowed to enter and get a glimpse of the religious practice and culture. Still for me it was somewhat overwhelming: people will not mind your personal space and push you along the stream of people, there ist a lot of loud praying and people bring tons of flowers and other offerings. Look out: In front of the main building there are many people who want to be your guide and tourists are guided to leave there shoes with some guard. We did not give them money because we think the entrance fee is high enough. And a guard is not necessary there. Pro tip: if you don’t want to stand out too much were white like the locals. If you’re not up to it don’t come during the ceremony times (around 10:30/ 11am and 17:30/18pm).

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If you are not a religious person that understands where to go, when and what's happening there at that moment, you won't enjoy the place much, neither the ceremony that happens at the place when it's open to the public. Not to mention that the place is a maze and it took me and my boyfriend some time to get to the entrance that we needed. Different prices for locals and for tourists are present also here, as everywhere else at Sri Lanka. The ceremony is a mass activity where a lot of people pushes themselves to a certain place at the temple, and you push yourself to get there also, since you don't know why are others pushing themselves so much. The fact it, the religious people want to give their offerings to the temple and to Buddha. You will end up in a room where everyone is packed, waiting to get to the room for offerings, where you won't get. So since you know about this now, you don't need to push yourself together with them and I have just saved you some time and nerves. Instead of pushing yourself with the mass, I recommend you to walk around the temple and the parts that are accessible for the visitors, and e.g. burn some candles as your offering outside. The place looks magical, especially in the evening when it's already dark outside. To burn something, you need to buy a special oil for that. I didn't figure out where to do that, unfortunately. What got me was a payment payment machine looking as an ATM that could be used for donations for the temple. Like wow. A way to go, The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic! This is what I call progress.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Considered as a sacred temple complex containing the sacred tooth relic of Lord Buddha, Shri Dalada Maligawa also known as Palace of sacred tooth. This temple is a must visit for every Buddhist. The tooth relic was originally housed in a rock carved temple in Anuradha pura before it was moved to the present palace / temple at Kandy about five hundred years ago. This centuries old temple is serene and the worshippers pray in silence. The temple was originally built as a royal residential palace by the royal family of Sri Lanka long time ago. The remarkable features of this temple is the renowned recital of Kandy drums is a joy to hear. The musical performance is unique for Sri Lanka.The musical instruments are two drums and a pipe instrument. The performance lasting about half an hour is precisely choreographed. The puja timings are fixed  lasting about half an hour three times in a day - morning, noon and evening. The temple premises are very well secured and spotless maintenance is visible everywhere. You need to be properly dressed to enter the temple. Ensure that your shoulder and knees are covered. The temple management treats every body equal. No preference seems to be given for any one. There is no shouting at or pushing of the pilgrims in the sanctum sanctorium. Everything is done in dignified silence. The temple is a must visit while you are in Kandy, Sri Lanka. Highly recommended.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Planning the visit is extremely important- given the ceremonies & limited window when doors are opened. We hired a guide & got there around 5.45pm- just in time for us to enter the central premises & visit other shrines. Guide helped us navigate & explained the different parts of the temple in details. Some tips for fellow travellers- 1. The tooth relic is not for public viewing everyday- only taken our during ceremony. Instead we get to see the golden caskets holding the relic from 6.45pm in the evening. So get there on the right time! 2. Several shrines are present inside temple premises, like Crystal budhha, Hari Krishna, original manuscripts, museum & royal elephant memorial. Taking a guide is best to navigate & not miss out key sights. 3. Golden Canopy above the relic is not to be missed- stunning sight in the evening light! 4. Moonstone entrances, beautiful paintings & carvings- despite the rush, take sometime to admire the place. 5. There are some ground rules for taking photographs- No selfies, no photos showing back to the Buddha statues, etc. So be mindful of them, while enjoying the temple. Entry fee for SAARC members is 1500 SLR per person. Ticket counter is next to the temple on side of the lake. Would suggest so spend atleast 1.5hrs to cover the entire temple.

To the point where we had to shout no and they wouldn’t take no for an answer. As foreigners we had to pay 3000 which was a lot we felt. A so called guide even followed us into the check in gate and got annoyed when we politely said no thank you. More persistence. Then we were told without a guide we wouldn’t understand. This is not true as just about everything is translated to English. There was a booth to leave our shoes at and when we returned we were hounded again for money for looking after our shoes. We already paid far more than we expected to get in so no thanks! A staff member followed us around when we were in a museum and made me show my ticket a number of times. It all felt like harassment. We are really not made of money, quite the opposite in fact. Something I thought was strange is even though you have to remove your shoes, all the staff didn’t which made me ponder what was the point. How can it be rude for us to wear shoes and not them? The tooth display itself was okay but of course you could Not see it so who is to say it was really there? Hey we can appreciate the religious/cultural significance - we aren’t made of stone but we had heard Sri Lankan people were welcoming: They are when they want your cash!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This place brings sanctity to Kandy. It is called Dalada Maligawa in the local language. The temple is golden-roofed. Locals and tourists visit the temple for prayers with flowers and incense throughout the day. The temple keeps the tooth relic of the Buddha in its main shrine. The premises also houses several shrines, museums, and temples. Museums include the International Buddhist Museum, Dalada Museum, Raja Tusker Museum, and Royal Palace Archaeological Museum The temple is open for tourists from 5: 30 AM to 8:00 PM. Pujas happen at three different timings – 5:30 AM to 6:45 AM, 9:30 AM to 11:45 AM, and 6:30 PM to 8:00 PM. It's advised to dress conservatively and wear outfits that cover your shoulders and legs.

Highy recommended place to visit in Kandy. And it is recommended to park your vehicles somewhere else in poya days and long weekends, since its own carpark is always full on such days. Another important thing is, you will not be allowed to enter the temple with shorts, short skirts and skinners.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Sacred Temple of Tooth is the most iconic place in Sri Lanka. It houses the sacred tooth relic of Lord Buddha and it is the holiest place of Buddhists. inside of the temple is exceptionally beautiful with ancient paintings and wood carvings.  The temple grounds spread out to many hectares and have several important spots under one head. The temple itself is located inside the ancient royal palace complex, which encompasses several devalas, and museums. International Buddhist Museum, Audience hall, meditation grounds, the Rajah Tusker Hall, and many more sights are the reasons for its ingenuity and grandeur. The spiritual power and awesome scenic beauty that surrounds this sacred temple will surely enchant you.

review_text: We attended the 5:30am (and least crowded) ceremony at the Temple of the Tooth. It was a real privilege to witness this special moment (although you don’t actually get to see the tooth) and later explore the riches the temple complex has to offer.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Very grand temple, different fees for locals and tourists, you can pay at the machine - ideally take the correct amount of change. The inside architecture and decor is impressive and the story of the ancient tooth relic is written on the walls. You can also light lamps outside in prayer or for blessings. I imagine it can be very peaceful. If you don't like crowds don't go at prayer time as it is really busy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited Temple of the Tooth in the evening and watched the Puja Ceremony. There are 3 ceremonies every day 6am, 10am and 6pm. Both men and women must have their shoulders and knees covered. During the ceremony drummers fill the air with rhythmic beats and  prayers.  People line up for the chance to catch a glimpse of the golden case with the tooth inside and offerings of flowers are laid before the sacred tooth’s chamber. It was very interesting to go at this time of the day and it had a real ambiance about it

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Visited on 18 February 2020 at 10.30am Dress decently. Very important is to wear cloths which cover the body and legs. No shorts or sleeveless tops allowed. For hot days carry cap/scarves. Please note. On Kandy sightseeing, this was the first stopover of the day. The entry tickets were arranged as part of the package which included a CD and souvenir. The location of this temple is beside a lake and approach road has many colonial buildings. The temple complex has many attraction within. Museum, floors, different portions dedicated to rituals and related things. Photos are allowed but not selfies. Respect the rules. This attraction will have long walks so suggest take a guide along and senior citizens must take rest breaks. There is a souvenir shop inside the Museum complex selling authentic Sri Lankan craft at appropriate prices. Authenticity is guaranteed.  Do use this opportunity to take few products back to your country. I bought Elephants (SLR 350), key rings (SLR 80) and fridge magnets  (SLR 200). Beautiful flower shops will amaze you when you exit the temple. You will feel a calmness and happy after visiting this place. Go and enjoy .

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We joined the queues during morning prayer. There are two queues to get in: one for the men and one for the women. Like most things in life, the men's line moved faster. This is mainly due to two things: 1) most women carry bags that need searching (most men don't) 2) the women perhaps face a little more scrutiny over what they can wear and must cover-up. Shoulders and legs need to be covered, so make sure you have a light scarf and sarong. Men too should carry a sarong to put on although some western males it seemed were managing to get through in shorts. Once inside make sure you follow the tourist crowds to the right and enter the temple through the tourist entry. Here you leave your shoes, you will be expected to tip after collection. Inside, at prayer, this place is busy. At times you are moved along with the crowd. The locals are of course queuing to leave gifts and to pray so don't feel too bad if you 'skip' queues and glide past those locals waiting on the stairs. The relic itself can't be seen. Instead, you can peer into the golden shrine where it is stored, but at this point in the temple, the crowds are at their busiest so you main only manage a cursory glance. The best part about the temple is exploring the grounds and additional rooms and buildings. The carvings and sculptures of Budha are beautiful, and in most spaces, you can take photos. Just be mindful of people worshipping and not to take pictures with your back to any Budha statue. The grounds of the temple are beautiful, and there is an elephant on the site too, which is used in ceremonies. Although, it is clearly an old elephant and seeing it so heavily chained doesn't make for the best view. At night time, around the temple and Lake, there is a cacophony of noise as bats and birds come to roost in their hundreds. It is the most spectacular site in Kandy and a must-see. The museum of World Buddhism, which is on the site is also worth a visit, and with a tourist ticket to the temple, you have access.

review_text: Always wanted to visit here as a highly regarded religious site. Had to wear a sarong as we tuned up in shorts. To be fair he showed us everything we wanted to see eg the temple of the tooth and other things in other temples including a stuffed elephant we wouldn't have known about. Temple was being cleaned when we visited so you ended up with very wet feet. The person holding the shoes also wanted money so the lack of materialism inside didn't stretch to the staff. Glad I went and would recommend if you have an interest in this sort of thing.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is another UNESCO World Heritage Site with interesting history and background. The site is located in city centre of Kandy right in front of Kandy Lake. Tooth Relic is believed to be sacred for Buddhism and the royal family was responsible for the safekeeping of the tooth relic. It is believed to be brought from Anuradhapura to Kandy Kingdom. Two storeys building was constructed for safekeeping the tooth relic. But the building was destroyed several times. Each time it was restored whenever it was destroyed. There will be ceremony everyday for the blessings by the devotees. We visited around late afternoon and waited for the ceremony around 6pm plus. Interesting cultural sights, but be prepared for uncontrollable crowds and haphazard situation during the ceremony. The tooth relic is said to be kept within a gold plated ornament, hence it cannot be seen by anyone even during the ceremony. The international Buddhism Museum within the compound is worth to check out too for the interesting architecture and interior design. Overall, it is still worth the entrance fee of LKR1,500 per person and appropriate attire is required and tight security check at the entrance.

review_text: We are a couple in early 30s with 9 and 10yr old daughters. Firstly we hadn't dressed appropriately so had to rent sarongs to cover up. The guy was nice enough but still 400rs down. It's a bit of a faff to get in, we went through one lot if security then you get your bag checked again before you go in. We had a tip off from the sarong guy that they take away your cigarettes and lighters so I hid them well in the bag. You have to put your shoes in a shoe storage area. Other reviews are correct about them asking for a donation, I was aware of this and just played deaf when they asked me, I had to assist my child... Oh and don't think you can put your shoes in your bag - that's not allowed! The ticket machines don't give change so you do have to have the right amount on you. There was an attendant who said we didn't have to pay for the children which was good and we didn't have the right change but he helped a guy behind us which then gave us the right change. So that was kind. First off you walk on boiling hot pavement in bear feet. Then I guess the rest is interesting if you like architecture and religious history. As atheists we were a little bemused by all of it. There's nothing to tell you where the tooth is. We assumed we were in the right place by the people praying on the floor... But there's no signs etc and we didn't have a guide. There's a museum which was a little interesting. The saddest part is the taxidermied elephant. Poor thing was captured and kept for a good 50years before he died. He's now stuffed in a glass cabinet. There's a photo timeline of his life since capture but it doesn't have any translation so we don't really know the story... If you like this sort if thing and are in Kandy then maybe pay it a visit... But I definitely wouldn't drive to Kandy for a day trip just for that. In my husbands words "I wouldn't go again even if it was outside my front door".

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I'm not a Buddhist so I'm reviewing the place and there it excels as it is designed to wow the visitor. In the viewing gallery there is a dedicated section for the faithful to sit and a walking route to see the Mounting Point for the tooth. When visiting please be careful to follow the viewing route as some guides send you through the faithful. Not really a highlight for me on this trip

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We were on a tour so were taken to this Temple. There is a lot of security there due to a bombing 24 years ago which killed a lot of monks, there are photographs of the damage that was caused. After dropping our shoes we walked through a big hallway where there were a lot of people praying and giving flower offerings. It was very interesting and well worth a visit but once seen I wouldn’t go again.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Overhyped and overpriced tourist attraction/temple that doesn’t seem to have much of an atmosphere or pays respect to a religion. It’s starts with paying the entrance fee, which basically feels like sponsoring the government. After dropping your shoes you enter the temple and don’t really know what a logical way is to start, especially since it’s super crowded. We went for the ‘ceremony’ but all it really was, was some guys banging a drum really loud for more then an hour. While that happend on the first floor on the second floor a queue of people pushing each other around formed to look in to a window (for not even a second) which apparently showed something important. I’m still not sure what it was. The temple has some pretty aspects but they mainly show in the hallways in the form of patterns and wallpaintings. After your whole ‘experience’ you’ll go and pick up your shoes and get to deal with the guys behind the desk forcing you to put money in a donation box while clinching on to your shoes. Kind of defeats the purpose of a donation doesn’t it?

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Our driver/guide took us to the 6:30pm pooja ceremony which was the perfect timing as it was very atmospheric, with the light fading and the temple coming alive with the ceremony. I would recommend having a guide to explain what is happening and to also guide you through the temple - it was very busy and could feel a bit chaotic if you don’t have someone with you to guide you through it, and to also take you to all the different rooms. There is a dress code where you need to cover your shoulders and knees, and you also need to take off your shoes.  Security is tight due to a bombing outside the temple a few years ago so give yourself time to get in to the temple. This is a must do when visiting Kandy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A bit of a hike from the nearest parking on a hot day. Shoes have to be left at a kiosk outside the temple and there is a dress code. No shoulders or knees allowed to be on show. There is a queue to see the tooth relic and you are not allowed time to admire it but ushered past quickly by security. We had a good guide otherwise wouldn’t have a clue what it was all about.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the Temple with our guide - the best way to have the inside knowledge. We went to see the offerings at 9.30am, at this time some separate rooms are opened which aren’t usually open during other hours. FYI you can’t actually see the tooth; it is well protected in a stupa which is behind a closed door but open during the offering time. It was quite busy but use your manners and getting around is fine. As it is a sacred place, clothing is more strict. Leggings for women need to be covered appropriately and men preferably trousers however my husband just wore a sarong over shorts. Shoulders are also covered accordingly. Make sure you take time to see the ancient paintings portraying the story of the relic and see the taxidermy elephant!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We were staying close to Kandy and knew that this was one of the biggest attractions in the area and our only available day to go was on a Saturday. We left early and got to the temple area around 9:30am. You must leave your shoes with a shoe keeper and buy your ticket in the same area. Make sure you are properly dressed as they will not let you in with any knee or shoulder showing (although you can buy a sarong right there if necessary). Women and men go through separate security lines and for us, the lines were extremely long and quite slow-I believe this was because of our timing. From there, you can make your way into the main temple and line up in a hectic, crowded, and sweaty manner for a VERY quick look at the golden casket which holds the sacred tooth of Buddha. From there, you are free to wander the grounds and look into the different buildings, including a museum with artifacts under glass, a room devoted to the famous temple elephant Raja the Tusker, and also some archeological artifacts. Altogether a very fascinating look into the passionate devotion to Buddha in Sri Lanka.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited this temple as part of an organised tour with Walkers tours and definitely benefited from having our guide, Sumith, giving his insight and sharing his expertise whilst we were there.  I don't think the experience would have been the same without this personal insight and informed commentary. Firstly, to be clear you do not see the sacred tooth! If you are lucky you may get a quick peek at the casket (with its separate 5 locks) where it is housed.  If you are a tourist you can reach this by one very quick queue where Buddhists who wish to leave an offering may queue for 3 hours to reach the relic.  The feeling of reference and respect is overwhelming and moving, just close your eyes for a moment and take in the sounds of chanting and drumming, the smells of essence and offerings, the emotions shown by people of faith.  I can honestly say I felt completely overcome and still shiver at the memory. On leaving this area there is plenty more to see which are less crowded and easier to view.  We particularly enjoyed the room with the pictures outlining the history of the sacred tooth around a statue of Buddha with another place for offerings a must do place in Kandy, particularly if you can have an insight as to why it is so important to the people of Sri Lanka

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic

Don't fall for this if he tries to do the same to you!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is a Buddhist temple in the city of Kandy, Sri Lanka. It is located in the royal palace complex of the former Kingdom of Kandy.  It is a very important Sri Lankan temple as it houses the relic of the tooth of the Buddha. We visited this temple as part of a G Adventures tour in the evening when the doors of the area where the casket that houses the tooth relic is open,  This allows the locals as well as the tourists to see this casket. Due to problems with possible terrorists, there are high security measures taken before you can enter the temple.  You must also be appropriately dressed with women wearing clothes that cover their shoulders and knees and men should wear full length pants.  Most of the locals wear complete white outfits to show their respect when visiting the temple. It is a very busy in this temple and you cannot wear your shoes in it.  I had a guide help me through the temple, which I would not have been able to do if he had not helped me up and down the numerous stairs you need to use to see the entire temple. The museum that is attached to the temple was also interesting to see as it held many sacred texts about Buddha's life.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The holy of holies for Sri Lankan Buddhists, the visit is a must though perhaps for tourists not at one of the scheduled pujas when you feel the crush of devotees attending to pray and offer food. If you want the atmosphere of a puja, drum beating will announce its start and continue throughout, the actual ceremony performed by the monks behind the closed temple doors with massive elephant tusks in front of it. The highlight is the ever so brief time you have looking at the large gold casket in the distance, devotees handing food and flowers over to the monks. Visit the library with its Buddhist texts on palm leaf and dazzle at some of the jewel-encrusted vases and the like. In another area you can get a history of the tooth relic over 21 panels. As you exit, the grounds are rather pretty. While there are elements of the visit that will leave you dissatisfied, try to soak up the overall atmosphere. You have to go through security.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Set in a large garden with several historic statues, this holy site is well kept, with an ornate building housing the tooth, but not much else. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It is the palace of the last Sri Lankan king in Kandy before Brirish arrived in Kandy in 1815.The king used the palace to keep and protect the tooth of the Buddha known as 'Dalada Maligawa'. there are lots of Sri Lankan history to be seen a very important place for those who are interested in history and knowledge about Sri-Lanka and its culture, religion and social aspects. to enter the palace one has to remove shoes and no cameras allowed, no shorts and appropriate clothes should be worn.There is a safe place to leave your shoes. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Religious site with a Buddha tooth relic with a newer building built over the original relic casket. Been told that at twice a day the casket door will be opened for special prayers. The temple was built circa  4th century AD. When we visited there were so many locals sitting on the floor for prayers. They offered white flowers for prayers. The tooth relic was brought over by the King and Queen, and she hid the relic in her hair, when the capital was moved to Kandy. Every year in August, the Festival of the Tooth is one of the grandest festivals in Sri Lanka and in the Buddhist world. It is held every summer in Kandy to honor the sacred tooth of Lord Buddha and to pay homage to old gods of Sri Lanka. For the people of Sri Lanka, it is a time to celebrate the country's rich culture and history

review_text: It so happened that we went there on Christmas day and seeing the long queues, we decided to go back later. But the crowds were still there when we returned in the evening. So we went early the next day. It is quite a walk from the main gate and the surroundings are really beautiful. Once we got in, we were surprised at the people inside. They were mainly devotees. We had to inch our way up through a crowded staircase to the main relic. I felt claustrophobic.You are allowed just a second and then you have to move. It was a relief to get out. .

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Get your information and timing right if you wish to visit this ancient and holy place. The door to the main relic is opened at specific timings, so check before you plan your trip. While the doors to the main shrine are closed, the crowds start building up, so if crowds scare you this place is an absolute no. Although the crowds are quite well behaved. Be sure to cover your shoulders and legs else shell out money to locals for giving you wraps etc. You need to buy tickets at the entrance from kiosks which need exact change. You will need to remove and deposit shoes at the counters outside. Once inside it gives you the feel of an ancient place but well preserved and maintained. Lots of devotees with offerings throng the temple every day. Do not miss the oil lamps lighted outside by numerous devotees. You are allowed to take pictures but take care not to have your back towards the main shrine - else you will be asked to delete them by the vigilant guards. You marvel at the architecture of the temple and palace and leaves you asking fir more. The gardens are huge and well kept. I would recommend going there in the evenings, and once the temple visit is done you can enjoy the beauty of the kandy lake and the hills in the background.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We saw that the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic was on every list when we researched things to do in Kandy.  It is, of course, a beautiful temple.  I especially liked the ceiling murals near the main entrance.  The main temple, however, was so crowded that it was hard to enjoy.  We happened to be there near the new year, when many people were coming with offerings. You will need to leave your shoes at one of two kiosks before entering the temple.  Therefore, the walk from the shoe kiosk to the temple can be uncomfortably hot on your feet, so plan accordingly and perhaps wear socks.  Also, there are ticket machines where you buy your tickets, and for some reason they require exact change.  Very bizarre.  There is a man sitting near the machines who will give you change, but it was an odd encounter because we didn't really know who he was or what he was doing. Overall, I was underwhelmed and went because it is so famous.  However, I feel our visit to Kandy could have been fine without this.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: As perhaps the most important Buddhist site in Sri Lanka, it is almost always busy, even when we went in the last few hours it was open. Yet, there is no denying it is a special place, with its ornate design (it was formerly the Kandyian king’s palace), and beautiful artwork within. It is a bit of a process to enter, multiple security checkpoints, a shoe drop off and automatic ticket machines that have several other visitors frustration (we agreed to let a gentleman who offered insert our payment and all was fine - these others seemed concerned this was a scam of some sort, it was not...). Bring your patience and you will be rewarded with a memorable visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The number one tourist destination in Kandy is surely this Temple. Easy to find in central Kandy. The entrance is adjacent to the old Victoria Hotel. Be aware that your legs and shoulders must be covered (no shorts allowed), so local sellers do sell some wraps or baggy loose trousers for a fee. Once in, a short stroll through the garden to the museum itself. If you are not native to Sri Lanka, you must go to the right to deposit your shoes in a locker/storage area before then queuing, searching and enter the temple. You also may want to pick up lotus or incense offerings before you go in too. Follow the crowds, it’s easy to navigate, and try not to take too many photos inside (which may offend) and pay the appropriate respects to those there for religious purposes. There is also a museum on site too towards the rear of the temple that’s worth a look too.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple shows how Buddhist worshippers from Sr Lanka and around the world show their devotion. We were there in afternoon to look at the different parts of the temple including the history of the relic being enthroned in the temple. At the back is a museum of Buddhist religions in the world (included in your ticket but no photos allowed). Our visit culminated with the afternoon prayers with monks bringing offerings into the chamber of the sacred tooth (off limits to worshippers). Visitors need to be appropriately dressed and leave shoes in holding places. Since the holding place for foreigners' shoes was far from the entrance, we left our shoes (in our shoe bags) in the locals' holding place which is nearer the entrance. Just show your ticket.

review_text: This temple is the main attraction in kandy for locals and tourists. However, they rip off the tourists with high entrance fees while the locals go in for free. review_text: The sacred temple of tooth relic is located right in d centre of kandy city. There are multiple entrances and we made d mistake of entering from d main entrance. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Sacred Tooth holds Sri Lanka's most sacred Relic, a tooth of the Buddha. Unfortunately we did not get to see the casket housing the Relic, but were still awed by the beauty of the architecture and the décor of the frescoes, moonstones and wooden frames. See the beautiful seated statue of a golden Buddha flanked by two white marble statues, other images and the ivory tusks, and then look to the ornamentation of the ceiling above. The Main Hall showcases man statue of the Buddha in various poses; suspended plaques over each give an explanation of he painted scene above. At ceiling height, above each statue, there is a sculpture of an elephant head and tusks, all coloured gold. Some wonderful features both indoors and to the buildings' exteriors. The complex was crowed with tourists and worshippers, sound muted as if all acknowledge the sanctity of the place.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We came to visit on a Saturday at around 7:00am. There were already lots of devotees coming in since it was a day of worship and offering for most of the locals. Upon entering the temple grounds, we went to buy our tickets and leave our shoes at the designated counter. Although I am not a Buddhist, it was still a very special spiritual feeling coming inside. Devotees mostly in white were already lined up to go to the top to give their offerings. While the relic room was not yet open, we went inside the other small rooms. One room housed many books written by Buddha himself. Wearing modest clothes is a must. Please also be mindful and respectful of the rules. This is their sacred place of worship and we are very lucky to be granted access inside. Read the signs around and be sure to follow them.

review_text: A delightful early morning visit here. It wasn’t too busy at 8am! location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Visited the Temple of Sacred Tooth Relic on an evening. Tourists entrance fee is 1500 LKR. I recommend getting there for 5:30pm and start with the museum situated on top floors showing artefacts and historical information, paintings and jewellery given to the temple over the past few hundred years and dignitaries and devotees. It’s quite impressive. Then come back down for 6:30pm when the veneration ceremony takes place. Tourists are allowed to watch and film. Then queue up to go to first floor to have a look at the relic. I won’t spoil the surprise, and it can’t be photographed anyway. By the way there is a replica in the museum upstairs ;-) ask one of the guards of the museum...

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I spent half the day at this by far the most relevant sightseeing spot at Kelly. I recommend to visit late in the afternoon if you get the chance to see the ceremony at 18:30. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Temple of the tooth, kandy is one of my favourite sacred places to visit. We visit this temple at least once a year. It houses the sacred tooth of Lord Buddha in a beautiful golden cascet. It was built during the time Kings ruled the kandy city so you can still see the architecture and paintings from the bygone era. So when you step inside you get the feeling of time travelling... Like a king or a queen might just walk by so that the Kings guard will announce all to bow down... If you can visit during the "thewawa" time you can vitness the grand ritual of offerings to the sacred tooth relic which includes a memorising drum play. If you do visit remember to dress in white and not to wear sleevless or short(above knee) clothes as a gesture of paying respect to the sacred tooth relic.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: As is the case throughout Sri Lanka, entrance costs are quite high (around 1500 Rps each if I remember correctly).  It soon adds up for a family of four. However, it was very interesting to visit the temple; particularly atmospheric as we arrived when the  the drums and music started playing. Being such an important Buddhist site, be prepared for queuing and a lot of jostling particularly at the relic.  You get closest to see the stupa housing the relic if you take an offering (you don't actually see the relic).  Otherwise, its more of a glimpse across the crowds. There are other parts of the temple to see too. For example there is the octagonal library and a gallery of wall paintings and other shrines (photo).  The visit was certainly more meaningful as our tour guide provided lots of explanations as we walked around. I'd suggest visiting quite early.  We arrived around 1000 and a lot of areas were closing as we were leaving (around 11ish).
