location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The most revered Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic of Buddha also called as Sri Dalada Maligawa humbles any one by witnessing the genuine devotion of people who walk with flowers and other offerings in their hands, mostly dressed in white clothes. I visited in the morning hours before it became crowded with tourists.There is a ticket that covers both entry into Temple premises and also to World Buddhism Museum. During Puja (prayers that happen four times a day), the main room in first floor opens for ten minutes but we see only a gold casket in the shape of a Stupa for a glimpse. The complex is a large area with numerous shrines and also new Shrine called Alut Maligawa(consisting of dozens of statues of Buddhas donated by Thai devotees), an Audience Hall, Raja Tusker Hall and Museum. It's better to engage services of a guide, available at entrace or at ticket counter and normal charge after negotiations will be 2000 Sri Lankan Rupee (less than 20 US Dollars).It's a sacred religious place and therefore dress code of covering legs and shoulders is a must.Shoes are not allowed.I wore a white shirt and I could see happy smiles on many faces due this simlple gesture. I had spent about three hours after visiting main shrine ( after saying bye to my guide).World Museum contains lots of pictures, explanatory information, models of sacred images of Buddha from across the world including India, Pakistan,Bangladesh, Japan,China ,Korea, Cambodia,Laos, Central Asia and other countries. Photography in not allowed inside the Museum. Not to be missed by any traveller to this beautiful country.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We went there at 6pm to join for the evening ceremony. Beautiful temple with lovely paintings, definitely worth a visit. Kandy wasn't our favourite place in Sri Lanka but if you there this place is a must. Ladies need to make sure to cover there shoulders and knees and gents knees. You can buy nice scarf outside temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I visited the temple due to all the positive reviews and considered a must when visiting Kandy. After arriving I was immediately hustled into buying over priced pieces of fabric to cover my arms and legs and so was my partner. Understand there are rules but some people had the arms uncovered but I wasn't allowed? Then we were charged a hefty price to enter the temple (which is men's to rise next September) once in the temple it was pretty in some areas but not anything special. My highlight was seeing a mum dog and her two puppies. We were told at 6.30pm an exciting ceremony would take place but it was just a 5 minute of some men drumming the same beat all looking very unhappy and bored. After leaving we were then charged another hefty price to retrieve our shoes. Over all was a lot of money paid out for a disappointing result. I would say come so you can see the temple but be prepared to pay out a lot of unnecessary money.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Take your time in the grounds and you could be there fir at least an hour. Ensure you have your shoulders and knees covered; both men and women as they are strict about it and can be refused entry. Scarfs can be bought just outside grounds if you need one to cover yourself. Head straight to temple and on the left is the ticket booth and shoe storage. Tickets are 1500. It is a one time use only so you can not leave and reenter. We stayed for ceremony at 6:30pm. Tourists line up, upstairs on the left to see the tooth. Locals line up on the right.   Music is played downstairs. Bit confusing as no one really explains what to do or what is going on. Sunset is nice from here and good view on giant Buddha on the hill

review_text: There is so much history to absorb on a visit to this temple that a good quality guide is essential. Be careful not to touch a beautifully carved elephant in the hall; apparently it can upset the worshippers. Bear in mind that shoulders and knees need to be covered at all times during the visit. You will be expected to walk barefoot so if this would cause you any problems with your feet don't go.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We normally avoid religious places like temples, mosques etc. unless they have historical significance. Therefore, we went to the temple of the tooth. We went on a afternoon and the temple was crowded with visitors. Despite the number of devotees, we did not feel oppressed by the crowds and thanks to a local guide (we paid LKR 500, but there are good chances that we over-paid) we were able to properly understand the significance of every corner of the temple. Less interesting is the museum upstairs which seems to be a collection of gifts to the temple. If you have lesser time, the museum can be skipped. The entrance fee for foreigners (even though saarc country members like us Indians pay a reduced fee) is FAR higher compared to locals. We thought this was a little unfair for a place of worship, but maybe they need the funds for maintenance.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple houses the most important Buddhist relic - a tooth of the Buddha. It is said that the tooth was snatched from the flames of the Buddha's funeral pyre and smuggled to Sri Lanka in the hair of a princess. It was first taken to Anuradhapura, and moved through the country on waves of history before it ended in Kandy. The tooth shrine receives many worshippers and tourists. During pujas the heavily guarded room housing the tooth is open to devotees and tourists. The tooth is kept in a gold casket shaped like a dagoba. You don't actually see the tooth.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We went to the temple after six o'clock on a day when the local holidays was ending. Thus closing time was postponed for an hour. Besause of the crowd we went there twice to see the chamber. It is really worth to see it. But still we cannot say how the opening works. We waited both times until they let us to glimpse inside. The inner place of the temple is beautiful especially in the evening with all the lights shining.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Temple of the Tooth relic is the most important Buddhist Relic. Proper attire is essential to enter the temple. Covering up to knees for the men; Shoulders and up to the knee for the ladies. It is free for locals and they charge for foreigners. Shoes can be kept at flower stalls before you enter the temple for a smaller price or at the shoe counters inside the premises. The casket is locked and displayed  after the daily rituals. You can see the relic early morning at 5.00 am or in the evening at around 7.00pm for 30 minutes. You may have to stand in long queues but its worth the stand. Your not permitted to take pictures while you worship the relic up close. Remember no back to the relic when taking photos. The temple is packed during full moon days since its a National holiday.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Lord Buddha is the embodiment of peace and Buddhism is practiced by a large population in the world.Nestled in the hills of Kandy is the Sri Dalada Malgawa where the holy tooth of the Buddha is enshrined and draws the faithful from around the world. It is a three hour drive from Colombo and the temple complex occupies a significant portion of the lakefront. As a mark of respect,one walks barefoot inside the main temple-there are shoe storage centres at the entrance.There is a fee for the foreign visitor which is used for the maintenance of the temple. please maintain silence and meditate as you approach the main shrine where the divine relic is ensconced in multiple bell shaped urns.there are some pictures describing the history of the temple and the relic.the humility and deep belief in the eyes of the pilgrims is inspiring.

review_text: We went at night after the Kandyan Dance Performance. Quick 10 minute walk to temple. Make sure you have temple socks (clothing appropriate and covering knee's for men, shoulders and knee's for women). You need to take your shoes off and check them at the shoe place. Don't pay in advance, only pay the 50 rupee fee when you return to collect shoes. The scared tooth relic is locked away most times and is displayed at night at about 7.20pm for 30 minutes. Queue is long and you get the pusher in's. Worth standing in the queue though, no photo's allowed when you walk past the relic. You can take photo's from a bit further away, but you will need a good zoom lens as the relic is brilliantly light in a very reflective case. Some of the other history in the temple is well worth seeing, but do this after seeing the tooth relic. Photo's are ok everywhere else. Remember no back to Buddah when taking photo's.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple and the surrounding buildings are very interesting, with some beautiful statues and some impressive views across Kandy Lake. The entrance price is quite high for foreigners (1500 lkr, going up to 2000 in January 2017), but locals give donations to the temple elsewhere in their lives, so you can't begrudge them paying a much lower amount. It also costs around 100 lkr to leave your shoes, but make sure that they give you the correct ticket, as we almost ended up with the wrong items! Also, make sure to go to the toilet before you visit, as otherwise you have a long and painful barefooted walk to some grubby toilets where you are encouraged to give another donation. Finally, avoid all touts trying to offer you a special discount to see a Kandy dance. They are a little shameless, as the bloke who was monitoring the shoes tried to get him to go with him for a 'special performance'. Overall though, well worth a visit and a good way to spend 60-90 minutes.

The complex is nice and with the right guide I'm sure a very interesting visit, unfortunately for us one of the lower points of our trip. Be sure to get a good guide I guess is the moral of this story.

review_text: We took a guide around the shrine: he'd welcomed the queen in 1954, took Prince Charles round and two days earlier had taken the head of Unesco so he was a great choice. The men carrying flags are prisoners who have been released for religious observance which is why they have a police escort.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Kandy the cultural capital of Sri Lanka and  home to the temple of the sacred tooth this is a stunning building built around 1687.   Our party of 7 were guided through the buildings with our trusty guide Manu  knees and shoulders must be covered on both men and women sarongs can be purchased for as little as 600 Rs £3.00 ish.  We visited at  8:30 on a Sunday morning it was busy, hustle a bustle as locals attend to pray and offer their gifts to Buddha usually a mauve water lilly the flower of Sri Lanka this placed under the Buda along with jasmine flowers. This was a very moving experience. Moving through the different rooms with people stand sitting and meditating the story of the sacred tooth is depicted on 17 paintings with explanations written underneath, The detail and ornate wood carvings and plaster work are truly beautiful  pictures can be taken  throughout the temple and grounds.We were fortunate as we had been to the Esals Perahera the night before the Elephants were kept in the grounds of the temple during this 10 day festival when they put on their glad-rags and join the dancers and jugglers in the nights festivities. This was well worth the visit and another great day out

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I have visited many Budhist temples throughout asia but did not find this to be a good one. As a westerner there was not enough information available to explain the history of this building and the tooth of Budda that it is supposed to house. I saw no evidence of the tooth fragment that is supposedly taken from Budda's mouth 2500 years ago after his cremation and could not find any staff that could explain anything to me despite having paid quite a high entry price. One member of staff did tell me that I should have my nose cut off for sniffing one of the flowers which I did not feel was in keeping with the budhist philosophy. Overall I felt like I had wasted my money and there are much better experiences available in Kandy in my opinion

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple and temple grounds were vast, and steeped in culture. You can see Buddhas here that have been donated from many different countries with Buddhist heritage, including Thailand and India. We ended up getting a tour guide who was persistent, but he ended up not being that great of a tour guide. He told us that the Sri Lankan President was coming that evening, and showed us where he had previously addressed the nation. We watched the ceremony at the main ground floor shrine, which involved men in traditional wear drumming as a precursor to the opening of the shrine (similar to a south indian hindu temple). There were lots of people and a huge line-up and so we did not line up to stay and watch the unveiling of the tooth (which we were told by the tour guide is ensconced in the centre of 7 boxes - and so we wouldn't have been able to see a tooth at all had we waited). The grounds are vast and worth a walk through. We also saw the taxidermy elephant display. Lots of elephants in the area - they were getting ready for the Parehra festival that evening (which we could not stay to watch). Make sure you are fully covered - one from our party had to buy elephant pants because he was wearing shorts. The way to the temple was lined with people queing up and grabbing a spot on the ground to watch the festival from. The way is picturesque, particularly with the Kandy lake acting as the centre point. Very beautiful, certainly worth a visit.

review_text: This is a place you are told to go and see, so of we went on part of our tour. You need to wear long trousers and your shoulders must be covered. review_text: As much as I love this place, remember that it is a very common tourist attraction as well as many locals visit daily. It is common to give an offering (they sell lotus flowers) very inexpensive and is local tradition. No shoes are permitted it's free to have them kept with the concierge. Walk around the temple as well as the grounds there are lots of shrine to see.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is a really beautiful and unique temple. In fact, you won't see a temple like this anywhere else. Unfortunately the photos on the internet don't capture much of its beauty. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Before you go,you must know that you can't wear shorts or sleeveless clothes. You have to be dressed modestly ( Applies to all) There is a fee to enter the temple and usually there is a small Que to buy it. Oh as you enter you may or may not be attacked my florist who will force you to buy the Lotus for the temple. Anyway, there are prayer offerings that happen early in the morning which you can attend but it is usually crowded by tourist and mainly locals. But it's a good experience as they perform some religious hyms. There is a museum at the end of the temple which you have to pay for separately. There are other smaller galleries of artefacts and pictures which are quite informative. The walk is long and it'll take you about 45 minutes minimum to cover the entire stretch on a crowded day. Over all, It wasn't the best for me but more of a "checked out of my bucket list" kind of thing.

review_text: We visited the Temple at late morning hours. The place was crowded with people. Security check you at the first steps. Walking through the grounds and then a ticket boot for foreigners, entrance fee is 1000 RS, children under 12 are free. You take your shoes off. We have brought socks and plastic bags to store our shoes in our bags. When you go in you walk with the crowds. You'll thank me in your hart for the socks tip. Going through the halls upstairs and downstairs.  I even was invited to saw an embroidery for a statue, with a group of devotees. Try to find a side wall at the last hall where the golden Buddha statue is, kneel and absorb the atmosphere away from the cell phone screen era  and modern life confusion. This is the time to relax and listen to some Buddhist chanting before going back to the busy streets of Kandy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: As a working temple this was mad busy during the perehera so it made sense to have a guide to show us round.  You only get a glimpse of the room containing the gold casket with the tooth but watching the procession of people and being able to understand a bit more about their customs was really interesting. There is a separate tusker exhibition (including skeleton) which was worth seeing and also the inside of the temple containing Buddha's from other counties. Because of the perehera we were able to see the elephant costumes and watch the elephants being washed in the temple complex. If you can go in August then do as the perehera is quite special!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We were there when they had their ceremony at 6.30pm so it was crowded with locals and tourists queing to catch a glimpse of the Tooth Relic. The window closes at 7.00pm sharp so be early.  Nothing much inside but admired the beautiful building inside the temple.  There is a Buddhist Museum next to the temple and its worth visiting if you have the time.  Its one of the largest museums in the world.

review_text: It's a spiritual place for the buddhists, however, it's over populated by tourists (me included). It must be annoying to the locals who come to pray. It's a big compound complex with various buildings and museums (with extra charge).

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Came here during Esala Perahera. Kandy is heaving with people. Went to the temple at 11.15am AFTER the ceremony had finished and it was quieter than during ceremony times. Came here 3 years ago in April during ceremony time and couldn't move for people. Coming after 11 is much quieter and I imagine outside of Perahera and religious days it's even quieter. We had no queues anywhere. This is a working temple though. The crowds are not tourists but Sri Lankans worshiping, praying and meditating. It cost 1000lkr each to enter and 1000 for a guide to take us round. (Always ask the price first. No one offering to guide you is doing it out of the goodness of their heart!) you need to remove your shoes to walk around- If you have a backpack just put them in there and carry them, rather than paying to store them. It's a pretty building and gives you information about the story of the tooth as well as some beautiful wall paintings and frescos. Outside the gates you may see the temple elephants working. During Esala Perahera the elephants are kept outside the temple before the evening parade. Up to 20 there!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Sri Dalada Maligawa is certainly worth a visit. Strangely, it has very little to do with the teachings of the Buddha or his actual life. A series of 20 depictions in the main hall dispense with the Buddha and the Dharma in three paintings- he was born, he taught something (we're not sure what) and then he died. The rest is given over to the history of the tooth taken from his funeral pyre. Interesting but nothing to do with Dukka, the cause of Dukkha and the path leading to the cessation of Dukkha. Go for the history. Try the Buddhist Publication Society if you want to learn about Buddhism

review_text: We were in Kandy at the time of the Perahera, so expected the Temple to be busy, particularly during one of the pujas. A mass of people wanting to pay their respects to the tooth casket. Check the puja times and join the crowds. Fascinating to observe.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: August in Kandy the city takes on a mystical allure - being the month of the Kandy Festival. The temple is the cornerstone of this quite literally. It was super crowded when I visited but takes on a special significance for the pilgrams and tourists alike. The tooth of Buddha is housed in a special "vault" for its protection the story goes it was transported from India to sri lanka for this reason. Be sure to buy some lotuses for a prayer offering.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is a must see place but I found it totally overwhelming due to the hundreds of people there. In July and August it is heaving with people so If you do not mind huge crowds then you will be fine, but I would recommend you go early morning, if like me, you don't.  There are big security checks which we found out are due to a bomb being exploded there back in 1998 where 16 people were killed - so they take it very seriously.  Men and woman are segregated at the security check entrance and men get through a lot more quickly so if you are with your family remember that.  Also remember that as with every buddhist temple you will be expected to take your shoes off and for women cover your arms and legs and for men your shorts need to be below your knees.  There are hawkers everywhere selling pieces of material should you forget - cost 2016 200 rupees to loan and 400 rupees to buy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Always inspiring to visit any religion's sacred places, with the added historic allure. Lots to see in the temple, so go early to avoid crowds, but make sure you stay long enough to catch one of the three daily ceremonies. Modest attire required (knees covered; not sure about tops, but perhaps not sleeveless; covering wraparounds available at nearby flower stalls). Separate entry fees for SAARC countries vs. other foreigners. Dedicated place to drop footwear (tip when collecting). Wish there was clearer info on the Web-site about exact timing of the each of the daily/weekly/etc. ceremonies/rituals. Also wish there was clearer info about audio-guide availability.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We didn't queue up to view the tooth (it looked like a looong queue) but wandered around and there was a lot to see. Beautiful statues and decoration and plenty of space to slow down and take it all in away from the (jostling) crowds.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: 1000RPs per head for foreigners is pretty steep as there is not a whole lot to see. Although it is nice, unfortunately the temple itself is quite small in terms of things to see and the surrounding buildings are just gimmicks with pictures stuck on the walls. I would recommend going to see the Golden Temple in Dambulla as it is built near the top of a hill and is far more impressive.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This temple is a must see. It can be very crowded during July and August because of their festival dedicated to Budha. Around the temple you will find great places for food and drinks, probably the best in Kandy. Entrance fee for foreigners is 1000r.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple is beautifully decorated and very well maintained. The security is tight and during the Perahara (a festival during which elephant procession with music band and Buddha's took is taken out at around 7 pm, the crowd is very large and hence one has to come early to get a front side view along the path of procession which is worth watching and a must for Buddhists!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I didn't know anything about this temple or that we were going to visit it until we were standing in front of it. Our guide brought us here. Who knew that this was going to turn into a couple hours long visit. I thought it was the usual pop in and talk about a few features and pop out. Nope, there is a lot more to it. First, we were told the whole history behind the temple. Then you have to take your shoes off so need to go to the booth that holds them for you (which had a gigantic puddle right in front of it so you were walking through who knows what that everyone was walking through, but I was on vacation so who cares). The we went inside to admire the art and decorations. We had of course arrived in time to watch the ceremony. It is interesting for those of us who are not Buddhist to watch and listen, but let it be known that the music is loud, especially when you are standing in the vicinity of the musicians. It's no joke when I say you might want to bring some ear plugs or protection if you plan to stand in that area. Then we went upstairs and this is where the chaos happens. There was a mass of people, some in a queue and then a lot more who are not (that was us). When they were finally showing the tooth (or what I assume was the tooth), this turned into just a huge crushing mass and you couldn't see anything anyways. I will admit, this part was not pleasant nor enjoyable. After the ceremony, we walked around a bit to see a few other halls and buildings. I still think it's an interesting visit, but it felt like every tourist in Kandy was in this temple right at that moment when you are being crushed by strangers all around you. I am not claustrophobic, but it would be a nightmare for those who are. It might be advisable to skip the tooth ceremony and just go at another unpopular hour of the day to get a feel of what the temple is about.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: As part of our excursion my wife and I visited this temple, we didn't realise how many people would be there at the prayer times and it was absolutely packed! review_text: We visited this temple with our driver who doubled as a guide. Being a Buddhist, he was able to guide us through the ceremony. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Visited on a Sunday morning which is apparently a busy time and my goodness, was it busy?! A real insight into Sri Lankan culture and some wonderful things to see and experience. The tooth itself is within a golden casket and means rather a lot to Bhuddists.  The temple is still very much worth visiting for non-Bhuddists or believers however. There is a museum and other buildings within the grounds too.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If you are a Buddhist you must visit this place. To observe what Kind of things that Kandy kingdom had and their Architectural skills Temple of the Tooth is the place. You can get more information about how important this place to Sri Lankans and for Buddhist people all around the world after you visit this place. Also you can see "Magul Maduwa" next to Temple of the Tooth, the place that sign the treaty with England and Sri Lanka leaders. Also you can visit to kings palace. Don't forget to watch the museum next to Temple of the Tooth. Foreigners, you have to buy a small ticket to visit this place and it won't cost you much. Strongly suggesting to visit this place if you are a visiter to Sri Lanka.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I guess this is one of three things to do in Kandy. Visit Tooth temple, Walk around the lake, and see the festival in August. The temple has two tours every day, one in the morning and one in the evening. We were the in the evening, I think it was around 18.00. Kandy as a city is hectic and noisy. If you are visiting Sri Lanka for the first time on a holiday I wouldn't recommend more than 2 nights in Kandy. We had a plan on staying in Kandy for 5 nights and go to different cities over the day and coming back to Kandy. This is not possible due to the roads and the amount of time it take to drive from Kandy to Ella for instance. You need guide/driver to take you to the different places. I can recommend our driver "Sagara" who is one of the best and most honest guides/drivers in the country. He drove us around the entire island and helped us with everything from finding the best restaurant and guest house within our budget, and even helped us with lowering the prices on hotels so that we could afford it. review_text: I told my guide that i did not want to visit many/any temples on my 11 day trip throughout Sri Lanka. Not prejudiced or a prude, but been in Asia many years and I am templed out. However, this is a good temple to visit, has historical value and many of the standard and above average features if you are interested in Buddhist architecture and adornments. My guide suggested we go for the 630 evening prayers, it was a good choice. The idea is that there is a tooth of Buddha encased in a gold cylinder and the adherents to Buddha come her to worship and pray. You see them by the hundreds, along with the tourists who stand in long line to get a 30 sec view not of the tooth but the encasement. Lots of lotus flower offerings. Wander around the room, see the worshipers, see the gold, statutes, mural paintings and get a picture of temple life. Not sure how expensive it was, don't think it cost much and at the end of a long day a nice pre-dinner event.

review_text: To me Kandy has two major highlights, one being the tooth temple ( and the other the botanical gardens).  A sacred temple, and place of worship for the believers. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Visited this temple as part of a two day tour to Kandy. Explained to Erish, our guide for two days, that we'd like to see a temple and he said we should visit this one. review_text: I was really excited to see this ... but it feels more like a tourist attraction than a sacred place of worship. Firstly, the security guard at the entrance was extremely rude. I was wearing a floor length dress and a shawl that completely covered my shoulders, upper arms and chest. I double checked with my guide and he said I was appropriately dressed. I was initially let through by a security guard before being yelled at by the second guard who told me that I wouldn't be able to go in looking so indecent. I therefore decided to wear a coat in the 40+ degree heat which seemed to appeased her. We first walked round all the smaller temples on the outskirts which was an enjoyable experience and we were made to feel very welcome by the locals. When we went into the main temple however the atmosphere was completely different. Tourists and locals were practically shoving each other out of the way in ques to see the tooth. The buildings were also extremely grand and decadent ... which although I can appreciate for it's beauty it did't seem to uphold the essence of what Buddha is about. Finally I was extremely saddened to see that all of the main alters are decorated with real elephant ivory. It was a complete shock to me to see something like this in a country that claims to be making protecting elephants a high priority.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Excellent place to visit while in Kandy. We witnessed a lot of active worshipers in the main hall. Brilliant architecture and enchanting interiors. There is a charge of 1000 LKR for a foreigner. Basically you have to pay a visit when around, its worth the name.

review_text: It's basically the thing to do in Kandy. There are a lot of sites combines around the temple and it's an active place of worship to this day. Hence it could be very crowded on weekends. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It is most visited attraction in Kandy. The temple is very beautiful and looks even more appealing in the evening with lightings. Don’t forget to wear long pants and long sleeves as they won’t allow to enter in sleeveless cloths, skirts will work. The entry to the temple is wonderfully landscaped and very clean. The entry price to the temple is a bit too high for tourists. The museum is great for history lovers. Definitely worth visiting!!!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: An undeniably beautiful group of buildings where the importance of the site is both obvious and powerful, yet it was such a shame. Our only option for visiting was on a Saturday morning, we had heard that there may be queues but decided to brave it for such a highly regarded point both in Kandy and Sri Lanka as a whole. We knew that foreigners had to pay while Sri Lankans didn't but put aside our misgivings as Buddhism isn't our religion so it seems fair that in going, we would be making it busier for Buddhists, so paying seemed acceptable. However, we did feel that 1000 rupees was a very extreme price to pay for the privilege, especially when you consider the average price of other attractions, food and travel in Sri Lanka. (It should be added that this price is just for the temple of the tooth and not for any of the other museums and galleries inside.) We paid up and went in where we were immediately herded, pushed and shoved every which way. I can safely say that after having travelled around Sri Lanka for three and a half weeks, it is the only place where I have found Sri Lankans to be rude and inconsiderate. When we finally got to the tooth, we were so busy being pushed around and forced through that we didn't see any teeth or parts thereof. All in, it was a thoroughly disappointing contrast to a country and a people we have found to he nothing but kind, open and friendly. A real shame.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We were in Kandy for a day and since this was the top place to visit on Tripadvisor, we decided to give it a go. The architecture inside the temple was nice and there was some information about the history of the tooth and temple. We did not get to see the tooth as we visited around noon. The place was crowded with locals and children on school trips. Near the exit, there is a small museum dedicated to Raja, a tusker elephant, which died in 1988 and has been preserved. Wouldn't go back again as there wasn't much to see. Not worth the entrance fee and you have to pay additional 100LKR when you collect your shoes at the end of the visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Temple of the Tooth charges different entry fees depending on ethnicity. As one of the locals remarked; "that's not very Buddhist, is it?" We didn't think so either. This is the first I have seen of this anywhere in the world, especially at a Buddhist temple. Even in Thailand's beautiful Old City, they're happy for you to walk freely throughout the temples as long as you're respectful and in the right dress. We didn't make it past the cashier.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: During the evening ceremony the tooth is taken out of its chamber. The temple is crowded with devotees and tourists. The atmosphere is special and people line up to catch a glimpse at the golden case. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A very important tourist place in Kandy, temple of the tooth is located in the centre of the town near the Kandy Lake. The temple can be visited around 7pm when there is a ceremony in the temple, though visiting it in the evening might make you miss the places around - (museum and the palace were closed by this time and we didn't have another day to come back). The entry to the temple is wonderfully landscaped and very clean. The entry price to the temple is a bit too high for tourists.

However once inside it is a massive crush as everyone gets pushed into the room where the tooth is located. If you are lucky you get a quick glimpse of the relic. Once out of the main chamber the rest of the site is worth exploring and is less busy.

review_text: The grounds and buildings in this temple are immaculate. A museum is also located in the complex as well as other historic learning opportunities. To enter, you'll need to go through a scanner (separate male and female lines) and have your clothing assessed at the entrance. I got turned away for wearing skin tones tights, even though they were full length and I was wearing an Indian below-the-knee-length kurta. Initially I was allowed in, but someone told the officer to come get me and escort me out. I had to leave and buy an overpriced sarong at a street vendor next to the temple grounds. You'll need to take your shoes off and leave them at the official shoe station... They give you a card with a number to retrieve them later. We tipped the guy 100 rupee when we picked our shoes up. You'll have to walk around the entire complex without shoes, including outside and in the museum. There's gravel and dirt around, so your feet may get dirty if you walk in some places. Its mostly paths and stone though. There's fresh drinking water available at various locations so you can refill water bottles. You need to pay an extra 500 rupee to get into the museum. Tickets for the temple are 1000 rupee but a price increase comes into effect in August 2016 and the price will be higher (can't remember but it might be 1500 rupee)

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Glad we visited the temple of the tooth. Learned about the history better from a guidebook than an actual guide. I'm glad we read so much as the experience would have been limited without any knowledge... The temple is highly used by locals and as such is not exactly suitable for a guided experience. You are more a part of the ceremony taking place than there to see to the history. Great to see Raja after reading so much about him. Incredible that he is stuffed and his remains are still there to view! I spoke to a friend who had been and as she was unaware of the history behind it she had not even seen the elephant. Well worth taking the time to research. We were fortunate to visit in the evening during the ceremony when gifts were being taken to the Temple and worshippers were allowed access to the tooth! When the door opens you can glimpse the casing with all its jewels and is quite magical the way the room behind the door lights up around the tooth. Probably the best temple I have visited. Quite surreal with all the hustle and bustle of hundreds of worshippers, but a sense of calm and wonder... Well worth a visit in the evening (dusk)

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Like most Buddhist temples, there is a sense of calm and serenity in the temple but that is all that is there to it . First of all i find it shocking that they have an entry fee, which makes it like a commercial place. Nowhere in my country have i had to pay an entry to a place of worship of any religion (even if they are popular with tourists) that too as high as 1k. Then, as u enter u get accosted by "official" tour guides for 500. The temple is popular as it houses the Molar tooth of the Buddha but we were sadly disappointed as it is not on display. It is exhibited once in ?5 years?? felt a little cheated about that. Temple and its grounds are well maintained. review_text: We had gone in at a time a lot of people had come in for prayers and it was a great feeling to see devotees from a different religion. Although one cannot see the actual tooth of Gautama Buddha, the temple is kept very clean and organized and it is a beautiful place

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple of tooth is a fairly large complex and it took us around 2-3 hours to tour the entire area . It's one of the most visited places in Kandy and hence its quite crowded . As we entered the main complex , there was a ritual going on with some drummers playing the dhaki and puja in progress . Also upstairs where the actual relic is kept was quite crowded with locals and one actually cannot see the relic . Our guide told us that its taken out once a year on the streets . Apart form these , there are also quite a few mini temples seeped in history , with lots of ancient and religious texts and holy scriptures . The walls are adorned with old paintings . Behind the main complex is another Buddhist temple with numbered paintings depicting the origin and movement of the tooth relic and the various wars fought by the kings over it . Above this , there is a three storied museum with lot of artifacts dating back to the origins of the tooth relic ,My only lament was that the preservation could have been better - there was lot of dust inside the display cases . artifacts of this historical importance should be only kept in air-conditioned and humidity controlled environment . There are also a few gardens in the complex where you can click pics . One of the things which all guides make sure they tell you is how the complex was bombed by militants some years back and the complex was completely destroyed . One can see the extent of the damage in the pictures in the museum which makes me wonder how much of the sustaining architecture is actually old. Nevertheless it quite interesting to know such an important piece of sri lanka's history and heritage

review_text: A must see in Kandy. This is a beautiful place and has lovely gardens too. We explored the temple and saw how the locals worshipped Buddha. We usually buy flowers from outside on the road for around rs100- rs200.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the temple of the tooth in Kandy for the 9:30 offering there are 2 others in the day make sure you go then or you will miss out! We went on a Saturday so it was extremely busy with mainly locals (about 95% of those attending). You enter through male and female gates which are next to each other to check you are suitably dressed. At this point we were approached by a guide who offered to go with us. We refused and he went on his way in the end it was a good choice you don't need a guide. You walk through the grounds upto the main building. You can just follow everyone else initially as everyone is going to the temple. You have to hand over your shoes they look after them and give you a ticket to get them back for a donation. Tickets to enter the main complex cost 1000 rupees however, be warned they go up to 1500 on Aug 1st then 2000 in Jan. Unfortunately foreign tourists pay a lot at Sri Lankan attractions. The ceremony started while we were in a tragic jam of people slowly pushing to the temple. Eventually we got to the temple to see the monk go in (no one else can) and the doors close. You then follow a mass of people up the stairs to see the tooth casket to the sound of drummers and pipe playing. There is no photography allowed of the casket and you file past glancing in a window to see the wonderful gold casket. After this everything calms down and you can leisurely look around the rest of the temple site. There are various other Shrines that are well worth seeing. The main museum is worth a quick look. Don't forget the Tusker museum to see Raja the stuffed famous elephant that paraded the tooth for 50 years before his death. Overall a great spiritual experience and an essential for any trip to Sri Lanka.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: 1000 rupiah entry and leave your shoes at the door. You get given a mini dvd with information - not massively helpful to find out about what you are looking at straight always. Apparently there was a wifi tour to download too, but I couldn't get it to work - I would have liked a little leaflet and map. Nice little market to buy beautiful flower offerings outside if you'd like to leave one on the alter - I haggled hard and got one in exchange for a cigarette! Lovely building inside, and nice gardens with lanterns and artefacts. The tourist toilet is way up the back to the side of the museum if you need it (museum costs extra to enter again so I didn't go in there). Be aware you shouldn't step on the golden band across the doorway thresholds to the holy rooms - I got told off as I wasn't aware! You must cover your knees and shoulders to enter - they policed this strictly and didn't provide anything if you weren't covered - brings scarves/sarongs.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: These temples in Sri Lanka are worth having a guide or someone who know's the temple to give you some history. Our driver is Buddhist and gave us as much detail as he could as we walked around. We entered via the side entrance which was next to the Catholic Church, this entrance led us to a Holy Tree and small budda statues, then we proceeded through the elephant height arch to the Tooth Temple. Inside was very insightful and if you time your visit for 9.30am or 6.30pm you will see the rituals of offerings. I don't think we would have thought it was that amazing if we weren't being told about the history and the meaning behind the artefacts as we walked around, but it was extremely beautiful and well worth a visit.

review_text: We arrived with a guide for the evening ceremony.  We found there is so much more than just the ceremony. On entering  you hear the loud rhythmic drums and a wind instrument. The priests go behind a guilded door, and that was a cue for us to explore the Temple complex. We were told of the legend of bring Buddha's tooth to Kandy, and that there area is firstly a palace, then a temple. Paintings depict the story of Buddha, and the history of the temple. There are Buddha statues gifted from various countries here, and a library of old manuscripts. The lily displays are beautiful, and you can light a prayer lamp.

review_text: One of Buddhists Religious temples having a relic from his body. The temple is made in pagoda style and there is a charge for going inside.Only those interested religious should spend money for entrance to the temple as the tooth is not on view.

review_text: We loved being part of the local scene.  This is a temple for the people, certainly not just for tourists.  However tourists are most welcomed as long as they respect the locals as they got about worshiping Buddha.  This is a must see while in Kandy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the temple the day before the full moon there were hundreds of devotees visiting the temple at this time. Just after we walked past it was closed so the queue of people behind us did not see in. The temple is still interesting to see and read the history.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It is beautifully preserved temple with a history. Legend has it that whoever holds the tooth relic of Buddha will rule over Srilanka. The last Royal to rule Sri Lanka was brought here as a prisoner  by the British and was made to sign the surrender documents in the presence of the head Monk. This was to sanctify the British rule over the island. The temple management has done well to preserve the pristine architecture of the temple. It is very well-kept and the staff is highly devoted to it. I also had the privilege to see the casket in which the tooth is kept since I was there at the time of Darshan.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is one, if not The, attraction in Kandy. The Temple is huge. There is a small fee for foreign visitors. No shoes are allowed in the main temple. And out of respect no shorts or sleeveless tops. There is a counter where you can leave your shoes. Be prepared for a HUGE crowd in the main building where Buddha's tooth is supposed to be. I say "suppose" because you can't actually see the tooth. It's safely tucked in a well guarded room. The tooth is kept in an inner room and at certain times of the day the door to the room is open for devotees to pay their respect. There is a ceremony before the doors are open and when it is open you will have to fight  horde of pushing and pulling people rushing to see something. A select group of people are allowed closer to the door but I'm not sure what you will have to do or how much you would have to pay to get into that line. But really even they don't get to see the actual tooth. And he line is constantly moving so you can't stop to actually get a good look at whatever is beyond the door. The place is worth the visit for the temple architecture.  Ut be prepared for the crowd. If you're in the city during Poya day, which is the full moon day, you can expect two-thirds of Sri Lanka to be in the Temple!

Palace is magnanimous and beautiful. It is sight worth seeing. Most of the palace, you can move around without paying anything.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Sri Daladha Maligawa AKA The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is one of the most sacred places in Sri Lanka and the world. It is situated in the centre of Kandy, one of the World Heritage Cities. Maligawa was founded by the Great King Wimaladharmasuriya 1st in 1595. It was the royal palace at that time and the person who holds the Dantha Dhathuwa (Sacred Tooth Relic) has the governance of the country. As the history says, King Wimaladharmasuriya 1st built a two-storey building to deposit the Dantha Dhathuwa but now those buildings are no longer exists. Many years later King Rajasinghe II (1635-1687) built another temple for Dantha Dhathuwa and King Weera Parakrama Narendrasinghe (1707-1739) modified that building. The octagonal Patthirippuwa was lately added to the palace by the Last King of Ceylon King Sri Wikrama Rajasinghe (1798-1815). History also says that the Paththirippuwa was designed and made by the finest Kandyan Architect "Deeveendra Muulaachaareen". Daladha Maligawa has its own traditions and customs. Many sound poojas at different times called "Thewawa" and Hewisi drummers and pipers create a traditional sound at that time. A nice and great place to visit and experience the Buddhist culture. Daladha Maligawa has few main areas to visit. The first one is the Chamber of Sacred Tooth Relic called "Weda Sitina Maligawa". It is located in the the second storey of the building. You can see many Buddhists who are worshipping in that area and loads of blessings and hopes are flying around. There are some certain times the Casket is displayed for public. From the other side you can see the Golden Canopy which is build over the Weda Sitina Maluwa. There are 48 Gold Lotus Flowers mounted to that canopy. The next area is the Paththirippuwa. As I earlier mentioned, Paththirippuwa was lately added to the main building. You can get a finest view of the city from there. But most of the time, general public cannot access the Paththirippuwa. One of another place to visit in Daladha Maligawa is "The Magul Maduwa" AKA The Ancient Hall. You can find the best Sri Lankan traditional stone and wood carvings from there. During the Kandy Esala Perahara season, there are some traditional dancing and sound displays by the dancers during the day time. There is a Museum in the memory of Tusker Raja, who was carry the Sacred Casket for 50 years in the Esala Perahera. The body of late tusker Raja was preserved  and you can see it on that museum. There are many valuable information and ancient pictures of Raja, the clothes which he wore on the Perahara, the jewellery which Raja wore can be seen in that museum. Raja was declared as a National Treasure by the Former Sri Lankan President Hon. J.R. Jayawardena in 1988 in recognition of his valuable services to the Religion culture of Sri Lanka. Sri Daladha Maligawa is open from 6am to 9pm. There are no dress code to the temple but I think that you know what Sri Lankan culture is. Best practice is cover 75% of your body before you enter to the temple. You can buy some fresh flowers and other things which need to worship from the small buttiques near the temple. Even some food outlets are there. If you are a tourist do not visit there on POYA days (Buddhist holiday). On POYA days Maligawa is absolutely crowded. In other days you can feel whole another feeling by just spend some time there.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Cozily nestled between serene Kandy lake in one side and lush Udawatta Kele forest sanctuary in the other, Sri Dalada Maligawa deserves to be the the highlight of a tourist's Kandy trip by its own right. The complex contains the Royal Palace of the last Sinhalese Kingdom of Kandy, a Vishnu temple, another hindu temple, couple of museums (including World Buddhist Museum) and of course the most famous of them all- Temple of the Tooth-relic. Kandy was declared World Heritage Site owing to this temple. Rituals/prayers are offered in the upper prayer hall 2-3 times (not sure) daily when devotees maintains blissful silence. The main prayer hall has intricate works and decorated with elephant head statues and tusks. The tooth-relic is kept hidden in a chamber beyond devotee's view. Esala Perhara festival in August should be the ideal time to visit this temple though many devotees as well as tourists visit round the year. We ourselves visited in the month of June- a couple of months ahead of the festival. Need to visit barefoot- leaving shoe near the ticket counter. Can hire a local guide inside if someone wants to.

review_text: Look, maybe I'm cynical because I've seen dozens of temples while living in SE Asia for the past six and a half years. Regardless, this place is incredibly jam-packed. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A great, atmospheric place to visit in Kandy.  Historic and pretty well kept. Beware that you are expected to hand in your shoes and they do expect a tip even though signs say it's "free". To get round this you could keep them with you in your bag. There's the Sri Dalada Museum inside over two floors which is interesting but we didn't go into the World Buddhism Museum in the complex as it costs extra. Overall a really lovely place to visit and take in the views over the grounds.  It can get quite busy inside so expect to be pushed and shoved a bit when people are trying to take photos! Tip: don't stand with your back to the buddha i.e. for pictures as it's seen as disrespectful. Spoiler: apparently the 'tooth' is not even kept there at all!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: When you get here you have to check your shoes in at a little stand on the left of the entrance next to where you buy your tickets. When you enter people will claim you get a free guide with your entry fee, while I do not believe this is true, it's up to you if you want to accept their "guidance" I don't believe you need it though. We bought some flowers at the entrance to use as an offering, despite being foreigners the man selling flowers seemed very excited to give them to me, so I figured I was not offending anyone. You must be quiet inside the temple which was fine, we walked around and it was quite peaceful. When we got to the main area upstairs we lay down our flowers on the alter, and again no one seemed to be bothered by us doing so. Apparently the tooth jewel is only visible once a day in the morning. We were there in the afternoon and did not get to see it but it was still very enjoyable and a great photo op.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Me and my partner visit Sri Lanka and Kandy last February. One of the highly recommended places to visit is the Temple of the Tooth (Sri Dalada Maligawa). The temple is on the center of the city by the lake (amazing location). Sri Dalada Maligawa or the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is a Buddhist temple in the city of Kandy, Sri Lanka. It is located in the royal palace complex of the former Kingdom of Kandy, which houses the relic of the tooth of the Buddha. Since ancient times, the relic has played an important role in local politics because it is believed that whoever holds the relic holds the governance of the country. Kandy was the last capital of the Sri Lankan kings and is a World Heritage Site mainly due to the temple. When you go in to the temple every room is full of flowers which are brought as offerings, you can feel the vibes and the positive energy of this sacred place, a lot of locals inside praying and worshipping. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This was part of our tour along with a few more historic sites around Kandy. Our guide wanted us to begin the tour about 5 pm but we asked to arrive later so we could see the drummers & horn blower. Shoes must be removed. Knees covered and no bare shoulders. You won't be let in other wise. Ladies are vetted by a female guard and like wise - male guard for men.  The art work is impressive & colourful on arched ceilings. The alter with large Sri Lankan elephant tusks either side is equally splendid. An area was cordoned off and one loud bang announced the music was to begin.  It is very loud. Crowds filled the stair well queuing to see the stupor shaped golden shine that houses the eye tooth of the first ever Buddha. Which was smuggled out of India in a princess's husbands top knot of hair. We were allowed to go up the stairs & into the area directly opposite the golden door, which opens only briefly for those queued to pass quickly in front & view. It is hot up there, fans blow cool air but very packed & jostling to get a good view. Our guide got us there just after for 6.30 and the golden door opened about 6.45. We saw the shrine and moved on to let the crowd see it. Rather a scrum, people pushing & shoving. It smelled wonderful though with a long table filled with water Lilly flowers which are offered as a gift to Buddha. After descending we visited the octagon room and back down stairs to collect shoes. I'm glad I have seen it but if you don't like crowds go earlier in the day. This is a serious pilgrimage temple, people have travelled many miles to visit & seeing that golden door open for only minutes is worth their wait.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple is very attractive and is a "must see" if you are visiting Sri Lanka.  Too many "worshippers" of the tooth of the Buddha for my taste. Religious relics are usually of doubtful validity and may be used to manipulate the credulous.  This one is surrounded by finery which is itself worth seeing.  You won't see the tooth.  They only extricate it from its many caskets once every 10 years or so and then only for selected devotees.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I think the appeal of this temple is more about the importance of the tooth relic to Buddhists than it is about the temple itself.  Meaning, the architecture and art are all fine, but not world class.  We attended the 6:30 pm ceremony, along with about three hundred other tourists, both Euro and (I’m guessing) Sri Lankan or Indian.  There was a non-trivial entry fee, which applied to foreigners only (foreigner based on appearance, that is), which surprised me.  Also, inside, they solicit donations by parading the full line of tourists, single file, past the tooth containment room, with the entrance (and therefore view) blocked by a monk and a money platter, all the while being watched by an audience of Buddhist locals on the floor in prayer a few feet away from you.  The ceremony was underwhelming and the temple interior OK but not impressive.  I would say the entire experience was below average, felt awkward, was crowded, and cost too much.  I wouldn’t visit if I weren’t already in Kandy for some other reason.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited here with our guide on a 4 day tour in Sri Lanka. To fully appreciate the importance of this temple and the tooth relic held within, one must take the time to learn the story of Buddha and understand the deeply held beliefs of his followers, who represent over 70% of the Sri Lankan people. From the moment we alighted our tour vehicle, we found ourselves in the most beautiful flower market where you could buy floral offerings to take into the temple. The fragrances and colours of the flowers were almost overwhelming and we were drawn into the hustle and bustle of those eager to pay homage. Having been instructed previously, we were dressed respectfully with shoulders and knees covered so as not to offend the monks. We had to remove our shoes and enter the temple barefoot, feeling the stones smoothed by millions of feet. Our guide advised us to step over the gold metal thresholds and not step on them, although many others were and he was quite upset by this. Firstly, we walked around the outside of the temple where the relic is housed and then went upstairs into a large worship area, where many laid their flower offerings and prayed. All around were statues of Buddha and on the walls were frescoes telling the story of Buddha and how the tooth relic came to be. We saw lots of babies here being placed onto the floor before the statues and our guide explained that this had to be done within the first 12 months of birth. We walked past the HUGE queue of those waiting for the tooth relic door to be opened and then spent some time wandering around looking at the stunning detail in the architecture, which was quite incredible and definitely worth looking at closely. We would also recommend that you take time to explore the beautiful gardens and areas outside of the temple; museum and area where incense is lit - very peaceful and spiritual. It's amazing that the moment you step outside of the gates, you are back in the hectic city again and we would recommend that you visit early as we left at 9:30 and it was heaving!

review_text: Built by the last King of Sri Lanka, this temple is the first place of worship for all Buddhists. The temple houses the tooth relic of Lord Buddha underneath a gold plated roof. The history of this temple could be seen in pictures in the new building where the museum is located. There are restrictions whether you are local or foreign to respect the temple. A lot of things could be seen in and around the temple which is a world attraction. If you are in Kandy or happen to visit Sri Lanka, this is a place that you must visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple and the surrounding complex are vitally important in Sri Lankan history, as is the tooth relic. This shows if you visit at a time when the tooth casket is available for "viewing" (You can't see the relic itself, but you can file past a window to look at the casket.) And when I say you, I mean you and half of the city, and every tourist in it. It's unsettlingly crowded, and made more uncomfortable by a loud drumming ritual performed enthusiastically by the monks - which would be captivating if it wasn't accentuating the claustrophobic nature of people cramming up against people to observe this casket. I'm glad I've done it, but I'd be happy to watch a video in future, sitting on a couch where the nearest person is at least 50cm away from me.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: When organizing our own trip to Sri Lanka, it became very difficult to find a company who would offer bespoke tours.  Fortunately whilst at a holiday exhibition we found the Earth Trip, based in London who specialise in holidays in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Seychelles, Maldives & Mauritius, and they arranged our four days stay in Sri Lanka to our own specification. Consequently as arranged our guide/driver was waiting for us at the time specified and we left our hotel in the centre of Colombo at 7.30 am on a Monday morning.  Despite the absence of traffic on the outskirts of the city because it was a public holiday, the 75 mile drive to Kandy took a little over three hours. On the last section of the journey after the parting of the ways, where the road turns off left to Jaffna in the north, we began to climb into the hills, Kandy being at an elevation of 400 feet above sea level. The public holiday, Navam Full Moon Poya Day, commemorated the appointment of Buddha’s two chief disciples, and is therefore of great religious significance to the Buddhists, the majority faith in Sri Lanka. Kandy is famous for the Buddhist shrine of Sri Dalada Maligawa, where the supposed tooth of Buddha lies in a casket, shown to the world, only on high days and holidays, although the casket is the only visible manifestation, as no one now sees the tooth.  In consequence the area surrounding the shrine was extremely crowded, not only with Western tourists, but also Buddhists from all over the world. It was obvious who were the pilgrims, as almost without exception, they were dressed from head to toe in white, men, women and children, some carrying what looked like lotus flowers/petals as an offering. Although temple admission was a modest 1000 Lankan rupees, the volume of pushing people decided us against going inside the building, the entrance to which was about 20 feet wide, with steep marble steps, and it is mandatory to go inside without shoes.  Crushed, trodden and burnt feet (the temperatures were not far short of 100 F) would be the least of your worries!  Myriad pairs of shoes were strewn all over the grass verges leading to the entrance to the shrine, mainly cheap flip flops, therefore Western footwear would stand out from the crowd and it wouldn't be the first time that returning visitors would find their shoes gone. There are of course "touts" who will look after your shoes for a fee, but we recommend taking a bag to carry your shoes around once inside. The exit from the temple takes you out by the side of the lake, in which are two small islands, one of which the reigning King used to retreat to for contemplation.  The other is used by the monks from the monastery on the opposite bank to the temple. A small oasis opposite the temple entrance is the Queen's Hotel, dating from the colonial era and is totally white.  An amusing feature on the hotel’s rooftop is that there are two replicas of old style British police helmets.  By virtue of being Westerners, we were allowed to enter the building unchallenged and make use of the facilities. The public holiday meant that the majority of shops were closed, the exception being those owned by Muslims.  Nevertheless, the town centre had plenty of shoppers, so one can imagine how busy the town would be when not a public holiday. In retrospect it would have been interesting to see Kandy when not in the midst of a very significant festival, when everywhere was completely chaotic, and we did not have the chance to meander the town and take in what was possibly a peaceful area.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A must not only for members of the Buddhist community but also for people who are interested in Religion, Culture, History, and for people of a Spiritual nature. During puja (offerings or prayers), the heavily guarded room housing the tooth is open to devotees and tourists. However, you don’t actually see the tooth. It’s kept in a gold casket shaped like a dagoba (stupa), which contains a series of six dagoba caskets of diminishing size. The entire temple complex covers a large area and as well as the main shrine there are numerous other temples and museums within the complex. You should check the times of the various Puja's.  We attended a Puja about 10.00 am and we were astonished by the devotion, amount of people and gifts being given.  We circulated with the 100's of people and offered our gift of Water Lily's.  The jostling and the enthusiasm of people we only found out afterwards was because the Temple Doors where the casket is kept is only open for a short period. The Temple Complex is very extensive and you should allow at least 2.5 hrs to participate and view the various museums and temples included on this site.

review_text: The temple of tooth was a nice break from the hustle of the kandy streets. This is a holly place for the Buddhist people to come and worship the tooth of there teacher Buddha. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Just walking barefoot changes the perception of a place.  Often unconsciously but more often consciously we judge people by their footwear.  Walking in lines of people with no shoes is some how so humbling.  It is a place where we are all equal and are made to show respect.  Whatever your faith or belief or lack of it, it is impossible to ignore the fact that so many people regard this place as the most important focus of their lives.  At its simplist it is so beautiful.  A stunning building.  At a much deeper level it is a place to think about our own lives.  Whatever we believe in or not, it is good to reflect sometimes on what we do and where we are going in life and our responsibities to others who share this small planet.  Please visit this wonderful place or wherever you are hunt out a place of faith, even if it is not your own.  I was in Rome recently and the first religious place I visited was the Mosque.  Not what many people would assume would be the first place to go but I was as moved there as here.  Again, it was the connection with people.  We can travel and hide away in our luxury beach hotel or we can go out and connect.  An important decision which adds so much to that two week break....

review_text: This is the "must see" sight in Kandy, and definitely worth a visit. Make sure you have your shoulders and legs covered (both men and women). There is a man outside selling scarves at inflated prices for this very purpose! The temple itself is beautiful- very colourful and covered in intricate paintings and statues. The casket holding the tooth is amazing to see, although be warned, you might only get a fleeting glimpse! Downside is that it can be incredibly busy (even early in the morning), and it can feel a little like you are intruding on the people who actually come to the temple to pray, not just look. We saw some kind of ceremony which was interesting but did mean it was even busier. The temple is part of a larger complex with a few museums and other mini shrines, so it's worth looking around and not just going straight to see the tooth.

It's a must visit if you are in Kandy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the temple with our tour group.  It was very atmospheric as we went at dusk, there were hundreds of giant fruit bats flying overhead.  You need to be dressed appropriately (ladies covered knees and shoulders) as you are entering a place of worship.  Footwear must also be removed.  There is also security on the gates.  Once inside you are amongst hundreds of worshippers bringing garlands and other floral tributes to the temple. The sight of the flowers alone is wonderful.   Towards the back of the temple is an interesting pictorial depiction of the story relating to the sacred tooth.  It was very interesting and just next to the lake in Kandy.  I can see why people throng there in their thousands.

review_text: A visit to Kandy will not be complete if you have not visited the 'dalada maligawa' temple of the holy tooth relic of Lord Buddha, a ticket for foreign visitors will cost approx $9/- (SAARC 50%) which gives access to the museum too, beat times to visit is during the morning or evening pooja ceremonies, make sure you are clad with proper attire no shorts, no shirts with arms cut, ladies long dress with chest covered it's a sign of respect, no slippers or shoes you better keep them in your vehicle as there is a place for shoe keeping with a charge why bother barefoot is good for you, busy during full moon poya days, parking can be a challenge as it is the Centre of the town, annual festival of glittering 10 days of pageantry takes place in JUL or Aug which is considered to be the most colorful religious pageant in the world, enjoy Kandy and don't miss the Dalada Maligawa.. review_text: Be aware you have to take off your shoes (obviously) but then have to walk a very long way on very hot concrete so don't go when it is very hot. There are too many people, and unless you have never seen a Buddhist temple or unless you are Sri Lankan and Buddhist I really don't think it is worth a visit. We have seen quite a few different temples and some are really amazing but I am not sure that this is one of them sorry.

review_text: We went whilst staying in Kandy during a tour of Sri Lanka on holiday. We had a guide on our tour who was very knowlegeable on the Temple and the history of the Tooth which really added to the visit.  If we hadn't had a guide it could be worthwhile to do some research prior to visiting in order to get the most out of a visit and to ensure nothing is missed.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The “Temple of the tooth” in Kandy, is of such significant importance to Sinhalese Buddhists, that it’s well worth a visit to view the beautiful paintings, carvings and architecture and soak up the mysticism and culture even if you are not of the Buddhist persuasion. The history of Buddhism and how a portion of the remains of Buddha travelled to Sri Lanka and Kandy, are told in a number of panels surrounding the wall of one of the buildings – the remains and the tooth itself are too sacred to be on show and are housed in a chamber on the upper floor of the shrine.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: OK, number one this is a HUGE complex and you have to remove your shoes at the very perimeter. So a) you need to be wearing thick socks (as well as covering your knees and shoulders and removing hats) and b) I recommend stuffing your shoes out of sight into your backpack BEFORE getting to the gate, as otherwise they force you to leave your shoes with them, for a fee. Number two this place seems to be absolutely heaving all day every day - just look at the number of reviews saying how crowded it is. We fought our way into the building housing the actual tooth relic, but the queues were enormous, and it seemed from observation that people were waiting for ages and then getting rushed past the relic at top speed, so we just didn't bother. The rest of the site is more interesting and slightly less busy. The octagon room (the library) is worth seeing, as is the audience hall. We were too tired to bother with the museums. If you haven't left your shoes at the gate, it's worth trying to exit near the lakeside (to your left if you're facing the lake) and popping to the local handicrafts centre just 50m from that gate, and then walking back towards the temple's main entrance along the lakeside which is shady. Overall this may be one of the holiest places in Sri Lanka, but due to the crowds it was one of the less inspiring visits on our trip.

review_text: This is a great place to visit, a very large temple with a lot to see. One of the few places in Sri Lanka that we came across large groups of tourists. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Had originally planned to visit the evening before but ended up going on Saturday morning. It was absolutely heaving with hundreds of people taking gifts to the Buddhist monks. There was no room to move in the actual temple on the top floor and you couldn't even see the casket the sacred tooth is kept in as it was behind closed doors that the monks opened then closed every time someone gave them a ' picnic' hamper. Also tourists standing blocking peoples way taking picture after picture to the point were you just couldn't move along . On a quieter day it would have been a peaceful more pleasant experience but it was just crazy. Note of advice beware the official guides that greet you as you pass through the security entrance to the grounds. One just hooked onto us and started telling us about the history etc following us up the gardens and when I thanked him for his interest and I explained we wanted to wander around at our own pace he held his hand out and said 'Then give me some money please'. Also we had paid our entrance fee and then had to remove our footwear in accordance with the customs of the temple and paid to check them in. When we came to get them back the attendant was reluctant to give me them back until I gave him some more money at which point I had to snatch them back. It's a pity they use the excuse of a religious site to try and extract further money from you but then it is a problem at a lot of similar places around the world. Also be aware of touts hanging around outside the gates who approach you.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If u come to Kandy, you will go to see it, coz in the end its the most important thing for the buddhist here.. The 'tooth' is hidden for most of the time except some period in the morning and the ceremony which starts at 6:30 pm. Anyway, even during this time, u cannot really see the tooth, as they push you to form a queue and wait the little window open. When it is open, everyone must walk fast and there is a monk in front of it asking for donations. No photos can be taken. In the end you do not even see a tooth, only a golden case where it should be hidden. Sincerely, not worth the waiting... During the day there are families, schools and workers praying, which makes it very crowded.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the Temple on a Sunday which was a mistake. This is because it being the day Srilankan families go to the temple to worship. I was fascinated by the history of how four of Buddah's teeth were taken after he was cremated and one of it is kept here. The place was packed with worshippers carrying lotus flowers and fruits, going up the stairs where the service was taking place at the holy sanctuary where the tooth relic was kept. the drummers were playing their drums. Mobile phones rang. Babies cried. People pushed and shoved each other holding their cameras or mobile phones high to take a shot as the doors opened to reveal the tooth relic (container). Some tourists even tried to take selfies with their backs to the holy sanctuary. It was very disappointing to see tourists behaving in a disrespectful way inside this Buddhist Temple. Worshipers should be allowed to worship peacefully without being pushed about. It would be better to ban cameras  inside places of worship or have organized tours for tourists at different times that does not interfere with local worshipers.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: There was something about this that felt very sacred and spectacular. After seeing the shrine itself you go into a room which shows in a number of pictures the story of Buddha and how his tooth is now kept in the shrine we had just seen. So from seeing this we then understood the importance of where we had just been. We saw many monks walking through and locals who seemed really pleased to be there and we spent around an hour and a half slowly walking around taking in the sights.
