review_text: Make sure you are not wearing a short when visiting the temple, otherwise you won't be able to get in. once you go inside you will remove your shoes and start following the people visiting the temple. i advise you to visit when a religion ceremony is taking place to have the best out of your visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If you're visiting Kandy a trip to The Temple of the Tooth is a must. The most sacred place for Sri Lanka's Buddhists who believe the a tooth of the Buddha resides there. This is an impressive temple which manages to be both powerful and serene at the same time. Take time to look around the series of pictures which depict the journey of the tooth to it's current resting place, though you're unlikely to see it as it's only on public once every four years. I don't think this detracts from the experience at all. There was also an interesting little museum to Raja, a tusker elephant, who had served the temple for 50 years.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of Tooth is an amazing place.  I would definitely recommend getting a guide as they explained so much that I would never have realised. The tour took about 40 minutes. It was busy and very hot so I would advise taking a bottle of water with you.  Overall a great visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We loved having the opportunity to visit this sacred place with so many devotees.  We went on a Sunday morning, so it was very busy, which only added the authenticity of the experience.  People brought lotus offerings to the tooth relic (don't know how Sri Lanka has any flowers left!), and waited in anticipation for the opening of the relic room, so we could glimpse only the enclosure for the tooth relic.  It's a shame people did not have any orientation to the superstition/beliefs that make this significant to the Buddhists in the country.  We were fortunate to have a fantastic driver/guide who shared his beliefs with us.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: According to our guide/driver, we visited on a relatively quiet day.  In which case, a busy day must be like Oxford Street, London just before Christmas. The Temple itself is beautifully decorated and the thrice daily ceremony (puja) in the Drummers' Courtyard is impressive, if somewhat cacophonous.  The Tooth Relic Chamber on the upper floor is packed with pilgrims and you have to queue to get in - and then get only a distant view of the shrine itself.  On the way out it is worth seeing the Rajah Tusker Museum with its stuffed elephant that carried the Tooth on its travels for over 50 years. If you are in Kandy, this is well worth visiting, but I'm not so sure that it merits a special trip, except to say that you have been there and 'done' this famous site.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth contains the remains of a tooth of Buddha. The actual tooth is stored in jewelled boxes inside a bell shaped casket knows as a stupor.  It is locked in an inner room but the doors are opened at certain times of the day. It is worth visiting in the evening for the atmosphere. Shoes have to be left at the entrance but the stones have been worn smooth after countless pilgrims have visited and are not dirty.  Outside the walls are plain white, carved to give a lacey/filigree effect at night time when they are lit.  Once inside the entire place is richly carved with inlays of ivory and gold. Inside is an inner chamber with a large wooden door ornately decorated with bronze and ivory. Huge elephant’s tusks stood in front of the square known as the Drummers Courtyard.   In front of this were men in costume drumming.  Try to get to the upper chamber early and  get your position for the ritual opening of the doors of the shrine being opened. Stand behind the long offering table opposite the doors. During the lead up to the ceremony monks in Orange robes and worshippers in white were wandering around and the sound of drums, conch shells and trumpets seem to reverberate round the walls. When the golden doors open you will  see the huge bell-shaped stupor covered in jewels. It is definitely something to remember.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited this Temple on Saturday.  It was very busy and raining so it wasn't very pleasant walking around with bare feet.  Carried along with the crowd but was attractive and interesting.  Guide attached himself to us but at least he showed us where to go and explained things a bit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Amazing how people from many continents and locals from all walks of life congregated at this famous temple on a Sunday morning. Lotus flowers were on sale, white and blue attracted me. I selected the beautiful blue ones . Huge rush of humanity, yet there was hardly any jostling. Huge drums and the trumpets echoed within the temple. Photography is allowed. Inner sanctum Santorum is silver, bedazzling! One has to take of shoes and park the at a designated place against a token. No payment required, yet some were paying handsomely (just to store shoes?). When I stood and prayed with my offering of flowers, no one jostled me. We all smiled readily at one another! Having walked around bare feet within the temple when I came out I expected my feet to be dirty, but they weren't. But there was a tap to wash your feet if you so wish. I came back filled with peace wondering, why can't the outside world be life this? Always?   ******* Shyamal

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I was looking forward to going here but came out with a slightly sour taste in my mouth. Although it is a very attractive holy place, as foreigners we could not help but feel exploited with the high entrance fee. For 2 of us we paid in total 2200 LKR for a half hour visit when the locals pay nothing. I don't like it when holy places charge a fortune to get in and discriminate against visitors. Plus they use the shrine to get money from locals by charging extra to get into the ante-room in front of it. Also not in it's favour is that it is mobbed by people including battallions of school children so it's probably a lot better to go at 5.30am like a friend I know did, if you can get up that early. I'm quite spoiled as I've been to Angkor Wat, Shwedagon Pagoda, the Taj Mahal and Hampi - but although they all charged foreign visitors more than locals, I felt they were worth it - not so with this place. Nicer to walk around it on the lake front and enjoy the pretty setting of Kandy for free.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If you go there during one of the set ceremony times, be prepared for a very large group of people (both local residents and tourists). It can get hectic, with a lot of noise, shoving (tourists with cameras and little consideration for others) and crying babies (many bring their children for blessings). The ceremony involves drums, and the sound reverberates around the walls and it can get uncomfortably loud. The temple is a beautiful structure to see, and the grounds have a lot of history to tell. Definitely recommend this, but if I had to do it again, I would avoid showing up during the ceremony.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: You can't really travel all the way to Sri Lanka and not visit the Temple of the Tooth. It is an extremely popular tourist attraction but naturally attracts many Buddhist pilgrims as well so it is crowded and quite hectic. Having said that I am glad I made the effort.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This was one of many temples we visited during our visit to Sri Lanka. We went in the morning and were there when the door to the room that houses the tooth opened to the worshippers. This was the one time we felt frustrated with the normally peaceful people. There was too much pushing and shoving and could not wait to get out! Beautiful statues and paintings of Buddha and his life. Interesting cultural experience. As with all the temples, shoulders and legs are to be covered. I wish we'd had our sarongs at this point of the trip. The stones were very hot and it would have been a good idea to bring socks to walk around after our shoes were stored.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It's better if you can go there before 7am in the morning. Otherwise it would be so much crowded. If you can go early without a rush you can see the beauty of this place and will feel how much it is sacred. It's very difficult to explain what I felt in every time when I'm there. You must go there, then you will know this.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: An interesting insight into Buddhism but you wont see the tooth.  We went at procession time and only managed a passing glimpse of the casket behind glass at some long distance amidst the vast crush of people.  You will get a good feel and understanding of temple life.  At times the mass of humanity did feel quite unsafe as we were swept along by the crowd.  Our guide forced a passage through for us which was helpful but did involve a lot of pushing and shoving.  If you have an aversion to being in crowds this would not be a place for you at procession time.  Also on the site are a  number of interesting buildings and museum. Note that men must cover their legs in order to get in, so take a pair of trousers or men's sari to put on. The temple is worth a visit but be prepared!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is more than just a temple. There are lots of different rooms and houses you can enter. There is small museum which reports about the history of the temple with a few antique originals. Most of the temple was destroyed and rebuild, but it is still nice to see. You cant see the teeth of Buddha because it is locked behind a few doors. The outside of the temple is very pretty, with lots of trees and plants. Also a lot of locals come to pray, so at least it is not a Tourist trap

review_text: So the tooth of Buddha is here but don't expect to actually see it.  It is hidden well back in the temple seen thru a window that opens once an hour, and you (and a hundred other) must be *right* in front of that window looking 50 feet down a vision tunnel.  But, just the show is worth watching.  Fabulous grounds and lots of people.

review_text: We knew about the Temple, but this wasn't a plan to visit it, just made a break in Kandy for a night before going from Segiria to Nuwara Eliya and went to look around in the evening. Fortunately decided to enter))) The ticket price is 1000 rupees, but for me the price was duble as I wasn't properly dressed - have to buy some stuff to cover shoulders and legs,but it is worth it, especially the area around the Temple - very consiliatory: lake, sunset, not hot, but the stones on the floor were nice and warm, which is good as you are not allowed to enter the Temple in shoes and need to give it for storage to a man who will ask for donation... so if you got stuck in Kandy and looking for harmony you have a chance to find it here,good luck!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited in late afternoon and attended the 6h30 ceremony. Our guide who is a buddhist took us to the right place and during the ceremony we lined up to go upstairs and you get to parade very briefly in front of the famous tooth. We then saw a few important parts of the temple. Going to that ceremony is great and this temple is truly amazing. A must see (and god knows we have seen a lot of temples on this trip).

review_text: A visit to the Temple of the Tooth really is something you should do when you are in Kandy.  However, if you go during the time that the tooth relic is on view then be prepared for crowds and for being sandwiched between tourists and Sri Lankans if you want to file past!

review_text: You will be able to see the sacred tooth relics of the Buddha once you entered the temple. We are also allowed to take photos with the tooth relics. Do not miss the Temple of the Tooth!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I'm used to taking pictures of everything when I travel, but at the Temple of the Tooth I had to put my camera away. Not because you aren't allowed to take photos there - you are - but because it didn't feel right. You're visiting this place as a tourist attraction, but the locals and people from all over Sri Lanka are coming here to meditate, pray and pay respect to the Buddha. When I entered the room where the shrine with the tooth is kept, I felt like an intruder, afraid to show disrespect. This is not to say you shouldn't visit. You should definitely visit. The temple is very much worth it and will leave a huge impression on you. Just realize this isn't just a tourist attraction but also a very active place of worship.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Went to visit this temple on our last day in Sri Lanka. Unfortunately it was new moon or full moon celebration day and it was packed. I mean absolutely jammed packed solid with people. It was a human stream from the entrance door all the way to the exit along which we just got carried. Didn't get any opportunity to break out of the flow and look around, not that we could have moved around much anyway. All we could really see was the ceiling and tops of the walls. I do have some great photos of the tops of people heads tho. Took us 45 minutes to just make our way through..   So top tip, avoid the festival day to visit this temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It is located in the royal palace complex of the former Kingdom of Kandy, which houses the relic of the tooth of Buddha. The best time of the year to visit is during the Esala Perahara season which falls in August. It is a grand festival with elegant costumes, elephants and much more.  It is the only time where the tooth relic is taken out of the royal complex and allowed the common public to see and worship it, outside the temple. The nearest place to stay near is the Queens Hotel. It provides an excellent view of the perahara (Procession). But it is extremely hard to reserve the place during that time of the year. And please note that gents should wear long trousers and shirts with sleeves. Shorts are not allowed in the temple. White or a light colour is preferred. For the ladies also above rule applies. The temple is opens at 5.15 am and closes at 8 pm.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: At the entrance to the temple anyone attempting to talk to you will be a guide. Even if they just seem to be trying to start a conversation. Politely but firmly say no thanks and walk inside quick! The temple is best enjoyed on your own unless you really need to know all of the history. It's especially amazing during the flower offering times.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Visited at night, when the temple is lit up and bathed in golden light. This does seem to be a popular time and the crowds are ferocious. The temple itself is beautiful (quite different from other Sri Lankan temples), with British and other influences. Don't expect to see the tooth, it only gets shown one day every four years.

review_text: Dalada Maligawa is a lovely place to visit along with family. We started early morning from colombo and reached Kandy around 10 am had breakfast, only sandwiches and tea available for vegans. Then we went around the temple, it was so unbelievable to see the tooth relic of Lord Buddha. It was a serene and subtle spiritual environment and one of the best holy places one must visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A lot to take in - drummers, the opening of the chamber where the tooth relic is stored, the pictorial story of the birth and history of Buddhism.  Be prepared to be jostled - it was extremely crowded, but still very friendly and gentle.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We were advised to arrive early as that's the best time, I'm still not sure why. My partner was wearing shorts so they used my scarf to fashion a sarong for him as, to our shame, we'd forgotten this wasn't appropriate attire. As we approached the temple it was charming to see lots of children in their white uniforms hurrying to join the massive queue before the security screening gate. We were ushered to a counter to pay separately and kept close to the entrance by security, I found this confusing, why were the locals being kept back? It became apparent. Whilst waiting you can hear the drums of the monks and it's all very atmospheric. A lady security motioned us forward, a man security stopped us and then the tide of locals running to get to the shrine first nearly took us out! I didn't realise Buddha gave his blessings on a first-come-first-served basis! We followed people up the stairs and I gave the offering of the lotus flowers to the monk, who unceremoniously tossed them onto a table to join the rest. I didn't know that that hatch is where you look to see the shrine of the tooth before being shoved forward by the throngs. Then I stood on a cockroach in my bare feet, not very Buddhist! For fear of sounding like an utter philistine a leaflet on what happens and where would have been helpful! As it was, most of the rest of the complex wasn't open at that time. It is a beautiful place and a unique experience.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This Sacred Budest Temple  is one of the most important Buddist sights in Sri Lanka, and is a must see in Kandy. Allow 2hours of your time and have a good guide, as it's very large and has a lot of areas to see. The museum inside has great information on the bombing of this sacred sight, and the exhibits are very interesting. (Make sure you are not wearing shorts and have scarves or suitable clothing before entering as the armed guides at the entrance will not let you enter). You will find this to be one of the busiest temples that you will see as its followers and tourists are in great numbers. Well worth a visit!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: While I dint really appreciate that they don't show the actual relic of tooth (creates a doubt that perhaps it doesn't even exist and this is all for getting donations and entrance fees like many temples across India?), it still is worth a visit. One of very few temples where entire history is depicted in few clearly designed paintings and writings. Beautiful architecture; looks even more scenic when it rains - imagine walking barefoot in small puddles of fresh rain water!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Family of four recently visit the Temple of The Tooth Relic, I had visited 20 years ago and had not realised the impact the bomb had made to outside the temple, it is actually much better for visitors with the railings & security around the temple, our driver had recommended we hire a guide and he was spit on, our driver booked our guide for us in advance & also booked us front row seats for the Kandy Dancing. Our guide for the temple was excellent, cost 1,000 rupees ( £5 ) he obviously knew all the main vantage points, short cuts & got us into prime positions to see many sights. He spent 90 mins with us and our two children found his talks fascinating and we all learned so much. We gave him £5 tip and he was so grateful. Allow yourself 2 hours and if you can do temple in afternoon before watching dancers, then if you wish you can go back over your tracks without your guide. You see so much once you know the story.

review_text: The most important Buddha's sacred place on Sri Lanka, Buddha Tooth relics temple. review_text: This is a two part review. Part one. The temple itself is a beautiful, historic landmark. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic

The approach to the temple has statues which commemorate important events in Sri Lanka's history and a good guide or guidebook helps the interpretation of these. I'm sorry Invictus (see below) didn't find Kandyan people friendly - we had a lovely rest in a little fresh-juice bar just by the temple while we waited for a young lad to try and mend my friend's mobile phone. The door containing the unbelievably ornate cask is only opened on occasions, but the feeling of calm and peace within the room is overwhelming, despite the crowds.  There are queues, so be prepared.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Visit timed to see the morning ceremony which was amazing- starts with devotee bringing the key to open the elaborate silver doors where the Budda's tooth relic is kept. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth Relic, at the top of the lake near Kandy town centre, is a very important part of Buddhist culture in Sri Lanka.  It is a very significant place of worship for Buddhists. The ceremony is interesting and it is certainly worth the visit. During prayers, the Temple can be very crowded, in the evenings in particular. You will also need to wear clothes that cover your legs and your shoulders, and remove your shoes - which are kept at the entrance for a small fee. Be mindful of guides touting their services though. Don't miss the ceremony of the opening of the lower chamber - rituals are performed three times daily. Only the monks have access to the inner chamber, but you can feel the history and importance of this place hanging in the air.

review_text: We visited early evening. There was a huge queue but once in the room containing the relic it became very dangerous with a terrible crush of bodies. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A small group of us visited at around 6:30pm just as a ceremony was starting. As soon as we entered the grounds a man told us he would be our guide. It was extremely busy due to the ceremony and the queue to see the tooth room was extremely long. It is quite difficult to work out what's going on so perhaps an official guide would have been helpful. It was an interesting visit but slightly spoilt by the overcrowding. We were there for about an hour. Quite nice to enter in daylight then see it all lit up once the sun has gone down.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It is important - historically and culturally, and it is the main sight in Kandy. That being said - the place is pretty boring, and also definitely overpriced for what you get. So my advice is - if you are on a tour around Kandy and you are interested in traditional culture / history; it is worth a visit. Otherwise there many more temples around Sri Lanka that are much less touristy - and allow you to see an actual ceremony and dive into the way locals visit the place.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: What's not to like? It holds a sacred tooth relic of Buddha, and therefore holds a significant importance to Sri Lankan people. It's no museum, it's where people of Kandy come every day to pay their respect and put flowers on table. Just being here and watching people come and go as they put flowers on and pray is really amazing cultural experience, the best experience you can have in Kandy. Most tourists just come around one of the ceremony times(three times a day) and see the tooth relic and go, but I suggest you visit a hour or so beforehand to fully comprehend its atmosphere. Don't forget to head downstairs before the ceremony is over so you can watch the real drummers playing those ceremonial beats during it takes place!

review_text: we had a problem - a bad guide (he pretended that the place is built by scottish slaves that Brittish have brought here, and that the last king of Kandy was killed by Englishmen with all his 1000 wifes and all his children, even babies). We were shocked - the guy had his licence but he has never read a book or site about the history of the kingdom of Kandy. The last king who was crowned as Sri Vikrama Rajasinha (when he was 18) was indeed deposed by the British in 1815 (ending over 2300 years of Sinhalese monarchy) but he and his 2 wifes lived calmly in Vellore Fort in southern India (as he was of Nayak Kings who were Telugu Buddhists and spoke Tamil). He died of dropsy in 1832 aged 52. As for Scottish slaves I'd like to assist this guide at his guiding somebody from Scottland... As for the sight, we were diappointed having expected more couleur locale. Well built, proportionnal, good stuff. The best place in Kandy. the tooth relic was brought from Kalinga, India by Princess Hemamali and her husband (her father was the intiator, the tooth was hidden in her hair) at the beginning of the 4th century (in Anuradhapura, of course), The builder of the present day temple, the king Vira Parakrama Narendra Sinha (1707–1739 AD) was the last Sinhalese King of the Kingdom of Kandy. He reigned for 32 years, had no children and that's why the crown passed to his wife's brother (from the Madurai Nayak Dynasty, southern India). The actual chamber which the tooth relic (within seven golden caskets) is called the "Handun kunama". The golden canopy is built in 1987.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth Relic, at the top of the lake near Kandy town centre, is a very important part of Buddhist culture in Sri Lanka and is a very significant place of worship for Buddhists. While you won't get to see the Tooth Relic itself (a tooth of the Buddha), as it is kept in a gold casket, the ceremony is interesting and it is certainly worth the visit. During prayers, the Temple can be very crowded, in the evenings in particular. You will also need to wear clothes that cover your legs and your shoulders, and remove your shoes - which are kept at the entrance for a small fee. Be mindful of guides touting their services though.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited this temple whilst on honeymoon in Sri Lanka. We were very fortunate to have a guide throughout our trip and this meant were able to get a good feel for the historical and cultural significance of the sight. However, the Temple itself has an audio guide and a few signs in different languages for those without a guide. At specific times during the day there are ceremonies where the monks enter a holy inner sanctum to worship (pay respect) and bring offerings. This is quite a spectacle, with ceremonial instruments being played throughout. Photographs were allowed, however we felt a bit uncomfortable with this. We also saw the Temple elephant who is commissioned to carry the relic, as well as a museum containing his stuffed predecessor. There is also a museum where you can see the devastating effects of the suicide terrorist bombings. It's insisted that all visitors entering the Temple take off their shoes and wear clothing that covers the knees and shoulders. This produced no issues, apart from areas outside where the ground was slightly hot (so maybe take socks). Overall, you can't come to Kandy without visiting the Temple and it has definitely enhanced our understanding of Buddhism.

review_text: We visited the temple after the Kandy Dance show which is held in the Red Cross Hall nearby along the lake. The setting is beautiful on the side of the lake and the history and architecture fascinating. The Temple was the palace of the last king of Kandy and the king also had a temple in the palace where the tooth, the most important relic in Sri Lanka, was kept. When the British defeated the king and took over the palace they moved out because part of the palace was a temple and the whole palace became a temple. The temple is beautifully maintained. It was busy because we went at a time when the room housing the relic is opened, but this emphasised how important this temple is to Buddhists.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is one of the most famous temples in Sri Lanka and it's easy to see why. When you walk in, you immediately get a feeling of calm. He also made it interesting and fun for our children whilst ensuring they remain respectful. Well worth a visit but take a guide to get the most out of it.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We had a very nice visit on the day of the election in Sri Lanka, so relatively less people.  Were arrived apparently at a good time, 9.15, the morning ritual was about to begin. A very friendly and enthousiastic guide led us through the temple and explained everything as good as he could. He spoke too fast at times but could be slowed down! When we reached the upper shrine, we were part of a large queue that led to a very brief glimpse of it, which made it enchanting and magical. Of course, the drumming should have been more passionate, his face was tiresome and bored. The same goes for the man who kept moving the queue forward (after 2 seconds) in front of the shrine. But not surprising when so many people come along and don't understand a thing and just take a look around for touristic reasons. Nice park with memorable monuments surrounding, beauitful view with the lake alongside. Demonstrative was the statue of a seemingly up in arms, throwing the British flag on the floor. Moving also the special museum in honor of the oldest tuskers of the annual Esala procession, Raja Atha. The guide, taking his time to lead us through the old and newer, international parts of the temple with gifts from many other countries, not rushing us and spending our money in the temple to give a little donation to guards to get through, finally  took us outside to a hindu (Tamil) temple which was smaller but demonstrating the broadmindedness of this place.

review_text: Is this the same a visiting Wat Pho in Bangkok? No, but then there are not all the touts trying to rip you off just outside the area either!  Is it an important historical sight that you should visit when in Sri Lanka - yes. The temple grounds are not that large.  Make sure to abide by the local Buddhist requirements - men to have pants that go below the knees, women to have shoulders covered.  Shoes are taken off and held in a storage area for 100Rs. It is a pretty quick tour once in the temple part.  There are hundreds of people (depending on the time of day there are special ceremonies taking place) awaiting the chance to get close to the tooth relic.  You do not actually see it, but there is a video playing of an earlier time that it was taken out for a ceremony by the guardian. Whilst you don't get to see the tooth relic, you do have many other interesting exhibits and parts to the temple that make it an interesting experience.  It is 1000Rs to visit, however, if the money is being used in the correct manner, then the payment is worth it.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is an obligatory cultural visit when in Kandy. This is so because of its importance in Buddhism worldwide and to the people of Sri Lanka. We attended the evening puja, which is very carefully choreographed, due to the large numbers of people attending, but very moving due to devotion of most of those attending. The lower floor has impressive drummers and beautiful surroundings. The upper floor is where the tooth is stored in its concentric gold caskets in an inner chamber. The closest you will get is the door of this inner chamber, 3 m from the casket, after a very long queue. Nonetheless, the casket is impressive. Despite the sheer numbers, the temple exudes calm, peacefulness and the devotion of the pilgrims. Do visit the octagonal tower, where a monk gives blessings every evening in a most beautiful room. It has to be said, however, that it is deeply disappointing to be charged entry fees to such an important religious centre, but Sri Lankans never miss a chance to relieve tourists of their money - it is truly a national sport. A pity, as they'd probably make much more from voluntary donations. The funniest thing during our visit was an ancient Sri Lankan gentleman encouraging visitors to sit down on a plastic chair by the shoe depository to put on or take off their shoes. This was next to a stone bench located there for the purpose. He'd then charge the visitor for the privilege of sitting on the chair that wasn't even his! Priceless!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This temple is where the tooth relic of Lord Buddha resides. This is considered as the holiest place of worship by the Buddhists. The temple consists of several  buildings which includes the inner  chamber (weda hitina maaligawa ) where the tooth relic is located ,outer temples a museum where the history of the tooth  relic  can be seen, special  museum where the body of the tusker "Raja " who served the tooth relic  for a long time during  the annual  perahera ,  and the temples dedicated to several    gods To see the replendent casket within the inner chamber you need to go to the temple during the "Thewawa" the service.  The times are daily at 05.30-07.00, 09.30-11.00 and 18.30-20.00 Monks of the two chapters of Malwattu and Asgiriya conduct daily worships in the inner chamber of the temple. On Wednesdays, there is a symbolic bathing of the sacred relic with an herbal preparation from scented water and fragrant flowers called “Nanumura Mangalya”. This holy water is believed to contain healing powers and it is distributed among those present.please have at least half a day set aside if you intend  to do the complete tour of the temple  and if you want to see the inner chamber and the casket  then you should time your visit to coincide with the times of thewawa.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Sri Dalada Maligawa was the last Buddhist Kingdom in Sri Lanka. The place is a sacred shrine as well as the palace where the Kandy Sinhalese kings resided. According to Buddhist traditions a sacred tooth of Buddha is required to ordain a king to rule as a Buddhist Kingdom. As such the name of the place suggest that "dalada" means tooth and "Maligawa" Kingdom. It's well worth the visit to see the beauty of the old Kandyan architecture. The history of the people is written in these stones. The Kingdom finally fell to the British, who took the reigning king to India to be executed as well as killed the next in line, a 9 year old boy. There the ruling line ended.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A visit  here satisfies just about every craving for Asian culture. The architecture, the ceremonies, religious observance, quirky exhibits and carnival madness. Give yourself over to the place but make sure you're there for one of the three daily ceremonies when the drums thump, the door to the Buddha's tooth repository opens and hundreds of devotees and tourists swarm for a glimpse (a glimpse, mind you, of the container only) which is another room. Don't miss the shrine to Rajah, the huge stuffed elephant who led the annual tooth parade for more than half a century. You may not turn your back on Rajah for a selfie. I would recommend visiting in August for the annual parade. It must be a hoot.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is a charming old Buddhist temple from around 1000 years back, The temple hosts the tooth of Gauthama Buddha which was smuggled into Sri Lanka during 300 AD. The relic is considered very powerful and is of significant importance to Buddhists and Sri Lankans in general. The temple is heavily guarded by SriLankan military due to multiple attacks in the past by extremist elements. The sanctum sanctorum is not very fancy and you will see a lot of people praying in silence in front of the Tooth relic golden room. There are couple of museums and places to see inside the entire Temple complex and can take a leisurely 2-3 hr walk to cover it all. Worth a visit if you are in Kandy. LKR 1000 to enter.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This temple is fantastic in its architecture and its significance to Buddhists. Entry fee is 1000 LKR for foreigners and 500 LKR for SAARC country citizens only. Carvings at the gates, pillars and wall murals are splendid in design. In the first floor, there is a golden casket which keeps the tooth of Lord Buddha and you can see only the casket itself which opens at specific timings only. Apart from that, there is a hall with large size Buddha statues, Buddhist museum and a life-size elephant (taxidermed actual elephant named Raja) to be seen. However the museum closes at 7PM though the temple remains opened. We have visited at 6:30 PM, at the prayer time and seen the golden casket but missed the museum and it got closed at 7PM. Quite a good size complex and you have to enter bare-foot (shoes can be kept in kiosk, separate for foreigners and you can just keep donation of LKR 20-50 later to the persons looking after the shoes). A must visit in Kandy.

Frankly I was expecting to visit, not a tourist attraction but a place of Buddhist cult, if you seek an atmosphere of peace and spiritual harmony, forget it, too many people around, who are there just recalled by the appeal of the Buddha tooth, you can walk around the temple just to spend your visit, appreciating the new architecture which is built  around the old sancta sanctorum where is preserved the relic. I was not impress by this visitation to the temple, except for the price of the ticket, the temple museum may offer more interesting attractions if you want to know about the Buddhist history of Sri lanka, and the temple regency. However next to the tooth temple you will find the walled perimeter which encloses the ancient temple, there you will finally please your expectations and have a chance to admire some golden statues of Buddha, in sitting and reclining position, that is the real thing which Buddhist come to offer their devotion.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Kandy is the second capital of Sri Lanka. Kandy is world famous for the Temple of the Tooth, which safe keeps the Lord Buddha’s Tooth Relic venerated by the Buddhists all over the world. There are also many sites with Kandy Architecture prominently displayed, specially at the Dalada Maligawa (Temple of the Tooth Relic) , Lankatilaka Temple and Embekke Temple, to name a very few. The traditional Kandyan Architecture consist of Temple Structures, Murals done on walls and on stone in many temples, Carvings and reliefs done on Stone and decorated Wooden Carvings on timber columns and brackets. Relics of the Lord Buddha is venerated by all Buddhists throughout the world and the relic at the Dalada Maligawa is the left Canine Tooth of the Lord Buddha which is one of the remains of the cremated body of the Lord Buddha after the Parinirvana. It is said to be removed by the Arahanth Kema, who is a pupil of the great Arahanth Sariputta and given to King Brahmadatta of Kalinga, India. For centuries it was venerated and homage was paid by the Buddhists of Kalinga. During the time of King Sirimeghavanna (301 - 328 AD ) of Anuradhapura, the Tooth Relic was brought to Sri Lanka by Prince Dantha (son of the King of Udeni ) and Princess Hemamali ( daughter of King Guhasiva ). During a war waged to obtain the posession of the Relic tooth by the nephews of King Pandu against King Guhasiva, this was brought to Sri Lanka by Hemamali and Danta in the guise of Brahmins and the Tooth Relic was hidden and concealed in Princess Hemamali's hair. Dantha_Hemamali A mural depicting Hemamali and Dantha bringing the Tooth Relic to Sri Lanka. The Lord Buddha Tooth relic which is presently at the Dalada Maligawa was brought to Kandy during the rein of king Vimaladharmasuriy I and he made a two storied Palace to place the Tooth Relic. During the first few centuries , it had been placed at Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa, Beligala Rock, Dambadeniya, Yapahuwa, Kurunegala and Kotte kingdoms. Due to Portugese invasion it was taken away by Buddhist priests to a mountanous region of Kandy and once Kandy was under the rule of the king, it was brought back again. Later King Vimaladharmasuriy II ( 1687-1707 AD) had made a three storied Tooth Relic Palace. King Parakrama Narendrasinghe ( 1707-1739 AD ) has also build a two storied temple for the Tooth Relic. The Last King of Sri Lanka, Sri Wickrama Rajasinghe made the Octagonal Building called “ Pattirippuwa” and the moat in front of the Palace. The approach to the Temple of the Tooth Relic and the views of Front of the Temple, the Moat and the Octagon Building or the Pattirippuwa.

review_text: The Temple Of The Tooth is an incredible place to visit in Kandy. As a tourist I decided it would be best to pay for a guide (600LKR after some bargaining) who took us round. We learnt so much about Sri Lankan history and Buddhism and would fully recommend this to anyone.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If you are interested in Sri Lankan culture, this is definitely a must see in Kandy - not just for the temple itself but to immerse yourself in the culture and observe a place of large significance for locals (and Buddhists) . While there are lots of tourists around, the best part for me was seeing the people pray and engage in their rituals. We did not use a tour guide, however our driver (YES - get a driver in Sri Lanka!! it is affordable and SO worth it if you are crunched for time. We have a reliable and safe recommendation if anyone is interested) gave us his own tour. People have stated they were happy to have gotten a tour guide, however I did not feel the need. There is a lot of walking if you choose to view the whole temple, so be aware if you go at the end of the day as we did, so tired :)

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is only decent to watch how Buddhists worship and admire something so sacred to them (ie Buddha's alleged tooth). The tooth is not actually for viewing. You pay 1000 Sri Lankan rupees (£5) to enter if you're not Sri Lankan (they pay 100 rupees- 50p).  This just gets you to see the tooth which is not actually on view. The thing we hated most was that you have to go inside barefoot.  In the pouring rain this means you get wet and very dirty.  If you do go, bear this in mind and take a cloth or towel to wipe your feet afterwards (or go wearing sandals / flip flops).

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I am not Buddhist however I appreciate visiting places of worship when I travel and believe I do so with quiet respect. The Temple of the Tooth was a place recommended, especially the evening service. We arrived at 6.30pm suitably dressed only to have our attire checked by a rude, dismissive lady as we passed through the corrals. Next we parted with 1000 rupees each at the gate. At this stage we felt herded along as the heavens opened (possibly a sign!). We had to part with our shoes at a stand with no shelter as many people tottered around wrenching off shoes while simultaneously trying to hold umbrellas for shelter. We handed over our shoes and received a tag. Next we slopped our way in the dark over dubious tiles to the entrance and the queuing. We were herded up stairs, through a room and literally pushed past the hole in the wall with a view through to the Tooth Vault. We were ejected from the other side and found our way through the torrential rain to the shoe counter where we could not retrieve our shoes until we paid more money for storing them!!! We parted with 100 rupees and that was clearly nor enough but we had our shoes and couldn't see anyone coming out into the rain to collect more from us. Next came the comedy of sharing umbrellas while putting on the shoes in the rain and puddles. I appreciate to some extent the significance of the temple and the only bright spot for me was the joy of the entire families who had come to worship, beautifully dressed and bearing gifts. Today I visited the Blue Mosque in Istanbul and the experience was in complete contrast to the one above a few days ago. We were welcomed, quietly checked for dress, it was free, bags were provided to carry shoes and covered seats were present. The interior was quiet and welcoming, it felt comfortable and I was very pleased to have made the visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Kandy originally called Senkadagala is the Mahanuwara ( Great city ) of Srilankan Kings  which is now a world heritage site . Temple of Tooth - Sri Dalda Maliguwa is the most sacred Buddhist pilgrim spot in the hill town. The temple built during the 17th century is now having a golden canopy. It is proudly located in the Royal Palace compound on the north of the Kandy Lake. The left upper canine tooth relic  originally preserved at Kalinga  after the nirvana of Buddha was brought to Lanka during the 4th century.  It was shifted to Kandy when it became the capital . One cannot see the original relic of the tooth which is known to be kept safe on a lotus flower in a jewelled gold casket mounted on a throne inside the inner shrine guarded by two big elephant tusks.  It is taken in procession once during the annual Esala  Perahera festival in August . Around the temple you can also see Alut Maligwa , Audience Hall , Rajah Tusker Hall , World Buddhist Museum etc.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: And as were based just around the corner, we found ourselves visiting this famous Temple on several occasions and each time we found something else to marvel at. Having visited some major religious sites around the World including the Vatican in Rome, Wat Pho in Bangkok, and The great Mosque of Kairouan in Tunisia, I'm always amazed at the grandeur of these places and this Temple of the tooth was no exception being the epicentre of the Buddhist faith. We first had a good look around in daylight to get our bearings and after paying an entrance fee of 1000 Rupees each made the big mistake of doing this on a weekend, as just about everybody in Sri Lanka turned up bus after bus load and we ended up in a chaotic scrum. But, first we had to hand our sandals in at the "Foreigners " counter, it would also be nice to see "Tourist" Or "Overseas Visitor"  instead of "Foreigners" .?   Making our way barefoot towards the Temple the crowds just got bigger and it bottle necked on the main steps, which was pretty scary going inside here, as it became quite crowded with people pushing and shoving .  As we went upstairs and joined the queue for the sacred tooth I was aware of the atmosphere and expected hysteria plus smiling excited faces all around me, and the crowd just kept pushing, as the little window opened they began filing and pushing past and you just get a small glimpse of the golden bell shaped casket containing the tooth, before being elbowed and bundled out the way and no pictures here but, if you stand further back you can click away quite happily. Moving around you can see musicians and monks wandering about, and you just have to admire the architecture along with the colours and paintings/carvings which abound here. Going outside there are small museums and the famous stuffed elephant Tusker, plus the views from the high walls across the moat and gardens are pretty good too. The one thing I found interesting were the amount of Sri Lankan's who came up to us including a family from Colombo and thanking us for coming, even taking pictures of us..? We decided to come back for the night time service the following day with my wife bringing some lotus flowers which you can buy for 100 rupees outside,  it was also now a bit quieter but still crowded and this time the crowd went crazy trying to see the aforementioned tooth, at over six feet I found myself becoming a tree as excited women climbed up me to get a better view, and I thought it was my good looks..Ah well.? The night service is also a lot better due to the atmosphere and the musicians however, as we were leaving the heavens opened up and a tremendous monsoon came down trapping everyone inside for a while. And walking around in one's bare feet I was aware of some kind person pointing downwards and It turned out I was standing just inches from a huge Black scorpion which had been washed down from the roof, talk about lucky here especially before my "Toe to Toe " with some Hornets I had later on up at Sigiriya..? Things to look out for are dress code, and you can buy some sarongs outside etc, and as some people have pointed out when returning to get your sandals, be aware of the "Donation" scam as these guys openly ask you straight out for cash. Just pop your shoes/sandals in a bag beforehand instead, and if you pick up a guide outside make sure he is what he says he is, as there are also the scamster's operating. As for us I never bothered as I read up on it before I left home. Now, I'm also quite perplexed at some people on here complaining that "It's just a tooth" etc,  perhaps they should stick to wandering around such "Historical " places like Benidorm or Magaluf .......?  C'mon, folks lets just enjoy this famous Temple and it's history of the Buddhist faith it's an eye opener and a once in a lifetime opportunity to show some respect..!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Kandy was the capital of the Sinhalese Kings from 1592 to 1815. Fortified by a terrain of mountains and the difficult approach Kandy managed to operate in independence from Dutch, Portuguese and the English till 1815. The city is a world heritage site declared by UNESCO, in part due to this temple. The Sri Dalada Maligawa or The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is a temple in the city of Kandy in Sri Lanka. It was built within the royal palace complex which houses the one of the two surviving relic of the tooth of Buddha, an object of veneration for Buddhists. The other tooth relic is believed to be enshrined in a stupa called Somawathi Chethiya. The Sri Dalada Maligawa in Kandy, the temple which houses the Sacred Tooth Relic of The Buddha, is possibly the most sacred Buddhist shrine in the world. It is venerated not only by Buddhists in Sri Lanka but by Buddhists all over the world.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Firstly dress appropriately, my partner had her shoulders covered but her top was slightly see through so she had to hire a shawl to cover. It's quite expensive to get in as a foreign tourist, especially as it is not relevant to our religions, but to locals and those of Buddhist belief, this is the most important place of worship and respect in Sri Lanka and that's great. On entering some bloke was cheesed of that we didn't want to hire a guide for an hour to give us a tour. From past experience of these guides in these places, you generally have trouble understanding them, and then they waffle on filling your head with names and dates and other such things that are meaningless to you and forgotten in an instant and you are bored after 5minutes but feel rude not to complete the lengthy tour and then end up paying the guide way too much than what you would have wanted to pay. We saw the temple of the tooth which is a door which somewhere behind is housed a tooth from a famous Buddhist. 2seconds a photo and that's that move on. We made the mistake of entering the kings palace which houses wooden artefacts and some guy there captured us and spent 10mins giving us a tour we didn't want and couldn't understand, then put out his hand for money and seemed displeased with Rs200 about £1, I mean we had already paid to go into the place at the entrance and we didn't want this tour of wooden artifacts. I mean he said, "this is a wooden window, this is a wooden stick etc" lost on me, I can see it's made of wood. I guess I shouldn't have gone as it's not my thing, but on a day tour of local places of interest, this is one of the places you go. I would have preferred to have a wander around the city streets. If your like me and temples don't float your boat, then 5-10 mins should be enough, I think it was £5 each to get in. Personally I saw a Burger King up the road and I would have enjoyed more a burger and proper orange juice and a wander of the shops and streets. Each to their own I guess. If you found this review helpful please give me a helpful tick Jamie of wisbech

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This historical religious site offers pretty good value for money for non-Buddhists.  Be prepared to cover yourself appropriately (men: hide your legs; women: don’t dare show your shoulders – strangely, the insistence of this attire is in stark contrast to the various paintings portraying worshippers of old who hardly wore a thing! If you don’t like going barefoot, too bad – ‘them’s the rules’). One of the more interesting aspects of our visit were a series of paintings in which the history of The Tooth Relic was illustrated in about 20 works of art, each with an accompanying line of text.  It can be quite amusing to see how poorly these are translated into English at most cultural centres. For example, #19 talks about the Dalada Floods and how Governor Edward Barns took a leading role to organize an exposition with “plomp and glory”. Great reverence is paid to this sacred object by the devoted followers of the religions, both in prayers and some serious cash.  There are opportunities to contribute your ‘blessing’ at various stages, including regularly spaced Till Boxes along a path by the side of the lake OUTSIDE the temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is a key attraction in Kandy and it is indeed a sacred place for Srilankans. Buddha's tooth is placed inside an egg-shaped box and this box is worshipped by the main priest everyday in a room with curtain on. This box can be seen by common people on a special occasion only once a year when it is carried on an elephant's back. The photographs are hung in the temple and that is how tourists get a glimpse. Like in Indian temples, there are donation boxes where pilgrims contribute money and you will see an array of lotus flowers offered by pilgrims. Stories about different Lankan kings who planned to destroy the temple and the tooth relic are depicted in the room where Buddha's statue is erected. Very interesting read. Make sure you do not take photographs with your back to the Buddha or tooth relic room. It is considered an insult to the god and your camera will be taken away by the temple officials. The temple is in the city centre, so you can plan the visit along with your shopping and lunch/dinner. The biggest surprise for me was an entry fee applicable only to foreigners - I don't understand why.

Avoid this ceromony until the monks take their responsibilities seriously and consider some effective crowd control and management to help  the devotees and tourists alike.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The family and I toured Kandy towards the end of our 15 days in Sri Lanka, having spent the previous week on a beach, lazing about; the contrast between that and Kandy during perahera could not be more stark! During the morning we visited the temple, a very finely decorated temple in the Royal Palace complex, which was fascinating - predominantly because of the two museums at the back of the temple. The one on the first floor has artifacts and royal costumes on display dating back over a millennium, and the second floor museum shows the effect of the two attacks on the temple that occurred over the past 20 years. The temple itself is obviously well loved and highly venerated - as well as being a major tourist attraction, it is a very busy temple which is packed with Buddhist worshipers making offerings, meditating and praying. Outside the temple is the Kandy Lake, with a small island in the centre that kings in the past had used as a little pleasure island, having their concubines rowed over for a little semi-public frolicking, and the Queen's Bath adorns the bank near to the temple. To be fair, the Bath doesn't do much adorning right now - it's very dilapidated and the usable parts of the building have been taken over by tour operators and various local organisations, but with enough imagination you can see how grand this would have been in its heyday! The actual mythology around the Buddha's tooth itself is fascinating, if a little morbid; apparently a Sinhalese princess stole the tooth from the Buddha's mouth as his corpse lay burning upon his funeral pyre, hid the tooth in her hair, and smuggled it back to Sri Lanka on the orders of her father. For much of the next 2,500 years, it was commonly held that whoever had the tooth ruled the kingdom, so the tooth took on great political, as well as religious, significance. Successive rulers generally built temples enshrining the tooth near their own palaces, and the last of these were obviously the rulers of Kandy. In the evening we returned and entered the temple grounds again, in plenty of time to get a seat in the stands. We discovered how important a good vantage point and a seat was when, 4 hours later, the perhahera parade was still going, and until it finished, we couldn't actually leave the complex! This, of course, is the downside of visiting Kandy during perahera - the streets in the centre of town are all closed, it's difficult to get around, and it's incredibly busy. The festival goes for two weeks at the start of August, and starts off small and gets much much bigger - we were there on day 3, and I can only imagine how crazy it must get later on in the festival! However, whatever downsides there might be, the dazzling, colourful displays of dancers, fire-twirlers, and elephants are totally worth it! It is just an overwhelming and wonderful show, with more elephants than you can believe, all bejeweled and decked out in wonderful robes, with their own palanquins atop their backs, emulating the one lucky elephant who actually has The Tooth on the palanquin display case on his back. Lots of fire, lots of drumming, lots of bells and traditional instruments, dance groups the next more extravagant than the last - great fun! Just be prepared, take water and some snacks for kids, but try not to need the toilet. Not enough there, and overused is an understatement!

review_text: Paying a ticket to enter a temple, is enough of a rip-off already. Temples are not supposed to be commercial enterprises in the first place. OK, everybody knows religion is a big business, with donations, property etc, but paying a ticket is over the top. Unfortunately in Sri Lanka you have to buy tickets almost in every single temple. A ticket of 6 euros for the tooth temple however, is insulting. It costs 4 euros to enter the temple of Poseidon in Sounion, a world class monument of ancient architecture, in the most beautiful setting possible, in a European country. 6 euros for the tooth is just too much. Having said that, this is not a visit you will remember for the serene atmosphere and budhist aura. Thousands of people flock here each day to offer flowers and worship the golden egg with Budha's tooth inside, among them hundreds of tourits. Architecture is beautiful and the temple is well taken care off but not really spacy. Head to the upper floors and you can enter the shrine, during puja you may even enter the inner shrine, but make sure your pockets are empty and your gear is safe. If you're looking for magical temple atmosphere visit India, the temple of Madurai for example. Vast, ancient, with beautiful art, and guess what: No tickets! Only a small donation IF you want to skip the line. For Kandy, I'd pick the botanical garden over the tooth temple any time.

review_text: The ambiance of the temple was lovely. We enjoyed seeing the families and worshippers arriving with their offerings and the ceremonial part downstairs. The viewing area for worshippers and visitors is quite small and as it got closer to the relic being exhibited it got to be a dangerous squash such that my husband pulled me out for fear of being suffocated. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple by itself is very historic and of great religious significance to Buddhists. The buildings are well maintained and the surroundings are very scenic and calm. Very spiritual experience for a devout pilgrim. But since they sell tickets  to foreign visitors (at higher prices) , all of whom may not be devout pilgrims of Buddhism, some basic measures need to be in place for ensuring a better experience for tourists . The following problems are noticeable : a) There is no  protection from rain in front of the ticket counter and in the adjacent footwear deposit counter. And from there upto temple entrance. So if it is raining , along with your footwear you will get thoroughly drenched. Since it rains most of the year, and there is an entrance fees being charged, I do not understand why they  cannot put up a  basic canvas roofing covering the areas leading from the road to  the ticket counter , the footwear counter and then upto the temple entrance - so at least the visitor does not get soaking  wet  before even starting the temple visit. b) Inside the temple you can see is the casket (which contains the tooth relic). The actual tooth is taken out only once a year. c) There are no signboards to tell the visitor clearly what times the casket is visible for viewing and hence different guides tell you different timings. Also, in the evenings it gets crowded and there is no proper queue management to handle the large crowds. So it can be frustrating. c) it is advisable to hire a guide - otherwise most of the history and significance of the various parts of the complex will not be understood. d) Vehicles have to park some distance away from the temple complex. So be prepared to have a fairly long walk in the rain back to your vehicle.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Sri Dalada Maligawa temple complex is situated with the Kandy Lake in front and the Udawatta forest behind it. For close to 1,540 years, the Sacred Tooth relic belonged to the Kings of Sri Lanka who treated the sacred object as their own property with the common man having no access to it. However, owing to foreign invasions and the belief that whoever possessed the Sacred Tooth would rule over the kingdom of Sri Lanka, the sacred object had to be moved from place to place nine times as a safety precaution. From Anuradhapura to Polonnaruwa, Dambadeniya, Beligal and so on till its final resting place, Kandy. Two bricks walls run around the temple complex with moat in between. The outer wall is called Diyareli Bamma (wall of water ripples) and the inner wall Walakula Bamma (wall of clouds) . There are holes in this wall to light coconut oil lamps. The main entrance gate which lies over the moat is called mahawahalkada. At the foot of mahawahalkada steps there is a Sandakada pahana (moonstone) which is carved in Kandyan architectural style. Mahawahalkada was totally destroyed in a 1998 bomb blast and rebuilt later. Elephants are depicted in stone on the either sides of the entrance. A Makara Torana and two guardian stones are placed on top of the staircase. The two storeys of main shrine are known as "Palle malaya" (lower floor) and "Udu malaya" (upper floor). A heavily decorated ambarawa (tunnel) leads to the pallemaluwa . The actual chamber which the tooth relic is kept is known as the "Handun kunama". The tooth relic is encased in seven golden caskets which engraved with precious gemstones and the caskets have a shape of a stupa. On the upper floor is the Pallemale Viharaya with bust of Buddha inside. Entrance to the Pathirippuwa (Octagon) is also located on this floor. Pathirippuwa was used by kandyan kings to address his fellow country men.

What I'm saying is you need to be patient and not in a rush or frustration will overcome you. Need to cover legs and as with most temples shoes off and minded for a small fee. You will not see the tooth but supposedly the gold casket that houses it but will need to join a long line to walk past (and here no photos) and stand 3 deep some distance away for a photo. Elsewhere around the temple is some great architecture and statues. Was worth the visit despite the crowds.

The complex is situated along the bank of Lake Kandy and the entrance is across the street from The Queens Hotel. Women and men have separate entrances, mainly for security reasons. Entry is free, but donations are very welcome. Although I have great admiration for Buddhism as a religion and way of life, I did not enter the buildings myself. It was very busy when we were there and everyone must be barefoot. That was a bit too much for me, with rather sensitive feet, as most people in the streets wear toe-slippers on their bare feet. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Heres a tip: if you dont understand the culture and cant respect religions just dont go. I read some of the one star reviews and they are ridiculous and made to sound like people are offended. This temple is one of the most important places for the buddhists so yes it will be crowded with pilgrims who actually come there to pray. No headwear or footwear is allowed inside temples as this is a way of respect in buddhism. This is not limited to hijabs, no headwear means nothing that covers your head including scarves, caps or turbans. Same goes with shoes. Its just religious etiquette. As someone else mentioned it is not necessary to pay for ur shoes to be taken care of. U can choose to carry them with u, or leave it at the sides of the temple, u only need to pay if u want someone to take care of them while u are away, which requires a payment - obvious. You are not allowed to wear anything short or tops which exposes too much skin. You will be asked to cover your legs and arms. About the tooth relic, as foreigners it may not be very significant to us, you may want to skip this if you are a tourist as the queue for the relic is very long. It is hardly visible and u will be rushed as the doors to view it is only open for a short number of minutes and everyone will be shoving to get a glimpse. I was told this is because it is important for the pilgrims to try and catch a glimpse and most locals at the temple have travelled from far to see it. No photography is allowed in that part so you might as well skip it unless it has any significance to you. The place itself i would give a 3/5. Then again its a religious place. Not an attraction. Go with someone who can explain what the murals means, i did and it was actually interesting to know the history.

review_text: This is a full scale worKing temple and as a visitor you may feel slightly out of place or trespassing slightly. We had a local guide ( recommend Dewmini Tours) which helps in negotiating your way round. Outside the temple building there are grounds to walk round, a small museum and a Hindu shrine nearby. Altogether an impressive experience to see what is a major cultural event locally. Definitely recommended.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If you happen to be in Kandy you must stop by the Temple. Security is tight, and unfortunately for Hijabis you will have to take off your scarf if you want to enter. We had a Malay friend with us and she went to the museum instead :( Entrance is 1000 rupees for foreigners, like most visit to the temple you will have to take off your shoes.  The temple consist of several buildings, the main entrance leads you to the main prayer hall.  The interior is very grand, with gilded lotus on the ceiling, brass door handles, and carvings on columns.  It is a place of spirituality and locals come here to pray, you can't really see the tooth, just a casket.  There is a newer hall within the compound at the back with a grander interior. There is a timber pavillion with elaborate carvings just next to the temple that is worth checking out as well.  We spent almost 2 hours here taking our time soaking in the elaborateness of the entire temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the Temple as a part of your escorted tour, accompanied by our guide / driver. We arrived  slightly before later morning worship, when devotees became to queue to go upstairs to see golden casket, where Buddha's tooth is supposed to be. We passed upper chamber shortly after the door were opened. In spite we are not Buddhist, we really enjoyed and shared the excitement with other people. I took a second tour, joined the left queue which allowed to see the casket even closer. There are many other parts of the Temple to visit. In summary, must to go place in Sri Lanka. Make sure that you will attend when the upper chamber will be opened.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It's a very enigmatic experience, as you wander through the temple grounds, as dusk is falling.  Worshippers gathering with their lotus flower offerings, children all decked out in white, the symbol of purity, candles in hand. The sounds of chanting and prayers echoing around the complex. The setting sun shimmering over the lake. You all file up the steps into the complex, and then to the inner temple to sounds of beating drums and beautiful lighting. Temple musicians play music, and devotees bow to the Buddhas. A little before 6.30pm you climb the steps to the upper chamber, and await the golden sliding doors to be pulled back. The large crowds start to press forward in anticipation. A few minutes later, the little doors slide back, and the golden casket comes into view. This is the vessel  containing Buddha's tooth. The devotees grasp. For some it's a life long ambition to see this. They surge forward to get the best view. You can't actually see the tooth itself. It's hidden inside the shimmering casket.... for the devotees that is enough.  Just to be in, or close, to its presence. A few moments later, it's over. You descend back down again and out to the evening air. I am not a.Buddhist, but can't help feeling that anyone would be moved by the atmosphere and the setting. Tip : you may may need your GoPro camera on a tall pole if you want to see it all! Tip 2 : get ready to push and be pushed. When those golden doors slide back, a  Mexican wave will surge and carry you forward.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Don't miss the opportunity to see one of Sri Lanka's most sacred Buddhist sites -- the temple that house a relic of Lord Buddha's tooth.   Relic veneration is a big part of Sri Lankan religious practice and this compound is a beautiful introduction to this tradition. The main entrance is right across from the Queen's Hotel.  You will be accosted by potential guides, who vary in quality.  I used a man named Gamage (0776230711) who is fluent in English and knowledgable about the site and Buddhism.  He also has a corny sense of humor which makes things fun. I paid him 8,000 rupees because he was a big help navigating the crowds waiting for the 9:30 ritual cleansing of the relic. You can buy lotus blossoms to make an offering and are free to take photos.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: You can go different times of the day and experience the temple in different ways. In the heart of the temple is a relic, a tooth from the buddha. Once a day they open the small shrine and you can stand in line to see, not the tooth, but the gold case that contains the buddha. The queue is long, the noise is unbelievable, and the vibrations of anticipation fill the  temple. Fantastic experience. You can also wander around the temple and see lots of statues and art work, check out the ceiling.Could be good with a guide for the basic story but be prepared to haggle for your price first. If you visit the temple at other times its much quieter but its also just to walk in the garden and see all the poeple meditating or in prayer. Most people go to Kandy to visit the temple and its historically ver important for all buddhists. If you are not a buddhist it is still a great trip.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Cover your knees and shoulders and you'll be fine. We ended up at this place on a Sunday. Wow. Chaos. An official temple guide (had a badge to prove it) offered his help out front and said he didn't expect any money but was happy to show us around the place. He also claimed to be the official BBC correspondent for Kandy. I'm glad we had him there because he whisked us through the crazy lineups and took us to all the important sections. I probably would've gotten lost and frustrated pretty quickly without him. We intended to give him a few hundred rupees tip for his little tour, but when we handed him five hundred, he scoffed at it and said he usually gets a thousand. I was astonished. My wife is a lot nicer than I am so she gave him the thousand he wanted. I don't regret letting him lead us through, but his dishonesty up front about the money was quite off-putting. Especially considering that (if he was honest) he has two well-paying jobs and shouldn't have to demand money from tourists. Odds are he was just a con man with a fake badge, as that would fit with most of the guides you find waiting for you at the entrance to Sri Lankan sites. My advice to visitors - If it's not a busy day at this temple, don't bother with the guide because there is signage. If it looks crowded, definitely use one, but be prepared to pay a thousand rupees even if they say no money is required. As for the site itself, its rich history and beautiful architecture are well worth the visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Firstly, this is a spectacular temple and worth visiting if only to wonder around and take it all in. I must say my rating is heavily influenced by the fact that we visited during the evening Puja which is a good experience with the drumming and feeding of the Buddah rituals taking place, however, it got to a point where the crowds were unbearable, especially in the upper room where they open the shrine for you to get the sneakiest of peaks at the casket which houses the tooth (you will struggle to see anything through the throngs of people). I think if we had visited the temple out side of ceremony hours and also wondered around the grounds my rating would be higher. Overall, the temple is magnificent and worth a visit. We especially enjoyed the room which tells the story of Buddah. However, I would not recommend visiting during Puja, there is really no added benefit. It would be much more relaxing, and allow you to take in more of the temple to visit outside these ceremonies and do things at your own pace.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The place is buzzing with activity since 5:30am on the day that I visited, Poson to remember the arrival of Buddhism into Sri Lanka.  Locals go in for free but foreigners are charged at hefty 1,000 Rupees but that comes with a free DVD.  You are not allowed to wear shoes in there and so, you need to have your shoes deposited.  To get your shoes back, you are expected to donate money into a charity box.  This Temple is a sacred place because it's where Buddha's tooth is allegedly located.  Devotees would come in droves to pay respect to the Tooth, to light candles and to pray for good luck.  World Buddhism Museum is tucked right at the back.  In Kandy, this surely is a place that you have to visit.  It's wonderful to savour the dance, the music, the elephants on festive days.  Commendable visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If you are in the city of Kandy, a visit to the Sri Dalada Maligawa  or the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is a must. The temple houses the  relic of the tooth of Buddha and is the primary reason why the city of Kandy have the status of UNESCO World Heritage site. The entry to the temple has a price, but if you are from SAARC country you are entitled to a discount rate, as is common in most place in  Srilanka. The temple is situated adjacent to the Kandy lake and the main temple complex is surrounded by a moat. Once you enter the main temple complex you can see the enclosure which houses the tooth relic. The tooth relic is taken out every year in a procession, but it is open for public viewing once in 5 year. You can see the Palanquin which is used to carry the tooth relic inside the temple complex. You can walk around the temple complex and see various statues and painting depicting the life of Lord Buddha. The is a hall which house a statue which is very similar to the one you see in Thailand. Will advice you to take a local guide. They don't charge much and will give you information and take you to certain parts of the temple which you may otherwise miss.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the Temple of The Tooth as part of our week long tour of Sri Lanka. Our driver acted as our guide for the tour and showed us around the various parts of the temple complex and explained the various historical and religious significance of the place. It pays to have a good guide, and obviously this can be some what pot-luck. If you wish to go around on your own there is an audio guide. We arrived around 9am, meaning that we were in time to see one of the three daily offerings. During this time the local Buddhist's bring offerings of flowers and food to Buddha, and the casket that houses one of the teeth of the cremated body of Buddha can be seen in the distance inside the inner temple. Learning about the spiritualism of the temple, and the country, is really eye-opening. My only somewhat ironic complaint is that the temple was really busy full of tourists, who are milling around whilst the locals are worshipping... I'd like to go back when it was a little less busy to really try and take in what was going on around me a little more. When you are there make sure that you take some time to walk around the rest of the grounds. In the land around the main temple are other smaller temples and shrines to other deities and some Hindu gods. These have far less, if any, tourists. These offered a real reflection of the way the Sri Lankan's worship - for example many woman and mothers were taking offerings and praying to the deity who helps fertility and children. There is also a Christian church next door, built during the time of the British colonisation of the country. As an observation I found the Sri Lankan people to be very tolerant of different people and beliefs. As others have said - be sure to cover up your shoulders and chest and legs down to your knees. You will also be required to take off your shoes. The floor can get very very hot in places, which is why it is often busiest early in the morning. It is acceptable to wear socks, so it might be worth wearing them, or doing what I did and taking a pair with you, just in case the floor is baking!
