location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the Temple in the evening as others have said. Our guide advised us to visit as it is the most interesting as so many local folks go there... so i would have to agree, it was a real experience. Yes it was crowded and for so many religious people in one place, there as a lot of pushing and impatience, which surprised me. Yes it was hot inside, but well worth the wait. Our guide hired at the entrance was excellent, the info was never ending and he was definitely well versed  in his knowledge. All in all well worth a visit. A word of warning, any one with serious balance issues, as with Vestibular Nerve involvement may have issues negotiating the crowds as did my friend. The loud drumming and noise of the crowds was totally disorientating and she had to step aside to gather her self numerous times. She still said it was well worth the struggles, but it was a big problem for her.  Again great to see this ceremony and one i won't soon forget! PS: you again have to take off shoes, and they store them for you very efficiently, for a small price and we stayed for the whole tour and by that time many had left so we had no issues getting our shoes easily and being on our way!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple is very beautiful and filled with amazing Buddhist art work and sculptures which tell about the history of Buddhism in Kandy. I understand this is a place of worship but it is also a very commercialized experience. I would have appreciated it if they have English translations of the signs that were written in Singhala everywhere. We were rushed through the line to see the pogoda which held the tooth relic so we didn't get to see what it really is. Every statue has a donation box or a monk with his hand out waiting for cash. Ruined the spiritual experience we were hoping for.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth has a very touristy feel about it. I much preferred our earlier tour of Anaradhapura. That being said, our guide was excellent - knowledgeable and friendly. I suppose everyone who goes to Kandy has to visit the temple but it is something of a gaudy monstrosity.

review_text: We went in the evening for the daily ceremony where they open the door to the casket where the tooth is stored.  It is “different” and very intriguing how much attention they give to Buddha’s tooth!  Whoever has possession of it is said to rule the city so it’s got a lot of history behind it.  The temple is beautiful and no matter how sure/unsure you are about the truth of the story is the myth or truth makes it a little magical I suppose.  It gets very busy so if you are sticking to a time know which order to see it in.  Otherwise take your time wandering around with the crowds.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic

review_text: There is a small entrance fee (RS25) and you also have to remove footwear. If you're bothered about the ground take socks... It's a busy place but the also tranquil. There are daily ceremonies that are very overcrowded so beware, check the times. Beautiful temple and grounds. Well worth a visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Interesting place to visit as had the story of the Buddha on the wall in one section and a few other little museum sections (we liked the elephant museum). Went in the evening to see the tooth relic ceremony but after about 30 minutes of loud drumming and nothing happening we left to see the devales. These were also pretty. A nice place to visit if in Kandy but not overly amazing.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: One is inclined to wear flip-flops in the heat, but do take socks to wear as you have to leave your shoes at the entrance. (25 rupees payable). You don't see the tooth of course, but the sacred atmosphere is entrancing, and the offerings of flowers add a heady scent.I liked the museum upstairs with effigies of the notataries through the years.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A welcome break from the chaotic streets of Kandy. We had a guide give us a short tour around the building, pointing out where we could and could not take photos. The temple had a nice story and well cared for building, but a lot of historical items (books, the relic etc) are all stored away and you can't see them. There is a nice hall towards the back of the temple where the story was told in maybe 18 picture boards with captions which was nice.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Fantastic to look around - the inside of the temple is stunning and although busy it is not crowded. There is so much to take in - getting a picture of where the tooth is actually stored is a little tricky due to the number of tourists and worshippers - and you can only see it from afar - but this didn't matter. Beware the guides who hang around outside - I said no to one but he then latched onto my partner and started talking to him. We agreed to have him as our guide as it can be a little confusing trying to figure out what takes place inside the temple - but he then asked for 3000rs for his services. Agree a price first would be my advice!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Most visitors come to experience one of the thrice daily pujas. Our guide ensured that we passed through the upstairs room in which the casket holding the tooth is held to experience the atmosphere and see the throngs of pilgrims. This early visit did mean that we did not see the actual unveiling of the reliquary but then we did not have to contend with the crush of hundreds of pilgrims desperate to see this event. We were able to take advantage to gain front positions for the actual ceremony below which is roped off to prevent crowding. Drummers and a pipe blasted the ears. Food was offered to the Buddha in the richly decorated and carved shrine. During this period we were able to enter other rooms including the library with a very old palm leaf book on display. Outside the main Temple there are other buildings and museums to investigate. If possible go during the week where the crowds are not as pressing.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: There are few points to remember for this temple: You should go inside with bare foot You should not smell the flowers you would take at the entrance for Buddha One tooth of Buddha is kept there but the other three which remained are in India. It worth to visit here for sure.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Visiting the place is okay if you are into visiting temples. Although I find it off putting that they have donation boxes in every corner. Even the guy who kept our shoes (because you are not allowed to wear shoes and revealing clothes) was asking for money. This place is a place for worshipping so its not good that the people looking after it is treating tourists like a bank. Sri Lanka is a beautiful country but if they want to attract tourists they should prevent from asking money this way.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I thought that the temple was nice.. you don't get to see the tooth, but it's interesting anyway. The tour guide was a bit of a con, he talked us around for 10 mins and expected a tip on top of his rate.. I wouldn't bother if I were you, after a bit of research I discovered most of what he said wasn't true anyway!! The museum at the top is interesting.. we also saw a culture dance show next to the temple which was nice! A lot of beggars surround the temple so beware.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: It is a very famous temple where a tooth of great Buddha is conserved n is of great devotional importance for Buddhists. It's situated alongside a beautiful lake. Entry fees 500 SLR for people from SAARC n 1000 for other countries. There's small museum also. Importantly they take d tooth out every five yrs n that will be in August 2014.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: By the time we reached Kandy we had spent three days viewing wonderful temples and sites so fatigue was setting in and the never ending shoe parking was getting irksome. Our guide was excellent and had us mobilised with military efficiency to be on time - quite an achievement in itself, he rushed us through to see all the key features of the ceremonies, the temple was very crowded and we would not have seen half the action without his experience. Wonderful carvings, images and real religiosity, so an experience to remember. It really needs longer than the 2-3 hours we spent there to see and absorb it all. We moved so fast to keep to the guides schedule that we probably missed a lot of the background information so a more leisurely visit would be more effective. Don't miss it!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Left Negombo at 9am for my first full day touring around & stopping at many other tourist attractions on the way, I eventually arrived in Kandy with my young excellent taxi driver late afternoon on Sunday 18/08/13, on arrival we had problems in finding a car space spending at least 30 min's driving around, eventually we found a space and had a 20 walk down towards the Temple to watch the beginning of the elephant festival, sadly didn't arrive earlier enough to take a look inside the temple. The Temple looks impressive with all the night lights during the festival, many crowds of locals & tourists. I managed to find a good advantage spot watching the parade of dancers & elephants, a most enjoyable experience attending this annual festival in Kandy. Spent around 2.5 hrs enjoying the atmosphere outside the temple & arrived back in Negombo at midnight after a very long enjoyable day.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The Temple of the Tooth is the heart centre of modern Buddhism in Sri Lanka and many parts of the world. We visited the temple for the evening service and were delighted to get a glimpse of the amazing Golden Casket that holds the relic of the tooth in an ante-room inside the temple. We had a young passionate guide recommended by Sangeeth of sangeethlanka.com who was fantastic. He explained in detail the history of the temple, the paintings, the rituals and most importantly the significance to the pilgrims in attendance that had waited 5+ years for the opportunity to attend the ceremony. They pay thousands of pounds to sponsor an offering and distribution of food to the needy on the day they attend. Our guide’s fee was 1000 rps/£5 and we gave him 2000 which was well deserved. I can’t understand why people would complain about paying a pittance to visit this hugely important site. You don’t get things for free in your own country so why object to paying for goods and services to people who are far needier than you’ll ever be? Our guide also told us how to ask for our inner heart’s desire while we had the ear of Buddha at the temple ☺. He told us how to make best use of a beautiful large room of contemplation, which had many statues of Buddha that helped us make a personal vow to change an aspect of our own behaviour. The whole experience was deeply moving for us and I’m happy to say that I’m keeping my vow to Buddha and enjoying my quasi connection to religion even tho’ I’m a dyed in the wool, atheist. The temple of the tooth was a surprisingly emotional experience for us and I think if you go with an open heart and mind, it will be emotional, thought provoking and memorable for you too.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Temple of the Tooth is a sacred place for Buddhists all over the world. It is a serene place of worship and the venue for the spectacular Kandy Perehara procession. It also has a beautiful museum that is well worth a visit. If you are non Buddhist, please be respectful, quiet, and patient when queuing. Be discreet when taking any photos. Cover arms and legs and take your shoes off.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Best to get there 9 a.m. to see the opening of the inner sanctum for puja. Although, truth to tell, you don't see a great deal (certainly not the tooth, which I understand may anyway be a replica of a replica....), it's an interesting spectacle featuring drummers and musicians. The temple is part of a complex which includes the audience hall where power was signed over to the Brits in 1815, and a museum of tribute to a particularly famous elephant. We also wandered round a museum of artefacts, where a chap who seemed quite knowledgeable supplied us with interesting facts about the exhibits - he might have been one of the dubious guides referred to in other reviews, but equally, he could have been the Director of the Museum. He didn't pressurise us for any money, so I'd prefer to believe the latter - it can be too easy to get suspicious about people's motives. We were there at the time of the Perahera, which meant that there were quite a few elephants tethered in the grounds awaiting that evening's procession - an interesting experience for our two boys, who were able to pose with a baby elephant, and to witness a senior tusker - what shall we say? - going to the toilet ! If you've never seen this, it's quite spectacular!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Temple of the tooth in Kandy is the castle of king Sriwickrama Rajasinghe who ruled the upcountry long years ago. However With the end of the Monarch  the castle was used to rest the tooth of the Lord Buddha brought from India. Srilankan kings have always safeguarded this tooth relic since it is considered as the symbol of their  holding of the power in the country. Srilanka being  a buddhist country, pays a high respect to this place and it is being visited by almost every visitor to the country. Temple of the tooth conducts a ritual annually (july/August) where the tooth relic was taken out and carried by a parade around Kandy town  . This parade is world famous and it is such a beautiful one with a lot of performers doing their acts in the night. Kandyan dancers, torch carriers ,elephants with lighted dresses , drummers are a few  of those.The parade consists of approximate 50 elephants dressed differently in a color unique to their origin (devalaya) and lighted with thousands of small LED bulbs. Nilame's ( Representing the traditional Devalayas) wear  dresses similar to what the old kings used to wear and unique to kandyan traditional VIP's.The most fascinating thing is the Tusker (Elephant with tusks) carrying the casket carrying the tooth relic of Lord buddha. This parade is a must see and one of the best i have ever seen.

What strikes you is, given the large number of worshippers, the noise is down to a minimum. The temple is very pretty with its exhibits and surroundings are clean.  The town and scenic spots are also very attractive. A visit this place is a must.

review_text: Buddhism is a living religion and Buddha is worshipped no matter what Mr Gautama would have to say about it. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the temple in the evening, after watching the Cultural Dance Show. We walked around the lake to reach it. After paying for the tickets and keeping our shoes on the rack we went inside. We were lucky to be there at the time of the Buddhist Cultural  Festival Esala Perahera. The whole place was lit up and beautifully decorated. Once inside we saw the huge elephant,which would later be dressed up with colourful clothes and brought outside.There was a lot of rush inside.People were praying in the inner chambers. The place where the tooth relic  is obvious  with its bright red and gold entrance topped with four elephant tusks with two stone lions guarding it. The whole area is surrounded by gold railings to prevent people getting too close.Around the hall are a series of pictures which follow the  scenes in the life of the tooth relic, showing how it was taken, supposedly destroyed but ultimately returned to safety.It was wonderful to be there.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A very important temple in Kandy, especially to the Buddhist. We arrived one day before the very important 10 day festival of Esala Perahera celebration. Crowds were large during this period, so have a little patience and understanding when you visit during important festivals. It is after all an active temple which is used daily and utmost respect is expected from visitors. Security checks are stringent, separate queue for male & females as you pass the gates but after that mixing is allowed, and bags are checked. Dress code applies, so be sure to wear decent clothings and if you are wearing a pair of shorts above the knees, bring along a sarong wrap to cover up. As you enter the temple, you need to remove your shoes/footwear but there is a shoe counter to deposit the footwear n tickets are given so there is no issue of misplaced footwear. It is good to have a guide to explain the temple's architecture and the rituals but not terribly important as you can read up in it before going.

review_text: This is the most holy temple in the Buddhist world and should certainly be on your agenda. 'Free' guides are ready to take you round, which takes a time, but their knowledge is worth it. They do expect, and deserve a tip at the end. You need to be covered, so take long sleeved clothes and be prepared to take your shoes off. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Speaking to non-Buddhists, if you must go to Kandy, then it's probably worth doing...but I wouldn't advise anyone else to take a detour for it. Expensive: 1,000 rupees each...plus lotus flowers, incense, candles and whatever other offering you may like to make...?? Guides are tricksters: some I'm sure, are educated and worthwhile. Ours however, gave dud information, couldn't answer basic questions appertaining to Buddhism, spoke poor English and charged a small fortune at the end...having already agreed a fixed price upfront. He rushed us through and ruined our experience, so be careful. Busy: so busy. The place is teaming with tourists...and worshippers. We disrespectfully walked into, past and around people making prayers and I felt awful and hugely intrusive for it. Surrounding the tooth chamber itself, were no less than 200 tourists with cameras and videos on tip toes trying to glimpse a shot, or posing in front of the chamber. To see in to the room with any level of clarity, you needed to stand in a further queue of about 150people, who were shuffling slowly towards and past it... However, the building itself is beautiful. The paintings that illustrate the history of the tooth are interesting and observing the sheer devotion and spirituality of those that have journeyed, pray, offer and worship the relic is an experience the older temples can't compare to in the same way: it's a question of whether you think that's appropriate or not. We spent some considerable time in Sri Lanka and impressive as it was for its religious history: speaking merely as a tourist, I'm afraid it was our most underwhelming temple experience.

review_text: We did an incredible tour of Kandy, Pinnawala elephant orphanage, Nuwara Eliya and the Hill Country with Indi from indilankatours.com. His knowledge of Sri Lanka is vast and his tour of the Temple of the Tooth was that much more personal as he is a Buddhist himself and could speak from his experiences and philosophy. It's easy to organise these trips while you are Sri Lanka and it doesn't matter where you stay.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Dalada Perehara which is 235 years old, is one of the grandest events we have in Sri Lanka. Many locals and foreigners look forward to witness this wonderful festival every year. This is held during the Esala month, in August, honouring the sacred tooth relic. Many foreigners who have been fascinated by the Perahera have written notes about it; among them is the famous British poet and novelist, D. H. Lawrence, who describes the Perahera as a "perpetual fire-laughing motion among the slow shuffle of elephants." Fa-Hien, one of the famous Chinese monks who arrived in Sri Lanka on a pilgrimage in the fifth century A.D. also gives a full description about the Perahera in his book, Fa-Hien Travel Records. "By the side of the King's Palace is the Vihara of the Buddha's Tooth, several hundred feet high, brilliant with jewellers and ornamented with rare gems. Above the Vihara is placed an upright pole on which is fixed a great Padmaraja (ruby). The Tooth of the Buddha was always brought forth in the middle of the third month. Ten days in advance, the king magnificently caparisoned a large elephant. A man dressed in royal robes on this elephant, who could speak distinctly, and the man went round it, beating a large drum, describing the life and the virtues of the Buddha, and announcing to the public; "Behold, ten days after this, Buddha's Tooth will be brought forth, and taken to the Abhayagiri Vihara. Let all, whether monks or laymen, who wish to amass merit for themselves, make the road smooth and in good condition, grandly adorn lanes and by-ways, and provide an abundant store of flowers and incense to be used as offerings to it." When this announcement was over, the king placed for exhibition on both sides of the road, the 500 different bodily forms in which the Buddha had appeared in his previous births according to the Jataka stories. All their figures were brightly coloured and grandly executed, looking as if they were alive. After this, the Tooth of the Buddha was brought forth, and was carried along in the middle of the road. Everywhere on the way, offerings were presented to it, and thus it arrived at the hall of the Buddha in the Abhayagiri Vihara. There the monks and the laity gathered in crowds, burned incense, lighted lamps and performed all the prescribed services, day and night, without ceasing till 90 days had been completed until the Tooth was returned to the Vihara. On Poya Days, the doors of the Vihara were opened, and forms of ceremonial reverence were observed according to the rules. Even during the Kandyan era between 1739 and 1815, the Esala Perahera was given much prominence. Four Devale Perahera, which was dedicated to the four guardian deities, Natha, Vishnu, Kataragama, and Pattini, was merged to the main Perahera during the Keerthi Sri Rajasingha Era. The Perahera is held according to some rituals coming down from traditions. They are known as ‘Esala-keliya'. This festival begins with the installation of ‘kapa' in each Devale. According to the ritual, for five days after installation of kapa, the kapuralas of each devale take it around every evening in a procession, accompanied by music and drumming and along with flag and canopy bearers and spearmen, and the sacred emblem of the gods.' This is known as the Devale Perahera. The Randoli Perahera begins on the 5th day. This is a lengthened version of the famous Kumbal Perahera. Palanquins of the four Devales which contains ornaments of the goddess, pitcher, and the sword are added to the Randoli Perahera. On the full moon day, this Perahera reassembles to go to Asgiriya temple, where the casket is placed. Then Devale Peraheras return to their Devales. Again, in the night, the Devale Peraheras make their way to the water-cutting site at the Getambetota. At the river, the ‘kapuralas' of the devales, go in a decorated boat, to some distance in the river. At this place, each ‘kapurala' slashes the water with the sacred sword and collects a pitcher full at the place where the sword touched the water. This water will be stored in their Devale for one year, and will be put back into the river, next year at a similar Ceremony. After seven days from the day Perahara, the ‘Waliyak-netuma', a shortened form of ‘Kohomba-kankariya' is performed at the Vishnu devalaya, along with masked dancing. On the seventh day, the Esala festival will be declared as over. The people of the ‘balibat' caste, who are sorcerers and exorcists, were the dancers in the Perahera during the days of our kings. It was a form of ‘Rajakariya' (duty) to the king. This time the Kandy Esala Perahera will be held in a grand style and will be a testament that Sri Lanka is ready for tourism after the peace!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Since it was first brought to Sri Lanka the tooth relic was the symbol of Kingship. He who held the tooth relic was able to govern the country. The tooth relic has been housed in many of Sri Lanka's medieval capitals and it last home in Kandy is where the Sri Lankan monarchy ceased to exist under British rule. However as a place to visit I do not rate it very highly the temple compound itself is modern and the tooth relic is kept closed and cannot be viewed. The temple has huge religious significance to Buddhists the world over and is a must visit if you are a Buddhist. But I believe there are other sites nearby which provide better value.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Beautiful temple ... reserve 2 hours for it and participate... stand in line to see the tooth relic (you will not see the tooth itself though, it remains hidden) and feel the magic. Photography allowed, great buddha-life-story paintings and more. I think the evening hours are a bit more 'magical' for a visit than the morning hours ... it's beautiful in the dark.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: When I say crazy I mean, if you arrive and you are not wearing something that covers shoulders and knees then they will make you buy something to cover them, they also check your bags like security and then charge you to go in. It's only about £5 even if your a buddhist! Once your in, at certain times you get to see the tooth. It's not the tooth you get to see it's just the container which the tooth is in, so don't go expecting to see the actual tooth! It's quite strange to see if you are not a Buddhist and don't know what they are doing because they lay flowers for Buddha which you are not allowed to smell. They light an oil candle and also incense. Which again if you want to do these you have to buy them before you go in. It is interesting to see what it is like but keep quiet and be aware that some people are actually there to pray and meditate, so have a little respect. But other than that I would recommend it!

review_text: What ever religion you worship, visiting Sri Dalada maligawa in the city of Kandy is some thing you should never miss. Why? Not only because it is a religiously important place for Buddhists. The serenity inside the great temple, The ancient sculpture you find inside the temple, the beautiful architecture and the wooden structural constructions where the inner chamber is placed, are all important areas for people who have different tastes. Most of the above mentioned artifacts runs in to many centuries exhibiting the talents of craftsmen of the olden times. For those tourists who are cumming from countries where many are Buddhists, it is one of the most religiously important placed within Sri lanka to visit. For two reasons it is important for them. While they would wish to worship the most secret tooth relic of lord Buddha , secondly any one would wish to be inside the temple and enjoy or experience the serenity. Just visiting the area where the inner chamber is not worth. Once the area of the inner chamber is visited, you can go to the museum, the place where the former tusker's stuffed body is placed which is a unique piece of art, and the ruins around the temple .Therefore one should take time to stay for at least one hour in and around the temple and visit all the key points. A tourist will be given a DVD where it will direct you to almost all the placed with a narration about each and every item . Also it may be cautioned that any person intending to visit the temple need to be properly attired as no person wearing  shorts and short sleeved blouses would be permitted inside  the temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The road from Colombo to Kandy is a very busy one: tuk-tuks, motorbykes, vans, buses, trucks, cars, bycicles, loud horns and pedestrians share the road on both directions. The traffic is crazy and heavy. Finally, three hours later, we arrived in Kandy, the former Sri Lankan kings capital, to visit the famous Sacred Temple of the Tooth Relic, housed in the Royal Palace complex. A magnificent construction, very beautiful, on the shores of Kandy Lake, great paintings on its ceilings, full of candles and offerings to Buddhist deities. Inside, the holy shrine that keeps the last physical relic of Sidharta Gautama: the canine tooth of  Lord Buddha, brought from India by Princess Hemamali and her husband, Prince Dantha, hidden in the hair of the Princess, to escape from hindu vandals. All right, it took us three hours get there, we paid an expensive entrance fee, hired a guide whose English was terrible, the place was overcrowded and we didn't even get close to the relic. The sacred tooth is only seen during the religious festivals of July and August. But I do not regret all the trouble. It was quite an adventure and one has to go through it all. Otherwise, it is not Kandy. Enjoy!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: As other reviews, make sure you agree a price when approached by a guide before engaging one. Should be about 1000 rupees (£5.50). We were asked for 2000 rupees at the end of our tour as there were 5 of us, but managed to negotiate 1500 rupees in the end - I think we were very generous looking back, especially as his strong accent made him difficult to understand! However, it was much better having a guide as you knew what you were looking at and the history and ceremony was explained. He also ushered us through the crowds very effectively and got a good picture of the casket containing the tooth relic for us. (You will not see Buddha's Tooth itself as it is only displayed briefly about every 5 years.) The Buddhist ritual which takes place 3times a day is interesting to watch but as we had already seen many Dagobas (Buddhist Temples) in Anuradhapura, we were getting a bit " Temple weary". Glad we went but possibly just do this one and skip the rest - other more interesting thinks to do in Sri Lanka.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I had an opportunity to visit this wonderful temple. I was lucky to visit the temple on 23 June 2013 which was a full moon day. It was an auspicious day for Buddhist followers. There were lots of people in the temple. The temple charges ticket for foreigners. For tourists from SAARC countries, Rs.500 Sri lankan rupee is charged and from other european tourists, Rs.1000 is charged. The temple is very big and beautiful. The Shrine inside is very peaceful. The sanctum sanctorium all glitters with the Gold which holds the tooth of Lord Buddha. The temple is also a good place for those who wish to research on Buddhism. There will be guides here who will ask 500 SriLankan rupees for showing around the temple. There is no need to take the services of guide. One can see around the temple oneself. A very good and lovely temple. I felt proud being an Indian where Buddhism took birth and also wondered that it has flourished to great heights in Sri Lanka.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: SKIP IT: The story of the tooth is something you can read about on line. The visit to the temple where the tooth is located, is mostly uninteresting. Upon walking on the grounds, you will be bombarded with nice men flashing official looking cards saying they will be your tour guide. This put me off immediately. The entry ticket is a USD $10 and even standing in line I was accosted by someone offering to help me. There is not much to the interior nor is it particularly beautiful (unlike the temples of Thailand). The interior building houses the tooth which is brought out for display only at set times during the day (so if you MUST see the tooth, pick your time). Behind the 'tooth' is a 3 story museum that while housing a bunch of relics and story boards was only moderately interesting. Following the path you're lead to the Museum of International Buddhism for which they wanted another entrance fee. At the return to the entrance, you pick up your shoes and there the man will demand a donation as well. Overall, Sri Lanka is a poor country and polished tourism hasn't yet arrived, often charming, but in the case of the temple a bit exhausting. If you must see it go, if it's not something you already know about, you likely aren't missing anything. Note: I'm mainly a visual tourist, perhaps the experience with a guide explaining everything would have improved the visit. However, it's not apparent the guides are part of a larger organization and quality could vary significantly.

review_text: We arrived at the temple just before sunset, making the monument even more picturesque. Eager to learn as much as we could at this majestic site we decided to take a 'guided' visit. We met up with the incredible Dinesh Duminda (adroit999@gmail.com) who welcomed us warmly, shared all his knowledge, answered all our questions about Buddhism and the service, and ensured that we not only understood, but genuinely felt part of the rituals as we wished to take full advantage of this experience. Our visit was perfectly timed so that everything was on display to view. It is great to see such a majestic site with the help of a passionate local. Be sure to look him up! There are some security checks at the gate before you enter. Facilities to leave your shoes outside the temple. Make sure to dress modestly. Photography is permitted within the temple.

review_text: There is quite a lot to see in the temple (the temple itself, surrounding areas, buddhist museum) although it is 1,200 entrance fee for foreigners. We planned to go for the evening puja but heard it would be very busy so went in the afternoon. This was probably the busiest place we went in Kandy. The shrine is pretty from the outside but you can't actually see the tooth casket. We also felt a little uncomfortable that we were allowed right up to where local people were worshipping and chanting. Taking pictures of them/ the temple felt a bit rude. Overall this is interesting and an important religious and cultural site in Sri Lanka but not the best or most impressive thing we saw.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple of the Tooth is a very large temple in Kandy. It is significant to world Buddhism as housing part of the funeral pyre of Buddha and has had a turbulent history. We went in the evening after dark, which was a good idea actually as there aren't many tourists and you get to see it as a working place of worship. It is all illuminated, which is nice, and they also don't charge you vast amounts to put your shoes away. There's lots to look at, but we only had a short amount of time so didn't get a guide. It really is very impressive even if you don't know the significance of everything you are looking at.

review_text: We visited during Sinhalese New Year and the location was super packed. Probability of becoming the victim of stampede was very high. Foreign Tourists should avoid these locations during religious Holidays. But the the Temple itself was beautiful. Plenty of ancient artifacts  that are well preserved. I bet it is very tranquil on a off day.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is most valuable place in the world. this place not only for Buddhist but also all the humans can go there and get spiritual freedom and feelings from it. When you go there you must wear proper cloth. don't wear shorts, short skirts etc... better if you can wear white cloths. Bring some flowers if you wish. spend some time with peace full environment. hear some traditional drum music at a particular times. visit museums (there are 2-3 museums).

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I went at 6AM in the morning, together with all the local people. It is a very spiritual place and I felt special to be there. Worth the visit, bring a lotus flower as on offering to Buddha. (You can buy them outside of the temple)

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The story goes that a young princess smuggles the tooth belonging to the great Buddha from India to the safe keeping of her palace in Sri Lanka. This temple in the palace grounds is devoted to the worship of that tooth. We were lucky enough to be there on a special Buddhist holiday where the pilgrims flocked here from all over the country to pay homage to 'the tooth' of their founder. It was an amazing spectacle - whole families dressed in white carrying offerings of lotus flowers to lay before the tabernacle which holds the tooth. Huge crowds filing patiently past the sacred sight in silence and utmost reverence, then spending time in the grounds to meditate or just 'be'. We were moved by such unquestioning faith.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We arrived mid day on a religious holiday which was silly, however it was our only chance given our schedule.  We took our shoes off (charges a fee for safekeeping - westerners only, everyone else left there's by the entrance) and where offered a tour by soooo many guides it was frustrating and very 'in your face'.  Basically it was so busy we went with the flow and were basically pushed through the temple having little say in what we wanted to spend time looking at.  Im still not sure at this point in time where the actual tooth was situated.  People were pushing me in the back trying to offer flowers and it was a very un-Buddhist experience.  Since ancient times, the relic has played an important role in local politics because it is believed that whoever holds the relic holds the governance of the country....I wish we had gone in the evening...we would have had a far better appreciation of the temple and a far more zen experience.  The wonderful glimpses of rituals being performed was humbling.  Well worth a visit but choose your timings.

review_text: drop by 5-7pm. you get to see the stuffed elephant, the golden relic and and the hoards of people coming in to devote their faith to buddha. theyll ask you to wear a white shirt, take off your shoes before entering and avoid taking photos inside the temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: True enough you have to believe that the most sacred tooth relic is enshrined there. Well, everything in this world is not only for your eyes to see. But visit when the temple does the daily offering to the in honor of the relic. You might be able to see at least the golden caskets covered with magnificent jewelry which contains the tooth relic. Dont rush when you visit the temple of the tooth relic. Wait to see how the people coming from all four corners of Sri lanka worship. Hear the drummers paying respects. Visit the new museum to gather more information. See the Majestic elephant Raja's preserved and mounted body  who carried the golden casket in the Kandy pageant many years ago.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: No visit of Kandy without this one... And the serene and respectful Buddhist atmosphere that surrounds this area strucks you right away. It calms you down, it makes you walk slower, it relaxes... It has impact, I enjoyed the visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: After seeing the other sites that form Golden Triangle, this was the least impressive. Legend has it, the Buddha's tooth is held in the temple. Unfortunately visitors don't get to see it. You just take their word for it. As a non-buddhist, it was a little underwhelming, but one of those things you just have to do I suppose. Average experience for me.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Temple of tooth relic is the most sacred place for buddhists. worth to visit the "thevawa" which is held at 6.00PM everyday and around 10.00AM in the morning. Please wear decent white clothes when visiting. Don't forget to visit the other historical buildings which belongs to the "Dalada maligawa".

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is the most important place of the city of Kandy. used to be the palace of the sri lankan kings. some of the buildings are older than 700 years. Tooth relic of Lord Buddha was brought here by the late kings and now it is commonly reffered to as the "Maligawa" which means palace. Please note that you muct wear decent white cloths if you're planning to go there. many buddhists visit this place everyday so it is a bit crowdy. Please don't forget to visit the museums to see the history of temple and palace. It shows the thousands of years old culture and the history of sinhalese.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The best way to get there is by tuktuk as there is a complicated one way system; we found this form of transport to be very reliable and cheap.  Be warned, you will not be allowed to enter if you are wearing shorts or a short skirt and there are vendors looking out for people dressed like this and will try to sell you something to cover yourself.  Also avoid touts who will try to act as your guide and at the end ask for a ridiculous sum of money. It is well worth going round the old temple outside. If you want a very nice authentic curry meal at a very reasonable price there is an hotel opposite the temple entrance; very friendly local people who use it so it is good food.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: One of the big attractions in Kandy, we really enjoyed visiting the palace and temple of the tooth. the temple itself was stunning but we took care not to pose for photos in front the temple itself as it is considered offensive to turn your back to the temple. After the temple itself we went around the accompanying museum which was loaded with the history of the relic dating back 2.5 thousand years and with tributes from around the world that people send to the temple.  We also paid a guard a couple of hundred rupees to let us go out onto a balcony at the back of the museum with views across the lake, and he also opened a window which allowed us to look down on the real gold roof over the temple which was donated by Thailand which was well worthwhile seeing.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I would recommend a visit here as it is an interesting cultural point. We went in the early evening, and found it extremely busy and quite manic, especially where you queue to walk past the window with the tooth behind it. I found other temples more interesting, as in here you are not allowed to visit all of it aside from 3 areas. Other temples we visited were much more interesting and less touristy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Great place to visit specially if you a Buddhist. There is a fee for tourists, but I hate that. But you will receive a valuable information kit with it. If you go after 7 pm you might be lucky enough to go without a ticket since most of the days ticket counters close by that time. This is highly religious site. Make sure that you dress with long trouser or frock / skirt. You will not allow to go in if it is above knee high. Avoid special dates like Full moon days, Year end, Sinhala new year in April.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: An amazing temple but so very crowded at the evening ceremony, to the point of possibly being dangerous. Men and women need shorts to the knees at least and shoulders covered. We saw many people declined entry due to improper clothing. As others have mentioned, shoes need to be stored and tip when retrieved. When you come out there is a room with the record of events regarding the tooth in picture form and worth following. A one of a kind experience.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I've never been so inspired by any temple!  It's not only the building that's magnificent, but the serenity and magnificence of the religion makes the experience even more memorable.  We had an amazing guide who not only took us round and explained everything, but impressed upon us the fundamentals of Buddhism.  Don't visit Kandy without going here!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Ticket: 1000Rs pp. Make sure you cover your legs below the knee and shoulder otherwise you ll have to buy an ugly shawl from the street sellers who are conveniently located just outside the temple entrance! quite few things to see at the museums and temple itself. take the free audio guide as it is useful.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple was pretty but not as awesome as I had hoped. A guide tried to adopt us and we had to be pretty firm in explaining that we did not want his services. An entrance fee is required (500 RS if I remember correctly) and a tip is very clearly expected when you pick up your shoes.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I didn't have really high expectations of this site based on reviews.  We even contemplated skipping it, but ended up having the time so we went.  I am glad we did.  It was a nice experience.  You do have to store your shoes before you go in and they definitely expect a tip to return them.  In addition you have to be covered below the knees - my husband had shorts on and I had a top of the knee skirt and we had to rent a sarong outside the gate for 600 rupees.  Don't go expecting to see a tooth - just go to see the temple.  I did feel awkward sightseeing in front of people praying, but got over it.  Our Sri Lankan driver went in with us and you could really tell how proud they are of this temple and it's history.  In the museum part he found someone who spoke english and provided us some information on the artifacts.  It was only about 20 mins and was informative - he wasn't obvious about expecting a tip, but we knew what was up so gave him a few hundred.  I am not sure if that was sufficient, but everyone in Sri Lanka seems happy with something.  (just plan to tip everyone that does anything for you - but not much 10% or just a token).  They do provide you a mini dvd with your ticket, which isn't bad at all.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Way back in 1963 (I think) the Queen visited the temple and our guide showed her around. He proudly showed us his photographs with The Queen. As you can imagine he was pretty old but still fit as a fiddle. He brought the temple to life explaining everything in very good English. The tooth was not on display as this only happens about every 5 years but the casket it is in is paraded twice a day. A very enjoyable tour made all the more interesting by our guide (who cost a fiver). Beware of chancers outside the temple who will try to attach themselves to you and be your guide. Wait till you get in where our official guide was waiting. Also buy a small bunch of flowers on the way in to present to Buddha they only cost a few pence. Stand on the moonstone.

review_text: We went for the 9.30am Puja. Only Rs 500 entrance fee. The temple itself is interesting and well worth a walk around. There are lots of people at the ceremony but in some ways that's what makes it special. The drumming is loud and really adds to the atmosphere. Walking past the room with the tooth casket makes you feel a real part of the event, although there's nothing much to see. Overall, we found it a really interesting experience and a "must-do" in Kandy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A blast of Buddhism and their culture... Wow... Had a amazing time spending over 2 hours inside.... Must see place and DO NOT MISS AT ANY COST.... Its all about Gautham Buddha and his preachings. They have a Tooth of Buddha and worship that as god. Interiors are quite impressive and antique. SLR 500 per Head (SAARC Country citizens) and it is totally worth it.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I is possible to be overwhelmed by the number of temples you can see in Sri Lanka, but if you have a list, this should be close to the top. We went on a special festival day; so the placement was packed, but actually this is how it is supposed to be seen, a queuing mass of humanity, all with offerings to give. No crowd control issues at all, small children and the very elderly all included. The architecture of the temple and the Kings palace and audience areas were a special experience in themselves. Definitely worth a visit.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Our guide took us to the Temple of the Tooth in the evening; this a perfect time to go. The temple is beautifully lit up and this gives the temple lots of atmosphere. With thanks to o ur guide, we managed to get a glimpse of the relic of the tooth of Buddha.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Nice location, serene atmosphere with a lot of locals praying, this is a must visit @ Kandy. The interiors are well maintained, the sanctum itself is not always open (when the tooth is displayed), but as part of understanding the local culture, spending time here makes sense.The museum inside is not so great, but if one is interested in artifacts, history etc, it's good.The Blue lotus is the national flower of SL, it's offered to the Buddha, so there's a crowd of flower sellers as you approach the temple, we also saw a group of monks arriving in a BMW! The adjoining lake is also a good place to spend some quiet moments.Lot of fish, quacking ducks add to the ambiance. Fees for members of SAARC countries is much lesser than Europeans & you need to take off footwear before entering the temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the temple for their evening "pooja" celebration. I just loved the beautiful temple nd the ceremonies. The drumming, the crowds, the flowers, the architecture of the building...all worth a visit and your time. It is lovely in the evening. Do not miss the buddha on the hill, all lighted. Surreal and unforgettable!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: You enter the site and start to queue up for the view of the Tooth Relic and you climb stairs and you are getting squeezed by hundreds of people. You buy offerings (flowers, rice, meat or anything else) and then there you are. 6 seconds in front of this tiny, narrow room where the relic is kept (and almost invisible) and everyone around you smiles and pray and is happy. A real experience!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A very pretty temple which changed with the time of day. I particularly enjoyed wandering round the lake on an evening, enjoying the sounds of the temple which mixed with the raucous sounds of the roosting egrets and the fruit bats circling overhead. A visit during the day is a great way to relax in Kandy.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Kandy is famous for the Buddha Tooth Relic Temple situated in the heart of the city adjacent to the Kandy lake. The legend has it that a piece of Buddha’s tooth was brought and kept here that is considered very holy by all Buddhists in Sri Lanka. There are regular ceremonies, rituals and offerings made at the temple as it is considered very sacred. The temple is very big with wonderful artfully built structures. There is library of ancient scriptures well preserved in the temple premises. This is a must see place for those who visit Kandy and gives peace of mind and solace.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We had heard about the tooth relic, having it visit our SE Asian city a few years ago.  Not being Buddhists, we didn't quite know all about it but knew it attracted a huge and devoted crowd.  It was a sight to see, from the building inside and out, and then getting to see a glypse of the gold covered relic.  You are one of a huge mass of crowd, but again its an experience seeing how devoted people are, hearing the music, the awe when the relic is exposed.  I quite enjoyed the actual building housing the relic and the whole experience in the evening.  One note, not only do you have to wear sleeves and longish pants/skirts, you do have to take off your shoes (as with every other Buddhist pagoda/stuppa/etc).

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The experience of the Tooth Temple was somewhat claustrophobic as there were massive crowds queuing to see the relic and much banging of drums to add to the confusion.  However the museum area beyond contained much of interest - well worth seeing if you manage to get through the crowds!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: An amazing place that was hot and noisy, but well worth the visit. We had an excellent guide and were able to get a good sense of the culture and history of the place. We arrived as the drums were playing and could visit the inner temples.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Kandy Tooth temple treated as the most valuable place for Sri Lankan Buddhists pilgrims.  Very prestige place, you better wear long dresses with sleeves or else you are not authorize to enter the premises. but you can get scarfs at front gate at a small cost to enter the temple.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: What every religion you are, this is a place in Kandy that you must visit. Architectural marvel, a beautiful structure. Buddhist consider the place to be of the highest value, having lord Buddha's tooth relic. Entrance fee of 1000 Rs. ( about $ 10) is charged. I do not think its too much as we spend a lot more on tickets at much less valuable stuff. You are getting a guided recording and a DVD as I can remember. Great place to be, a must visit at least once in a life time.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited the Temple of the Tooth, not knowing what to expect entirely. However, we were charged to get in 1000 Rupees each, which was very high (although you do get an accompanying mini - DVD to watch at home), and the temple was very very crowded, there was a lot of people in one space queuing to see the Buddah and we wern't very excited by what we saw. We had visited a more traditional temple which is off the tourist trail more, where we offered fruit, which was a much more authentic experience, if still a bit crowded! I wouldn't re-visit the Temple of the Tooth and I felt a it was a bit intrusive on the Sri Lankan people who are there to genuinely worship, whilst we tourists stand around and take pictures.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We arrived here around 6pm, the area was busy and very much alive, and the whole atmosphere was electric.  We explored the area before entering; being meet with the sounds of drums, the heat of the other tourists, pilgrims and Buddhists monks. We lined up to see the Buddha’s tooth which is a light of its own; you are hustled along and hopefully get a glimpse of it the doors soon close ending the showing. There are pilgrims waiting to go inside and wait patiently then the Buddhist monks wait as well after the public viewing. In one of the halls the story of the Sacred Tooth is shown and explained. This is a most sacred place for the Buddhists so remember to respect their beliefs wear long trousers, shoulders covered, no hats and no photo’s with your back to the Buddha’s. I found this Temple very interesting so much to see with so much history, the library is also amazing.  Not to be missed.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We have been to many Buddhist temples in Thailand but this is one of the most important temples for Buddhists and to see the extravagant container with the tooth and the story was fascinating. To see the reverence devotes pay to the tooth relic is special.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This temple is huge and very beautiful. It was really crowded but there was a lot to see. We got to see the area (not inside though) where the Buddha's tooth is right before they shut the doors for prayer. The story of how the tooth got there was really interesting. We also got to see the high priest run up the stairs. It really was a neat experience.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: To choose just one of the many exploits during our honeymoon then our visit to the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy has to be the one in first place. We visited the temple at night, during the last of the offerings... this made the approach to the temple very special indeed. We were also VERY fortunate in being present when the temple was opened for view, and we could see the casing that holds the tooth of Buddha. The drums (played throughout in the lower chamber) got louder and faster as the anticipation of the opening of the inner temple approached. We were accepted as being a part of the proceedings, with the place packed with local pilgrims and their lotus flowers. If you want to experience Sri Lankan culture at its best, visit the Temple of the Tooth. You won't be disappointed.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: I visit Sri Lanka on end of January 2013, weather in Colombo was warm & weather in Kandy is so windy that it just perfect for travel, approximately 19°C . I and my friends only have 5 days to stay in Sri Lanka so we can only focus on places nearby Kandy. If you want to travel to north Sri Lanka also please prepare to stay more than a week, because in 5 days our schedule was extremely packed. All my friends are backpackers, so we ACTUALLY planned to travel by our own, but when we reach train station tourist info counter, we were told that we aren't possible up to north part because we are lacking of time. The Sri Lankan officer 'insisted' us to purchase their tour package (he himself owned a travel company & guest house) & refused to advise further on our planned schedule. He first recommend us his own tour package with the price of USD430(train to Kandy because his guest house in Kandy, bed, breakfast and transport to all destinations within 5days), but all we have in our pocket was approximately  USD480, since its already 3.30pm we were actually considering even its so freaking expensive! Because me might just lost our first day just like that... He refused to reduce the price until we walked out the tourist info counter, he reduced USD430 to USD150. So now the deal is on! haha From Airport - Colombo Town Take tuk-tuk 1. Around 1hr 15mins 2. Around 1000 Sri Lanka Rupee (SLR) per person (personally think worth it, because in my     country 1hr journey by Taxi could up to Malaysian Ringgit (MYR) 150++ or more. 3. MUST bring a mask, air pollution was bad especially in Colombo town. Colombo train station - Kandy Take train 1. Around 3hrs 40mins 2. Fare included in USD150. 3. The view along the journey was so beautiful with the sunset! So its extremely recommended to take train in evening, our train start 3.50pm. Bear in mind nice view only start after an hour after train start, so you can take a nap first. Haha.. I'm love to take photos so I was waited for it LOL. 4. Bring your own insect repellent since the journey is hilly and many trees. 5. Prepare long sleeve jacket since at night it can be quite cold, and your up the hill 6. Do not put your head out the window to take photo as the train could enter the tunnel in speed. Local people told us that there was a number of accidents before. When we reach Kandy it was almost 7.50pm. We wait for our driver to pick us up to guest house. Blue Heaven Guest House 1. Staffs all very friendly (they even woke up at 4am to prepare breakfast for us when we need to rush for our planned schedule) 2. Hot & cols shower (I guess in 14°C night you would need a hot shower :)) 3. WIFI!!! haha 4. Mosquito nets 5. Do bring some of your own snacks as the breakfast is going to be the same everyday. (two eggs, toast, tea, coffee & fruits). To me the portion was large, I only drink hot chocolate & have a bun for my breakfast normally. But do try their papaya, its so sweeeeet!!! 6. We had dinner in the guest house cafeteria, food served was OK, but the price was slightly more expensive than town. So do go to town to try GOOD food and pay a cheaper price. Try to avoid restaurant with a lot of tourists, price was high & with tax (normal restaurant that locals goes doesn't apply tax), service was extremely bad!!! We asked them to take order & wave our hands in front of them, they doesn't even look at you!! We waited for 15mins and no one cares, at last we walked out the restaurant. So this is my first day itinerary in Kandy, please browse or read my second review in Kandy when I'm done with it k? Thanks for reading everyone :) Hope it helps~

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This was one of the best places that we visited on our holiday in Sri Lanka. We had an excellent guide who seemed to know exactly where we should be and when. We timed it to coincide with the 0900 ceremony and were able to file past and see the casket and witness the monks going in to the ceremony. It was a fascinating visit and we feel privileged to have had the chance to go there. Don't miss this!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This was my second visit after 8 years, and it was just as memorable. About 12-15$, (men - remember to wear pants & ladies with covered arms). Many arrive around 9-930 am for the morning ritual prayers. You can opt for a guide, or not, for a couple of $. You will line up to purchase your ticket and remove your shoes - they are tagged and kept for you like a bowling alley (much different than the mayhem 8 yrs ago with shoes strewn about everywhere!). This is an active temple and the Sri Lankans are incredibly polite to the touts of rude tourists pushing their way through and snapping pictures. If you step back and take time to appreciate the incredible structures, architecture, art, and history - it's a different experience. You can wander around the large "complex" - visit various pagodas, sit under large trees, listen to prayer. There is a room which depicts the story of the "tooth" in english that you can follow along. There is an elephant there, chained of course, which is gutting to see for some, including myself - please be respectful. It's a beautiful experience here if you allow yourself to see more than getting that great picture!

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Tooth temple is the most revered place for Buddhists around the world. It is also the foremost attraction for tourists visiting Sri Lanka. In ancient times, it was believed that the person having the tooth relic would control the kingdom of Sri Lanka. According to the legends, the left canine of Lord Buddha was retrieved by one of his devotee in India and subsequently it was transported to Sri Lanka, to save it from invaders and enemy. Kandy being the last capital of the ancient Lankan Kingdon the tooth relic is preserved there. The temple is situated inside the Royal Palace dating back to 6 century BC and to the one side of the temple is the Kandy lake. The way to the temple passes through a large well kept garden with flower beds and big trees. To visit the temple, devotees need to be decently dressed and have to remove their shoes outside the temple. We visited the place on Sunday and there was long queue at the entry and as well inside the temple. Sunday, being holiday, locals visit the temple being revered place. The temple is constructed in unique pagoda style, with the tooth preserved inside a gold chamber shaped like stupa. There is a museum at the back of the temple, which depicts the  legend behind the tooth relic and its journey from India to Sri Lanka. There is also another museum inside the complex, devoted to 'Raja' - the elephant, who was for decades carrying the tooth relic on its back for the annual procession in Kandy. The place is well kept and must visit to seek blessings of the revered Lord Buddha.

review_text: This was one of the first things I had to see when coming to Kandy. A guy attached himself to us immediately upon entering.  Normally I would have discouraged him from staying with us, but he was so pleasant, I had no problems with him showing us around.  Oddly in the end he never asked for money and when I gave him a few bucks it seemed awkward.  I just hope I did not offend some custom I was not aware of. You do have to remove your shoes and there is a place where they will store them for a very small tip (less than a dollar).  The walkway after removing your shoes was either very wet or very hot.  I wore socks and was happy as my feet where not burning on the pavement, but I had to hopscotch around the many puddles to avoid soggy feet.  Just keep that in mind. I did not actually see the tooth, but it was quite nice inside and cool from the hot sun.  There were several people praying and I could not resist taking photos of the flowers and other offerings.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: A trip to Kandy is not complete without visiting this, one of the most important Buddhist temples. We visited during the evening drumming ceremony, and it was as busy as we'd expected - I think the tourists must have outnumbered the locals by 3-1. The exterior and garden spaces are worth a wander round, and the areas where lots of candles and incense being burnt are lovely. You are given a ticket pack on entry which contains a DVD of the complex - nice souvenir to keep. The drumming and fanfare ceremony takes place downstairs and there's a reasonable amount of room to be able to watch, although most of the ceremony takes place behind closed doors. Upstairs is where worshippers pay homage to the relic and queue with offerings. This part is very crowded and unfortunately brings out the worse in some tourists and their guides in trying to push their way through. It would be good if everyone had a little respect for those who are there to pay their respects. As with any other temple you need to leave your footwear at the entrance - there is a booth where you pay a small fee to store them but you'll need to hold your nose if you're at all delicate (smells like a very unclean changing room). Definitely worth a visit despite the hoards of other tourists.

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We knew this was a "must see" in Sri Lanka, but I have to confess the pre-publicity we had was not good! My mother, when living in Ceylon as a teenager in the 1920's, was taken to visit by her father, and many years later I remember her still moaning of how dull it was, although she adored Sri Lanka.  A number of friends who had recently hoidayed there, echoed her view. However, our wonderful driver/guide (who knew everyone and everything) suggested we visit in good time for the 0930 Puja. It is not cheap for foreign tourists, but then none of the major sites in Sri Lanka are.  He found a parking place (which seemed to be at a premium) and ushered us through.  I think you really have to approach it in the spirit of it being someone else's very important religious site, rather than a tourist event.  We were impressed by the lack of hideous, tacky religious artefacts that are so common outside the great cathedrals & shrines of Europe. Obviously proper dress and sensitivity to the devotees is a given, and we found the sound of the tabla drums outside the main door, the overpowering scent of the various flowers & incense on sale for puja, and the many bees around the flowers, to be very evocative.   People were organising their puja by family groups, (usually a grandmother in charge) and lots of very young new babies were being brought - apparently it is the first outing they have after their birth.  We didn't find the queues at that time too bad, and although you do whip past the open doors showing the actual reliquary pretty quickly, our guide took a picture for us from behind the little enclosure which has a good view of the altar/reliquary,  which wealthy devotees can pay to sit in.  The devotees were quiet, respectful and there was remarkably little pushing and jostling. We visited the various other rooms of shrines, and saw the golden roof (rebuilt after the terrorist attack of 1998).  As museum freaks,  we visited the upper floors, where there is a good museum, with a number of interesting exhibits regarding the British take-over of Ceylon.  We went out on the upper balconies and were able to se the wonderful carved overhanging roof and saw where all the bees came from - huge honeycombs attached to the roofs with buzzing bees everywhere - they are never removed.  You could see right out over the lake, and view the bathing pavilion and remains of the royal palace.  We rather enjoyed the shrine to Raja the elephant - him being a national treasure and all, and the various children were certainly enjoying it. We found the whole experience quite fascinating. Each to their own however, and if you are expecting to see the actual tooth, then you will be disappointed (We saw a replica in the museum, and if Buddha had a tooth like that, then he had some serious dental problems!  There are of course heretics who say a buffalo's tooth was substituted many years ago.)

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: If you have done any research you will know that the Temple of the Tooth (Sri Dalada Maligawa) is the most important temple in Sri Lanka, revered and visited by buddhists from all around the world.  It houses the Sacred Tooth relic of Gauthama, the Lord Buddha. You will NOT see the Tooth itself.  This is kept inside seven gold/silver caskets, placed one inside another, and secured upstairs behind closed doors.  Our travel agent and guide both recommended that we visit during the one of the thrice daily Pujas when the doors are opened for 15 minutes allowing visitors a glimpse of the casket. We opted to go for the evening Puja at 18.30 which is probably the busiest time (evidenced by our difficulty finding a parking space). Admission is slightly higher than other attrcations but this includes an informative mini DVD.  You will get more from your visit if you have a guide. Local guides or an audio guide are available for a small fee (you need to enter through main front gate for this).  As is the case elsewhere in Sri Lanka, there are separate queues and prices for foreigners and locals.  As for all temples, you must dress respectfully (legs and shoulders covered; hats and shoes removed but you can wear socks).  Also, you must not stand with your back to, or have photos taken alongside, Buddha statues or frescoes). You have to pay a small fee (about 25p) for shoe storage. Security here and at the Bo Tree is tighter than at other attractions in Sri Lanka (a result of the bombings in 1998) and there separate lines for men and women. Downstairs in the main temple there is a covered hall with a striking and colourful entrance way  to the shrine.  During the Puja, drummers stand either side of the door.  To see the Tooth casket you have to queue to go upstairs.  We were constantly being hurried along and whilst we appreciate this was done to ensure that everyone had an opportunity to see the casket, this did spoil the expereince. We saw the casket for a fleeting second; no time to take a photo (you could go instead to the praying area directly opposite the shrine and take a photo from there when the door is open but this is quite intrusive to local devotees). On the way back downstairs there is set of steps up to another shrine room/museum with some early scrolls written on leaf and other artefacts.  A visit to the main temple will take no more than 1 hour (up to two during the Puja because of the queues) but I would recommend allowing extra time to enjoy the tranquil setting and views around the wider complex and man-made lake. The golden roof is striking especially at sunset.  Within 5-10 minutes walking distance there you can see the Audience Hall (you can’t go inside but worth a photo) and three devales (the Vishnu Devale has some colourful shrines and you get a superb view of the main temple from the top of steps at the entrance). With hindsight we would not have visited the main temple to coincide with a Puja.  Yes, the drumming is atmospheric but too much queuing and chaos for us for the brief glimpse we got of the relic casket. An unexpected thunderstorm meant that the audience hall was even more crowded than usual as people were staying inside to shelter from the rain.  We spent most of our visit walking through puddles in bare feet and wet clothes which we then had to wear during the 1 hour transfer back to our hotel. (Tip: even if the weather seems fine, take an umbrella if not a light raincoat!) If you do want to go for the Puja, then make sure you go early to get in the queue up the stairs and remember to allow time for parking, admission, removal of shoes, security etc.

review_text: We drove 2 hours out of our way to see this. So my disappointment is elevated by additional time spent in the car. Be respectful, decently dressed and also do not take pictures with your back turned to the statues. We went during a rain storm and while we got to see a lot of the sights it was quite crowded and the museum had closed, we were also not able to see the stuffed elephant. Perhaps it was the rain but the whole temple seemed a little disorganised and a little stressful to be honest with worshippers and tourists scattered helter skelter, a tonne of pictures, long lines and loud drumming. location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Sri Dalada Malikgawa or The Temple of Tooth relic is situated in Kandy Sri Lanka and is a UNESCO world heritage site. This Temple has a range of buildings which houses the relic of the tooth of Buddha.Temple of the Tooth building complex. this building complex and surrounding consists of following buildings and places. Mahawahalkada (The main entrance) Moat Pattirippuwa (Octagon) Handun kunama Golden canopy New Palace Royal Palace of Kandy National Museum of Kandy Old courts building Kandy Lake Biso ulpen ge (Queens bath) Diyathilaka mandapaya Udawatta Kele Sanctuary This is a most sacred place for world wide Buddhists and you will have to remove your shoes before entering the temple. If u a man you should wear a sarong or long trouser and women should wear a adequately covered cloth if not they( at the gate) will provide u a cloth to cover your body. People are expected to behave very very decently once you enter the temple. The sacred tooth relic does not show every day, it shows only in special ceremony only and most of the time once a year. during that period people from Sri Lanka and all over the world line up for hours to worship this most sacred tooth relic. Esala Perahera (the festival of the tooth) is the grand festival of Esala held in Sri Lanka. It is very grand with elegant costumes. Happening in July or August in Kandy, it has become a unique symbol of Sri Lanka. It is a Buddhist festival consisting of dances and nicely decorated elephants. There are fire-dances, whip-dances, Kandian dances and various other cultural dances. The elephants are usually adorned with lavish garments. The festival ends with the traditional 'diya-kepeema'. So this is very important for Buddhists and people from other religions who do not have a proper understanding about this place may find it is another temple in the country but please keep in mind its not so.it should be respected for the fullest

location_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We visited this temple this morning fully aware of its significance to Buddhists. We chose to go first thing in the morning because we had been told that there were fewer people at that time. The crowds were large and there was very little lack of organisation in ensuring all those in attendance were funneled through past the Dagoba holding the sacred relic. It was chaos and a lot of pushing and shoving occurred as tourists and pilgrims struggled to get a glimpse of it. In the end we were glad to escape the melee for the relative peace outside. Those that did manage to see the relic were hustled by in a few seconds. For 1,000 rupee each, it was both  waste of money and time. I also object to having to pay a shoe minder when the locals were free. Just another grab for the tourist $. The headsets available with the ticket purchase worked intermittently and as the noise in the temple was so great with drums and horns sounding continuously, it was not possible to hear the audio. Altogether an unpleasant experience and very disappointing.
